The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

We begin with the taut string met in chapter 13. There the string was at rest, and it had a wave equation, modes and frequencies. Now the string does not only move sideways, it also runs along its own length through two fixed eyelets, small rings that it slides through. What running means is shown by a piece of material: after a time \(\tau\) the same piece is farther along by \(v\tau\), while the eyelets are where they were. The chapter shows what changes because of this, and it uses what we know from chapters 8 and 10, where we treated systems with finitely many degrees of freedom.

The words of the title mean something simple. A belt (jermen) is a band that runs over wheels and carries motion from one to another. Axially (aksialno) means along the axis, that is along the band through which the material runs, as the arrows \(v\) show, and not across the band. A moving continuum (gibajoči se zvezni sistem) is a body that we describe not by a few points but by all its points at once, and that moves as a whole: all points run along the band with the same speed \(v\). The title therefore says: we treat a belt as a continuous body through which material flows without end.

Why does this matter? A belt in a machine, a band saw between two wheels and a cable car between two towers are all such systems. For a steel strip of length 1 m, running at 40 m/s lowers the first frequency of vibration from 56.61 Hz to 49.55 Hz: in figure 26.22 these are the orange dots at \(v = 0\) and \(v = 40\) m/s on the curve \(f_1\). At a high enough speed the frequencies fall to zero, all three curves at the same speed \(c\), and the string loses stability, which a string at rest does not predict. Why exactly there is told in section 26.4: material that runs along a curved path needs a force toward the centre of curvature, and at the speed \(c\) the tension of the string is just enough for that, with nothing left to pull the string back straight.

The chapter promises three things. First, from the balance of a piece of string we derive the equation for the running string and show that the waves in the two directions travel at different speeds. Next we find the modes of vibration, the speed at which the frequencies fall to zero, and a quantity that is conserved while the string runs. Last, we extend the equation to a belt with bending stiffness, turn it into finite elements and apply it to a drive with two pulleys, saying what our model leaves out.

26.1 The moving string (gibajoča struna)

In figure 26.2 the belt runs tight over two wheels, and on its upper part, the span, the transverse oscillation is drawn dashed. At the speed \(v\) the matter flows along the belt, and this is what separates this system from a string at rest.

A magnetic tape runs past a head, a band saw runs over two wheels, a cable car pulls its cable over two pylons, a fluid flows through a pipe, a chain and a belt run over pulleys. What they share is that matter flows along its own length and at the same time can oscillate sideways (WM1990, PDF p. 1, read). We call such a system an axially moving continuum (aksialno gibajoč se kontinuum), where a continuum is a continuous system from chapter 13. The chapter treats belts, so we take the simplest part of a belt, the span (razpon) between two pulleys, and write it as a string that runs. The question of this section is simple: does the wave equation of section 13.1 hold for such a span, or must it be changed, and how does it change?

From history

The methods for axially moving materials reach back into the nineteenth century: WM1990 (PDF p. 1) names Skutch, who in 1897 published a work in Annalen der Physik und Chemie on pages 190 to 195 (the year 1987 in the text on page 1 is a printing error, the reference lists of WM1990, PDF p. 6, and of CHEN2005, PDF p. 21, have 1897). The title of the work is German and in free translation reads the motion of a taut thread that is forced to run at constant speed through two fixed points and between them oscillates sideways with small amplitude (WM1990, PDF p. 6, CHEN2005, PDF p. 21). This is exactly the model of this section. According to CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2) Skutch was the first to study a moving string without excitation.

Let us return to the span between the pulleys. The story told what the model is: a taut thread that runs through two fixed points. Here we build it and derive the equation ourselves, on a steel band that we choose as the running example.

We draw the span in several steps in figure 26.3. First we take the axis \(x\) and on it two eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). An eyelet is a small ring through which the thread runs, as a thread runs through the eye of a needle, and the word means a small eye. The eyelets stand in space and the string runs through them. In this way we replace the pulleys: the span is clamped at a pulley, so the transverse displacement there is zero, and what happens to the belt on the pulley itself (wrapping, friction) the model does not ask about (idealization 6 below). We draw the string blackwhite: at rest it is a straight line along the axis \(x\), and during oscillation it is a curve \(w(x, t)\), where \(w\) is the transverse displacement of the point at \(x\) at time \(t\), as in section 13.1. The slope in the figure is strongly exaggerated so that the curve can be seen. Outside the eyelets the string runs on along the axis: the arrows \(v\) show that it enters on the left and leaves on the right, and all points of the string move along the axis \(x\) with speed \(v > 0\) in the direction of increasing \(x\). The number \(v\) in m/s we call the transport speed (hitrost transporta). In addition the string moves transversely in \(w\).

Now we can say what it is that moves. On the string we imagine a mark, like a coloured line on a thread: a material particle (točka snovi) is a piece of the string that we follow as it runs. Two dots at \(a\) and \(b\) at time \(t\) are two such particles, and the blue part of the string between them is a material piece (kos snovi): the same pieces of matter all the time, wherever they are. The lower row of the figure shows time \(t + \tau\). The material particles have moved by \(v\tau\) along the axis \(x\), since they run with speed \(v\), and the material piece now lies over the interval from \(a + v\tau\) to \(b + v\tau\). Meanwhile the shape of the string has changed too: the dashed grey curve is the string at time \(t\), the blackwhite one the string at time \(t + \tau\). The neighbouring parts pull the piece with force \(T\) along the tangent, each force starting at the point where it acts, as in section 13.1. The forces are drawn at both times.

The model has eight idealizations (idealizacije). We name each and give it a measure. The example is a steel band that we choose ourselves: thickness \(0{,}9\) mm, width \(50\) mm, with span length \(L = 1\) m and stress \(\sigma = 100\) MPa. Bands are found on band saws (WM1990, PDF p. 1), the dimensions, stress and speeds are our choice, we have no data on real belts (the project sources contain none). The cross-section is \(A = 4{,}5\cdot 10^{-5}\) m\(^2\), the density of steel \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\) and the elastic modulus \(E = 196\) GPa (BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100), so the mass per unit length is \(\mu = \rho A = 0{,}3510\) kg/m and the tension is \(T = \sigma A = 4500\) N. For each idealization we say why it holds here, when it does not hold and what it costs. Idealizations 2 to 4 speak about the force at the end of the piece, so we first draw this end from close up.

  1. The string is homogeneous: \(\mu\) is constant. Since all points of the string move along \(x\) with the same speed, the spacing between them along \(x\) does not change, so the mass per unit length stays \(\mu\) also in the running flow (WM1990, PDF p. 1: the axial speed is approximately \(V\)). This is shown by the blue piece, which is equally long along \(x\) at both times. It does not hold for a belt with a joint or with teeth, where the mass per length is larger at the joint: there \(\mu\) at a fixed place would change every time the joint runs past, and the equation would get coefficients that depend on time.
  2. The string has no bending stiffness, so the force in it is along the tangent: at the right end of the piece, the point \(b\), the neighbouring part pulls the piece with the force \(T\) along the string. For the band \(EI = E\,b h^3/12 = 0{,}595\) N m\(^2\) and the ratio \(EI/(T L^2) = 1{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\), which is an order-of-magnitude estimate and is small. It does not hold for a thick or short band, where this ratio is not small. We include bending stiffness later in this chapter, with the moving beam.
  3. The tension \(T = 4500\) N is constant along the span and in time. When the string moves it stretches and the tension changes. For our band, \(EA = 8{,}82\) MN, the strain at slope \(5\cdot 10^{-3}\) is at most \(1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) and the tension changes by \(EA\cdot 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5} = 110\) N, which is \(2{,}4\) % of \(T\), and the wave speed by \(1{,}2\) %. For the wire of section 13.1 the estimate at slope \(0{,}01\) was \(1{,}8\) %. The tension in a real belt depends also on the speed and on friction at the pulleys, about which the project sources have no data: \(T\) is here a given number (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, assumption 2).
  4. The slope is small, \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) (stricter than \(0{,}01\) for the wire, because the band is much stiffer under tension). The tangent then makes with the axis \(x\) an angle \(\theta\) of less than \(0{,}29^\circ\), which we drew large. So we may write the vertical part of the force \(T\sin\theta\) as \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), with a relative error of at most \(1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\), and the horizontal parts at the two ends of the piece differ by at most \(56\) mN (step 2 of the derivation below). It does not hold at large amplitudes: for the shape \(\varepsilon\sin(\pi x/L)\) the largest slope is \(\pi\varepsilon/L\), so at \(L = 1\) m the bound allows an amplitude up to \(\varepsilon = 1{,}6\) mm.
  5. The axial speed of every material particle is \(v\), constant and equal for all (WM1990, PDF p. 1), as the arrows \(v\) show, so the shift \(v\tau\) is the same for all particles. It holds because the band is one piece and hardly stretches (idealization 3), so the particles keep their spacing and run together. If a particle ran along the arc with the same speed, the component along \(x\) would be smaller by at most a relative \(1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) at slope \(0{,}005\), which we neglect.
  6. The eyelets are fixed in space, \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\). The connection of the span with the pulley (wrapping, friction, oscillation of the pulley) is neglected (CHEN2005, §2.4.2, PDF p. 4). It holds when the pulley is rigid and heavy compared with the span. It does not hold when the pulley itself oscillates or when the span talks through the pulley to another span of the same belt: then the end points are not points at rest and the span exchanges energy with its surroundings, which the model does not see. How large this influence is we cannot say here with a number, because the project sources have no data on pulleys.
  7. Weight is neglected: the weight of the span \(\mu g L = 3{,}4\) N is \(7{,}6\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the tension force. It does not hold for a long and slack span, where the weight is not small compared with the tension and the span sags already at rest.
  8. The transport speed \(v\) is constant in time, because a drive in steady running holds its speed. It does not hold during start-up and braking. Then the acceleration of a material particle, which we derive below, would get one more term \(\dot v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (our computation with the same chain rule). For a start-up from \(0\) to \(40\) m/s in \(4\) s, \(\dot v = 10\) m/s\(^2\), and at slope \(0{,}005\) this term is \(0{,}05\) m/s\(^2\), while the local acceleration of the test motion below reaches \(97\) m/s\(^2\). We require only \(v > 0\). The ratio between \(v\) and the wave speed \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4) we shall restrict only where it is needed.

For the example \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu} = \sqrt{\sigma/\rho} = 113{,}23\) m/s. The ratio \(v/c\) at \(v = 40\) m/s is \(0{,}353\). We write this ratio simply as \(v/c\), with no new letter. For a reader of the sources: WM1990 writes \(\nu\) for \(v/c\), \(P\) for \(T\) and \(\rho\) for \(\mu\), and CHEN2005 writes \(c\) for the transport speed. With us \(v\) is the transport speed (not the deflection as in chapter 5, the deflection here is \(w\)), \(c\) the wave speed and \(T\) the tension force (not the kinetic energy of chapter 9).

Before we ask about the acceleration, let us ask about the velocity: does a material particle rise just as fast as the string under it? No, and why not we see from close up.

We draw the axes \(x\) and \(w\). From close up a short piece of the string is almost straight, so at time \(t\) we draw it as a straight blackwhite line, and on it the material particle. After a short time \(\tau\) the particle is higher for two reasons. The first: the string rises. We draw it orange, at time \(t + \tau\). At a fixed place it has risen by \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\tau\), since \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the rate of rise at a fixed place. The second: the particle does not stay in place, in the time \(\tau\) it runs \(v\tau\) forward. The string is inclined, and the triangle says what the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) means: one step forward, \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) up. Whoever goes \(v\tau\) forward therefore rises by \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\tau\), like a walker going uphill. There the string has meanwhile risen by another \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\tau\). The two vertical segments on the right together are the whole rise of the particle:

\[\text{rise in the time } \tau = w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\tau + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\tau , \qquad \text{rate of rise} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}} .\]

We may take a straight line because the time \(\tau\) is short: the curvature would move the particle only by a term with \(\tau^2\), which after division by \(\tau\) vanishes as \(\tau\) shrinks. In the velocity we therefore do not feel the curvature, but it returns in the acceleration.

What remains from section 13.1? There the acceleration of a point of the string was simply \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), because the point stayed at the same \(x\). A material particle of the moving string does not stay at the same \(x\). How large its acceleration is, is shown by figure 26.6, which we build in three panels. In all three the same string at the same time, bulging upward, and on it one material particle, the blackwhite dot at \(x_0\).

In panel (a) we ask: what would be the acceleration of a point that stayed at the same \(x\), as in section 13.1? The string moves in time \(\tau\) and the dashed curve is its position at time \(t + \tau\). The point at constant \(x\) would rise, its acceleration is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), called the local acceleration (krajevni pospešek), because it is the acceleration at a fixed place. The arrow \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is drawn upward for the case where the curve rises ever faster. That the curve rises says only that the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is positive, the acceleration points upward when this velocity grows. In panel (b) we take the point to run. The tangent to the string at it has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), and since the shape changes, the slope changes with rate \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), the tangent turns like a rod. The point runs along the tangent with speed \(v\), like a bead on a turning rod. A bead on a rod that turns with angular velocity \(\Omega\) and runs along it with speed \(v\) relative to the rod has, besides other terms, an acceleration \(2\Omega v\) perpendicular to the rod (Coriolis acceleration, Coriolisov pospešek), as school physics knows it. At small slope the angular velocity of the tangent is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), so the acceleration is \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), drawn upward, because the slope grows. In panel (c) the point runs along a curved curve. The circle that fits the curve best at this point has by definition 5.16 radius \(R = 1/|w_{\mathrm{xx}}|\), and whoever runs along a circle with speed \(v\) has acceleration \(v^2/R\) toward the centre of the circle (school physics, uniform circular motion). That is why this term is called the centripetal acceleration (centripetalni pospešek): Latin centrum means centre and petere to seek, so an acceleration that seeks the centre. At small slope the arrow toward the centre is almost vertical and equal to \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The curve bulges upward, \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} < 0\), so it points downward.

Where does the two in the term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) come from? The school formula \(2\Omega v\) only brings it along. We see the reason if we return to the rate of rise \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The acceleration is how fast this velocity changes, and each of its two terms, \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), changes for two reasons: because time runs and because the material particle arrives at another place. Per unit time:

\[\begin{aligned} w_{\mathrm{t}} &\ \text{changes by} \quad w_{\mathrm{tt}} \ (\text{time runs}) \quad + \quad v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}} \ (\text{the particle arrives elsewhere}) , \\ v\,w_{\mathrm{x}} &\ \text{changes by} \quad v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} \ (\text{the slope grows}) \quad + \quad v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} \ (\text{the particle arrives at another slope}) . \end{aligned}\]

The first term is the local acceleration of panel (a), the last the centripetal one of panel (c). The middle two are equally large, each is \(v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), and together they are the Coriolis term of panel (b). Since these are two different reasons, we draw each separately.

On the left we draw a piece of the tangent and on it the material particle. The tangent turns with rate \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). So its points do not rise equally fast: at the particle with rate \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), further right faster. In the time \(\tau\) the particle runs \(v\tau\) and arrives at a place that rises faster by \(w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,v\tau\). Per unit time this is the first half, \(v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}}\).

On the right we draw the same piece of the tangent with the material particle, which runs along it with speed \(v\). The slope is \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), so the particle climbs with rate \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), as in figure 26.5. After the time \(\tau\) the tangent is steeper, the slope is larger by \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\tau\), and the particle climbs faster by \(v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\tau\). Per unit time this is the second half, \(v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). The halves are equal because both describe the same turning of the tangent: that the right part of the tangent rises faster than the left is the same as the slope growing. In the computation this is the equality of the mixed derivatives, \(w_{\mathrm{tx}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}}\).

The above are explanations from the figures and school physics. The exact computation with the chain rule is given by the lemma that follows.

Lemma 26.1 Velocity and acceleration of a material particle of the moving string (hitrost in pospešek točke snovi gibajoče strune)

Let \(v > 0\) and let \(w\) be a function on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\) with continuous partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tx}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) (definition 1.26). Let \(s\) be a number and let the material particle that at time \(t\) is at \(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = s + vt\) lie in \((0, L)\) during an open interval of times. Then its transverse displacement is \(W(t) = w(s + vt, t)\), its transverse velocity is

\[\dot W = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}} \tag{26.1}\]

and its transverse acceleration is

\[\ddot W = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \tag{26.2}\]

both at the point \((s + vt, t)\). The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are in turn the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal acceleration.

Proof

We must show the first and second derivative of the displacement along the path of the material particle \((s + vt, t)\). We get each with the chain rule, the second by applying the same rule to the velocity.

  1. The material particle is at time \(t\) at \(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = s + vt\) by idealization 5, so \(x_{\mathrm{p}}' = v\). Its displacement is \(W(t) = w(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\), which is \(w\) along the path \(\Phi(t) = (x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\), whose derivative is \((v, 1)\).
  2. By the chain rule (lemma 8.30, point 1, where \(D\) is an interval) \(\dot W = w_{\mathrm{x}}\,v + w_{\mathrm{t}}\). This is equation (26.1).
  3. The function \(g = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) has continuous derivatives \(g_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{tx}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(\dot W(t) = g(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\). The same rule applied to \(g\) gives \(\ddot W = g_{\mathrm{x}}\,v + g_{\mathrm{t}} = v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\).
  4. The mixed derivatives are continuous at every point, so by the theorem on the interchange of mixed derivatives (theorem 8.31) \(w_{\mathrm{tx}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and from step 3 equation (26.2) follows. These are the left and the right half of the Coriolis term in figure 26.7, which are equal.

Source: WM1990, PDF pp. 1 and 2: the transverse velocity is \(U_{\mathrm{T}} + V U_{\mathrm{X}}\) (PDF p. 1), the terms of the acceleration are in turn the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal (PDF p. 2). CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (the same description). The proof by steps is not from the source.

The acceleration therefore has three terms, not one, as in panel (a) of figure 26.6. The computation has confirmed the explanations of panels (b) and (c): the second term is the Coriolis one, the third the centripetal one.

Let us check the lemma on numbers, which the material particle in figure 26.8 shows. Let \(v = 40\) m/s, which is \(v/c = 0{,}353\), and let

\[w_*(x, t) = \varepsilon\,\sin\frac{\pi x}{L}\,\cos(\omega t + k x) , \qquad \varepsilon = 1\ \text{mm} , \quad \omega = \frac{\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\Big) = 311{,}32\ \text{1/s} , \quad k = \frac{\pi v}{c L} = 1{,}110\ \text{1/m} . \tag{26.3}\]

We chose the function so that it will be a motion of the span. Why exactly these \(\omega\) and \(k\), the section on the modes of the moving string shows later in the chapter, here it is only a test function.

At the point \(x = 0{,}3\) m at \(t = 0\), \(w_* = 0{,}765\) mm and \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 1{,}452\cdot 10^{-3}\). By the lemma the three terms of the acceleration are \(-74{,}10\), \(-36{,}17\) and \(-15{,}72\) m/s\(^2\), which we draw to scale head to tail, all pointing downward. So the transverse acceleration of the material particle there is \(-126{,}0\) m/s\(^2\) (SymPy), and not only \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -74{,}10\) m/s\(^2\). The largest values over time and \(x\) of the terms are \(97{,}0\), \(78{,}2\) and \(17{,}8\) m/s\(^2\), so the Coriolis term reaches \(81\) % of the local one, and the centripetal \(18\) %. At \(v/c = 0{,}353\) we therefore must not neglect them: the Coriolis term is almost equal to the local one (panels (a) and (b) of figure 26.6).

Now we can write the equation of motion of the material piece. The law of motion of a body (definition 8.78), integrated over the points of the piece, says that the resultant of the forces on the piece equals the integral of the mass density times the acceleration. The piece of section 13.1 was over an interval that did not move. Now the material piece is over an interval that moves with speed \(v\), as the lower row of figure 26.3 shows, so in the law we use the acceleration from the lemma.

Derivation 26.2 Equation of motion of a material piece of the moving string (gibalna enačba kosa snovi gibajoče strune)

Goal: for a material piece that at time \(t\) is over the interval \([A, B] \subset (0, L)\), \(A < B\), to write the law of motion in the transverse direction. The assumptions are idealizations 1 to 8 and \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) on \([A, B]\).

1
\[\text{material piece} = \{\text{material particles } s \in [a, b]\} , \qquad a = A - vt , \quad b = B - vt , \qquad m = \mu\,(b - a) .\]
Hint

The material particle with label \(s\) is at time \(t\) at \(x = s + vt\) (idealization 5), so the material piece with labels from \(a\) to \(b\) lies over \([a + vt, b + vt] = [A, B]\) at time \(t\), and over \([a + v t', b + v t']\) at time \(t'\) (the dots at the ends of the piece in the upper and lower row of figure 26.3, below shifted by \(v\tau\)). All particles run with the same speed, so the length of the blue piece along \(x\) does not change, it stays \(b - a\), and the mass is by idealization 1 constant: \(m = \mu\,(b - a)\).

2
\[F_{\text{navp}} = T\,\big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t)\big) .\]
Hint

The forces of the neighbouring parts are by idealization 2 along the tangent, by idealization 3 of magnitude \(T\), so the sum of the vertical components, \(T\sin\theta_{\mathrm{B}} - T\sin\theta_{\mathrm{A}}\) with \(\tan\theta = w_{\mathrm{x}}\), equals this, with a relative error at \(\sin\theta\) of at most \(1 - 1/\sqrt{1 + 0{,}005^2} = 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) (step 3 of derivation 13.1 with the bound \(0{,}005\)). The horizontal resultant, \(T|\cos\theta_{\mathrm{B}} - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{A}}| \le 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\,T = 56\) mN, would accelerate the piece along \(x\), but by idealization 5 this speed does not change, so we neglect it. We do not count the weight (idealization 7). The forces \(T\) are drawn in the upper row of figure 26.3, and the right end from close up with its vertical part and horizontal part in figure 26.4.

3
\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,\ddot W_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}s = F_{\text{navp}} , \qquad \ddot W_{\mathrm{s}}(t) = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} \quad \text{at the point } (s + vt, t) .\]
Hint

The law of motion of a body (definition 8.78) for the material piece, which is a body because it is the same matter all the time: the mass density per label \(s\) is \(\mu\), because the spacing between the particles does not change (step 1), the transverse acceleration of the particle with label \(s\) is by lemma 26.1 equation (26.2), these are the three accelerations of figure 26.6. On the right is the resultant from step 2.

4

The resultant of the tension forces at the ends of the piece equals the integral of mass times acceleration over the material piece:

\[\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big)(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t) . \tag{26.4}\]
Hint

The change of variable \(x = s + vt\) at constant \(t\) (lemma 9.95, point 2, shift) turns the integral over \(s\) from \(a\) to \(b\) into an integral over \(x\) from \(a + vt = A\) to \(b + vt = B\), that is over the interval between the dashed verticals under the ends of the piece at time \(t\). The function is the same, only the argument is shifted.

Equation (26.4) holds for every material piece that at time \(t\) is over the interval \([A, B]\). For the piece with labels \(a = A - vt\) and \(b = B - vt\) this is a piece that stays in \((0, L)\) for a time around \(t\) if \(A\) and \(B\) are interior points, so the equation is a condition for every interior pair \(A < B\). For the end points we extend it by continuity of both sides.

Source: WM1990 (1), PDF p. 2, and CHEN2005 (1), PDF p. 2, obtain the equation with Newton's second law (Swope and Ames, 1963) or with Hamilton's principle for travelling media (Archibald and Emslie, 1958, Benjamin, 1961, WM1990, PDF p. 2). The derivation with the material piece and with the error bounds is not from the source.

With this the model is fixed. Let us write it as a definition in which it gets its name.

Definition 26.3 Moving string (gibajoča struna)

Let \(L\), \(\mu\), \(T\) and \(v\) be positive numbers: the span length in m, the mass per unit length in kg/m, the tension force in N and the transport speed in m/s. The moving string with length \(L\), mass \(\mu\) per unit length, tension \(T\) and transport speed \(v\) is a motion described by a function \(w : [0, L] \times [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) that has continuous partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tx}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) (definition 1.26), satisfies \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) for every \(t \ge 0\) and for every \(A < B\) from \([0, L]\) and every \(t \ge 0\) the equation (26.4). The function \(w(x, t)\) is the transverse displacement of the point at \(x\) at time \(t\) in metres. The model holds with the error from derivation 26.2 as long as \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) and idealizations 1 to 8 hold.

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2 (first paragraph of section 2.1: "uniform, flexible, axially moving string of linear density, tension and transport speed that travels between two fixed eyelets"), CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (section 2.1.1, assumptions 1 and 2). The error measures are ours.

Equation (26.4) is one condition for every pair \(A < B\), as for the string of section 13.1. Does the equation at every point follow from it? Yes, and also conversely, as in theorem 13.3.

Theorem 26.4 Equation of the moving string (enačba gibajoče strune)

Let \(w\) be a function with continuous \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\). Then for every \(t \ge 0\) equation (26.4) holds for all \(A < B\) from \([0, L]\) if and only if for every \(x \in [0, L]\) and every \(t \ge 0\)

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \tag{26.5}\]

which with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4) is equal to

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.6}\]
Proof

We must show that equation (26.4) for all pieces is equivalent to equation (26.5) at all points. We write the difference of the two sides as an integral of one continuous function and use that a continuous function with zero integral over every piece is zero everywhere, as in theorem 13.3.

  1. Fix \(t \ge 0\) and let \(f(x) = \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}})(x, t) - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, t)\). The function \(f\) is continuous, because the derivatives are continuous.
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55, point 1) \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t)\). This is the difference of the slopes at the ends of the piece, where the forces \(T\) act.
  3. By step 2 and linearity of the integral (lemma 3.54) \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the difference of the left and right side of equation (26.4). The equation holds for the piece \([A, B]\) if and only if \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  4. If (26.5) holds, \(f = 0\) and every integral is zero, so by step 3 (26.4) holds.
  5. Conversely let (26.4) hold for all \(A < B\), that is for every piece, however short. By step 3 \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for all \(A < B\), so \(G(x) = \int_0^x f\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) for \(x \in [0, L]\). The function \(G\) is differentiable with \(G' = f\) (theorem 3.55, point 2), because \(f\) is continuous, and it is zero, so \(f = G' = 0\).
  6. From \(f = 0\) follows (26.5). Division by \(\mu\) gives \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} = c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which is (26.6).

Source: WM1990 (1), PDF p. 2, CHEN2005 (1), PDF p. 2. The proof with an arbitrary finite piece is not from the source.

At \(v = 0\) the arrows of speed vanish and equation (26.6) simplifies to the wave equation (13.2): the string of section 13.1 is a special case of the moving string. At \(v \ne 0\) the Coriolis term adds the mixed derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and the centripetal term changes the coefficient of the second derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(c^2 - v^2\) instead of \(c^2\).

Let us test the theorem on numbers. The function \(w_*\) of equation (26.3) at \(v = 40\) m/s satisfied equation (26.5) by SymPy: the residual of the left and right side is at five points at most \(1\cdot 10^{-14}\) N/m in magnitude, so zero up to rounding. For the material piece over \([0{,}2\ \text{m},\ 0{,}5\ \text{m}]\) at \(t = 0\) the left side of equation (26.4) is \(-13{,}142\) N, the right \(-13{,}142\) N. At \(t = 4\) ms the piece is over \([0{,}360,\ 0{,}660]\) and both sides are \(3{,}629\) N (numbers by SymPy). The equality is no accident: we chose a function that satisfies the equation, and the theorem says that then it holds for every piece.

The theorem is tied to the material piece. Would it not be simpler to take an interval that stands in space, as in section 13.1? Let us try, and on the same motion \(w_*\).

A window (okno) is an interval \([a, b]\) that stands in space: such was the piece in section 13.1. In figure 26.9 the blackwhite row is the window and the blue row is the material piece. At time \(t\) they have the same matter, as the upper row of the figure says. At time \(t + \tau\) the window is still over \([a, b]\), but the material piece is over the interval from \(a + v\tau\) to \(b + v\tau\). So the matter in the window is not the same: the left orange area, of width \(v\tau\), is matter that entered through the left edge, the right orange one, also of width \(v\tau\), is matter of the piece that left the window through the right edge. The window is therefore not an unchanging set of material particles, so the law of motion of a body for it does not mean that mass times \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) equals the force: matter enters the window and leaves it and carries momentum with it.

How much this amounts to we measure on the motion \(w_*\) and draw to scale.

If we write the equation of motion as in section 13.1, \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(B) - T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(A)\), then for the motion \(w_*\) and \([A, B] = [0{,}2\ \text{m},\ 0{,}5\ \text{m}]\) at \(t = 0\) we get on the left \(-8{,}027\) N, on the right \(-13{,}142\) N. Missing are \(5{,}115\) N, which is \(39\) % of the force. The wave equation (13.2) itself is not satisfied either: the residual \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} - c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is at the point \(x = 0{,}3\) m \(51{,}9\) m/s\(^2\), at \(x = 0{,}5\) m \(38{,}6\) m/s\(^2\), not zero. The window therefore does not give the law.

What is missing is told by the momentum of the window. Let \(P_{\text{ok}}(t) = \int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}x\) be the momentum in the window (by equation (26.1) \(\mu(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\) is the density of transverse momentum). At \(t = 0\) its derivative in time is \(-9{,}764\) N. The second part is the flux of momentum through the edges. In the time \(\tau\) a strip of matter of length \(v\tau\), with mass \(\mu v\tau\) and transverse velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), leaves through the right edge, so it carries away the momentum \(\mu v\tau\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\), per unit time \(\mu v\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\) at \(B\). Through the left edge a strip of matter in the same way brings in the same expression at \(A\). The flux, the expression at \(B\) minus the expression at \(A\), is \(-3{,}377\) N. The sum is \(-9{,}764 - 3{,}377 = -13{,}141\) N (the deviation from \(-13{,}142\) N is rounding), and this is exactly the left side of equation (26.4), the upper blue bar. The momentum of the window therefore changes because of the force, which is \(T\) at the edges, and because of matter that enters and leaves through the edges. Only the second part is missing when we use the window with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\).

At \(v = 0\) the flux is zero, the material piece equals the window and equation (26.6) is equation (13.2). For a string at rest the window is therefore a material piece, and so in section 13.1 it was correct to take an interval that stands still.

Equation (26.5) can be read from one more side. Let us move the centripetal term to the right:

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} = \big(T - \mu v^2\big)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} .\]

The right side looks like a string at rest with a smaller tension. How much smaller, we draw to scale.

The whole tension is \(4500\) N. Of it \(\mu v^2 = 0{,}3510 \cdot 40^2 = 561{,}6\) N goes into making the matter turn along the curve, which is the centripetal term of panel (c) of figure 26.6. For bringing the string back toward the straight position there remain \(3938\) N. What happens when the remainder runs out is treated by the section on the critical speed later in the chapter.

The section has set up the model of the moving string: a span between eyelets that runs with speed \(v\), a material piece with the same matter, and the acceleration of a material particle with three terms. From this followed equation (26.6) with the mixed derivative \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), which at \(v = 0\) equals the wave equation. For our band of the example \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, the speed \(v = 40\) m/s is \(0{,}353\,c\) and \(T - \mu v^2 = 3938\) N instead of \(4500\) N at \(v = 0\). The next section introduces the material coordinate \(x - vt\), which finds solutions of the equation in the form of two waves that travel with different speeds.

26.2 Two waves in a moving string

A string at rest has, by lemma 13.5, two parts of its motion: a shape that runs to the right and a shape that runs to the left, both with speed \(c\). A band that runs through two fixed ends carries along everything that lies on it. Do both parts still run with \(c\), and are there still two of them?

From history

Skutch, whose paper of 1897 on a running taut thread we met in section 26.1, found the natural frequencies of the string without excitation by adding two waves that travel in opposite directions (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2). In 1954 Sack excited the same string by a harmonic motion of one end and found the natural frequencies from the resonance condition (CHEN2005, PDF pp. 2 and 21). Both obtained the same natural frequencies (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2). The path of two waves is the path of this section. For d'Alembert's string (section 13.1) the boundary conditions linked the two shapes, and since the end is fixed, here too a wave that arrives at it must become another wave there. The calculation begins with the question of what two fixed ends do to the fact that the band runs.

Let us return to the steel band of the running example of section 26.1: the span between the ends is \(L = 1\) m, the tension \(T = 4500\) N, the mass per unit length \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m and hence \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu} = 113{,}23\) m/s. The dimensions, the tension and the speed are our choice and not data of any real drive. The transport speed is \(v = 40\) m/s, with the idealizations of definition 26.3.

Let us draw what the band does. In the left picture we measure horizontally the place \(x\) along the band from the first end and vertically the time \(t\). The ends stand at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) at every time, so they are vertical lines. A particle of the band that is at \(x = \xi\) at time \(0\) is at \(x = \xi + vt\) at time \(t\), because the band runs with speed \(v\). Its path is the dashed oblique line \(x = \xi + vt\). The particle with \(\xi = 0\) would reach \(x = L\) at \(t = L/v = 25{,}0\) ms (above the top edge of the picture, which reaches \(14{,}7\) ms), and a particle with negative \(\xi\) enters the span only through the first end. The number \(\xi = x - vt\) does not change along such a path, so it labels a particle and not a place in space. That is why we call it the material coordinate (snovna koordinata): the Slovenian word snov means material, and \(\xi\) is the label of the piece of material that we follow.

Let us choose the event \(P\), the place \(x = 0{,}6\) m at time \(t = 11{,}78\) ms. We draw the same event in the right picture, where we measure \(\xi\) horizontally. Every particle now has a constant \(\xi\), so its paths are vertical, and \(P\) lies at \(\xi = 0{,}6 - 40\cdot 0{,}01178 = 0{,}129\) m. The ends have turned around: \(x = 0\) means \(\xi = -vt\) and \(x = L\) means \(\xi = L - vt\), so each of them flees to the left with speed \(v\) and runs past the particles, just as the band runs past the ends when we look from outside.

Why is this view useful? By Newton's second law the force determines the acceleration of a particle, that is the change of its velocity as we follow it. We follow the particle with \(\xi\) along a vertical line of the right picture. Its transverse displacement is \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\), its velocity \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) and its acceleration \(u_{\mathrm{tt}}\). Section 26.1 computed the same acceleration as \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (lemma 26.1). We show that the two calculations agree and that the view from the band turns into the equation of a string at rest.

We write the equation of the moving string in the form (26.6) (theorem 26.4, \(c^2 = T/\mu\)) once more:

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.7}\]
Lemma 26.5 Material coordinate (snovna koordinata)

Let \(c > 0\) and \(v \ge 0\) be numbers and \(w\) a function with continuous partial derivatives up to and including second order on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\). For \(t \ge 0\) and \(-vt \le \xi \le L - vt\) let \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\). Then, if the derivatives of \(w\) are taken at the point \((\xi + vt, t)\):

  1. In the right figure \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\xi\xi} = w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  2. The function \(w\) satisfies equation (26.7) exactly when \(u\) in the right figure satisfies \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2\,u_{\xi\xi}\), that is the wave equation of a string at rest (theorem 13.3).
  3. At the ends \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) holds for every \(t \ge 0\) exactly when \(u(-vt, t) = u(L - vt, t) = 0\) holds for every \(t \ge 0\).
Proof

We must show that the view from the band turns all three parts of the model. We obtain the derivatives of \(u\) from those of \(w\) by the chain rule and then compare the two sides of the equation.

  1. The function \(u\) is composed of \(w\) and the linear map \((\xi, t) \mapsto (\xi + vt, t)\), which carries a point of the right picture to the same point of the left one, like the event \(P\), so by the chain rule (lemma 4.43) \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 1 + w_{\mathrm{t}} \cdot 0 = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot v + w_{\mathrm{t}} \cdot 1 = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The term \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) has its reason in the picture: the particle that we follow along its line moves by \(v\tau\) along \(x\) in the time \(\tau\), so its displacement changes because of the place too and not only because of the time. These two derivatives are again continuously differentiable.
  2. The same rule for \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) gives \(u_{\xi\xi} = w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which we get along the line of the particle, it gives \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = (w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}}) + v\,(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}})\), and since the mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 1.131, the derivatives are continuous), \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). This is item 1.
  3. The left side of equation (26.7), read in the right figure, is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} - c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} = u_{\mathrm{tt}} - c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\) by step 2. It is zero exactly when \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\). This is item 2.
  4. The end point \(x = 0\) has \(\xi = -vt\) at time \(t\) and the point \(x = L\) has \(\xi = L - vt\), and \(u(-vt, t) = w(0, t)\), \(u(L - vt, t) = w(L, t)\). This is item 3.

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2: the acceleration of a particle has three terms, which the source calls the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal acceleration. The passage to the material coordinate and the proof are not from the source.

The lemma says what we drew. In \(\xi\) the equation is the one that chapter 13 solved for a string at rest, and every acceleration is the acceleration of a particle. The only difference is the ends: instead of resting at constant \(\xi\), they flee along the oblique lines of the right picture. The reason for this is Newton's law: an observer sitting on the band moves with constant velocity and his acceleration is zero, so he sees the same forces and the same accelerations as an observer on the ground, and for him the string is at rest.

A string at rest has, by lemma 13.5, solutions \(F(\xi - ct) + G(\xi + ct)\), and in \(x\) and \(t\) we have \(\xi - ct = x - (c + v)t\) and \(\xi + ct = x + (c - v)t\). Are these all the solutions? Lemma 13.5 proved only that such shapes are solutions, not that there are no others. Where the speeds come from we see from the left side of equation (26.7): the operators \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} + (v + c)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} + (v - c)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\) multiply to \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + 2v\,\partial_{\mathrm{t}}\partial_{\mathrm{x}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}^2\). The first annihilates \(F(x - (c + v)t)\), because its derivative with respect to time is \(-(c + v)F'\) and with respect to place \(F'\). The second annihilates \(G(x + (c - v)t)\) for the same reason. That there are no other solutions is shown by the proof with the new coordinates \(p = \xi - ct\) and \(q = \xi + ct\).

Let us draw where these coordinates live. In the picture we measure \(p\) horizontally and \(q\) vertically. Since \(q - p = 2ct\), the initial time \(t = 0\) is the line \(q = p\), and later times lie above it. From \(\xi = (p + q)/2\), \(t = (q - p)/(2c)\) and \(x = \xi + vt\) we get \(x = \big((c - v)p + (c + v)q\big)/(2c)\), so the end \(x = 0\) is the line \((c - v)p + (c + v)q = 0\) and the end \(x = L\) the parallel line \((c - v)p + (c + v)q = 2cL\). Everything that happens between the ends after the start is the shaded region \(D\) between these three lines. The proof will need one single property of this region: a horizontal line at constant \(q\) cuts it in one piece, and so does a vertical one at constant \(p\).

Lemma 26.6 Converse of d'Alembert's solution (obrat d'Alembertove rešitve)

Let \(c > 0\) and \(v \ge 0\) be numbers and \(S = \{(x, t) : 0 < x < L,\ t > 0\}\) an open strip, which the \((p, q)\) plane shows as the region \(D\). Let \(w\) have continuous partial derivatives up to and including second order on \(S\) and satisfy equation (26.7). Then there exist twice continuously differentiable functions \(F\) and \(G\) of one variable, \(F\) on the interval of values that \(x - (c + v)t\) takes on \(S\), and \(G\) on the interval of values that \(x + (c - v)t\) takes on \(S\), such that

\[w(x, t) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big) + G\big(x + (c - v)t\big) \qquad \text{for every } (x, t) \in S . \tag{26.8}\]

Conversely, for any twice continuously differentiable \(F\) and \(G\) the function (26.8) satisfies equation (26.7). For \(v = 0\) this is the converse of lemma 13.5: every solution of the equation \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the sum of a wave running to the right and a wave running to the left.

Proof

We must show that equation (26.7) turns into the equation \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = 0\) for the new coordinates, and that a solution of this equation on a set whose sections are intervals is the sum of a function of one coordinate and a function of the other.

  1. By lemma 26.5 (items 1 and 2 use only derivatives at a single point, so they hold on the open strip too) the function \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\) is twice continuously differentiable on the strip between the ends, the set \(S' = \{(\xi, t) : t > 0,\ -vt < \xi < L - vt\}\) and satisfies \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\).
  2. We introduce \(p = \xi - ct\) and \(q = \xi + ct\). This is a linear map with the inverse \(\xi = (p + q)/2\), \(t = (q - p)/(2c)\), because \(c > 0\). Since \(\xi = x - vt\), we have \(p = x - (c + v)t\) and \(q = x + (c - v)t\). The image of the set \(S'\) is the set \(D\) of points \((p, q)\) for which \(q > p\) (this is \(t > 0\)) and \(0 < (c - v)\,p + (c + v)\,q < 2cL\) (this is \(0 < x < L\), since \(x = \xi + vt = \big((c - v)p + (c + v)q\big)/(2c)\)). This set is open. Let \(\omega(p, q) = u\big((p + q)/2,\ (q - p)/(2c)\big)\), twice continuously differentiable on \(D\) by the chain rule (lemma 4.43).
  3. The derivative \(\omega_{\mathrm{p}}\) keeps \(q\) constant and \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}}\) keeps \(p\) constant. By the chain rule \(\omega_{\mathrm{p}} = \tfrac12 u_\xi - \tfrac{1}{2c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}} = \tfrac12 u_\xi + \tfrac{1}{2c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\). Next, \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = \tfrac14 u_{\xi\xi} + \tfrac{1}{4c}\,u_{\xi \mathrm{t}} - \tfrac{1}{4c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}\xi} - \tfrac{1}{4c^2}\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\). The mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 1.131), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = \tfrac{1}{4c^2}\,(c^2 u_{\xi\xi} - u_{\mathrm{tt}}) = 0\) by step 1.
  4. For a given \(q\) the set of values \(p\) with \((p, q) \in D\) is determined by inequalities that are linear in \(p\) (and \(p < q\)), so it is an interval. The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}}(\cdot, q)\) has on it the derivative \(\omega_{\mathrm{qp}} = \omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = 0\) (theorem 1.131), so by corollary 1.86 it is constant. Its value is a number \(g(q)\). At every point \((p_0, q_0)\) of \(D\) we have \(g(q) = \omega_{\mathrm{q}}(p_0, q)\) for \(q\) near \(q_0\), because \(D\) is open, so \(g\) is continuously differentiable.
  5. Let \(G\) be a primitive function of \(g\) on the interval of values of \(q\) (theorem 3.55), so \(G' = g\) and \(G\) is twice continuously differentiable. The function \(\omega - G(q)\) has derivative with respect to \(q\) equal to \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}} - g = 0\). For a given \(p\) the set of values \(q\) is an interval for the same reason as in step 4, so by corollary 1.86 \(\omega(p, q) - G(q)\) is independent of \(q\). We denote it \(F(p)\). Since \(F(p) = \omega(p, q_0) - G(q_0)\) for \(p\) near \(p_0\) and fixed \(q_0\), \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable.
  6. Hence at every point of the region \(D\) \(\omega(p, q) = F(p) + G(q)\), which is equation (26.8).
  7. Conversely let \(w = F(x - (c + v)t)\). The derivatives are
    \[w_{\mathrm{x}} = F', \quad w_{\mathrm{t}} = -(c + v)F', \quad w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F'', \quad w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -(c + v)F'', \quad w_{\mathrm{tt}} = (c + v)^2 F''.\]
    Insert into the left side of equation (26.7):
    \[\big((c + v)^2 - 2v(c + v) - (c^2 - v^2)\big)F'' .\]
    Factor out \(c + v\):
    \[(c + v)\big((c + v) - 2v - (c - v)\big)F'' = 0 .\]
    For \(w = G(x + (c - v)t)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = G'\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = (c - v)G'\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = G''\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (c - v)G''\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = (c - v)^2 G''\) and
    \[(c - v)\big((c - v) + 2v - (c + v)\big)G'' = 0 .\]
    The equation is linear, so the same holds for the sum.

Source: CHEN2005, PDF p. 2: Skutch obtained the natural frequencies by adding two waves in opposite directions. WM1990, PDF p. 5: for the motion considered, a forward wave with speed \(1 + v\) and a reflected one with speed \(1 - v\) (in dimensionless units). The proof is not from the source.

The proof did not need the ends, only the interior of the strip. It matters that the sections of the set \(D\) are intervals, like the blue and the orange segment. For a strip between two straight ends this is always true, because all three borders are straight lines. It would not be true for a region with a hole: for a set with a gap in a section, \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}}\) in step 4 could be a different constant on the two sides of the gap, the number \(g(q)\) would not exist, and the solution would not have the form (26.8).

The lemma also fulfils a promise of chapter 13. There we knew only that the waves \(F(x - ct) + G(x + ct)\) are solutions of the string at rest, here we know that there are no others, and the string at rest is the case \(v = 0\), when the paths of the particles are the same in both figures. But where do the shapes run? This is told by the shift of the values of a shape, which we draw.

Let us draw what happens to the two shapes in the time \(\tau\). In the top row we measure the place \(x\) horizontally. The blue shape \(F\) is drawn twice, solid at time \(t\) and dashed at \(t + \tau\), shifted to the right by \((c + v)\tau\). The orange shape \(G\) is also drawn twice, but the dashed one is shifted to the left, only by \((c - v)\tau\). The grey arrow is the path \(v\tau\) of the band to the right: the shift of the blue shape is this path and \(c\tau\) more forward, the shift of the orange shape is \(c\tau\) backward and this path forward. In the bottom row we see the same in the material coordinate \(\xi\), where the band is at rest: both shapes are shifted by the same length \(c\tau\), the blue to the right and the orange to the left.

Corollary 26.7 Wave speeds (hitrosti valov)

Let \(0 \le v < c\) and \(w(x, t) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big) + G\big(x + (c - v)t\big)\) as in lemma 26.6. Then:

  1. The shape \(x \mapsto F(x - (c + v)t)\) at time \(t + \tau\) is the shape at time \(t\), shifted by \((c + v)\tau\) towards larger \(x\), that is in the direction of motion of the band. We call it the forward wave (val naprej).
  2. The shape \(x \mapsto G(x + (c - v)t)\) at time \(t + \tau\) is the shape at time \(t\), shifted by \((c - v)\tau\) towards smaller \(x\), that is against the direction of motion of the band. We call it the backward wave (val nazaj).
  3. In the material coordinate \(\xi\) both waves go with speed \(c\): \(F(\xi - ct)\) travels towards larger \(\xi\), \(G(\xi + ct)\) towards smaller.
Proof

We must show that the value of each shape at time \(t + \tau\) appears shifted. For this we insert the shifted place.

  1. \(F\big((x + (c + v)\tau) - (c + v)(t + \tau)\big) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big)\). The value of the forward wave at the point \(x\) at time \(t\) is therefore the value at time \(t + \tau\) at the point \(x + (c + v)\tau\).
  2. \(G\big((x - (c - v)\tau) + (c - v)(t + \tau)\big) = G\big(x + (c - v)t\big)\). The value of the backward wave at the point \(x\) at time \(t\) is the value at time \(t + \tau\) at the point \(x - (c - v)\tau\), because \(c - v > 0\) is a shift towards smaller \(x\).
  3. By lemma 26.5, \(x - (c + v)t = \xi - ct\) and \(x + (c - v)t = \xi + ct\), which is lemma 13.5 in \(\xi\).

Source: CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (superposition of two waves), WM1990, PDF p. 5 (forward wave with speed \(1 + v\), reflected with \(1 - v\)). The proof is not from the source.

The names have a reason: the forward wave goes forward, in the direction of the band, the backward wave goes backward, against it. The speeds \(c \pm v\) are a sum of speeds as in every motion on a moving base. The waves run with speed \(c\) relative to the band (item 3, where the band is at rest), and the band itself with speed \(v\) relative to the ends. Someone who walks on a moving walkway with speed \(c\) in the direction of the walkway is seen from the ground with speed \(c + v\), and someone who walks against it with speed \(c - v\), if \(v < c\). The first is the forward wave, the second the backward wave.

Example 26.8 Two shapes that are not a wave of the string

For the steel band of the example, \(v = 40\) m/s, take the shape \(F(s) = \varepsilon\sin(\pi s/L)\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\) mm and move it with speed \(V\) through space: \(w = F(x - Vt)\). The slope is at most \(\varepsilon\pi/L = 3{,}14\cdot 10^{-3}\), below the limit \(0{,}005\) of definition 26.3. In the picture we measure the speed \(V\) horizontally and vertically the factor that step 1 computes.

  1. For every speed \(V\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = V^2 F''\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -V F''\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\), so the left side of equation (26.7) equals \(\big(V^2 - 2vV - c^2 + v^2\big)F'' = \big((V - v)^2 - c^2\big)F''\). The factor in front of \(F''\) is, as a function of \(V\), a parabola with its vertex at \(V = v\).
  2. The factor is zero exactly when \(V - v = \pm c\), that is \(c\) to the right or to the left of the vertex: \(V = v + c = 153{,}23\) m/s or \(V = v - c = -73{,}23\) m/s. These are the speeds of the forward and the backward wave of corollary 26.7.
  3. The speed \(V = c = 113{,}23\) m/s was the speed of the waves on a string at rest. Now the factor is \((c - v)^2 - c^2 = v(v - 2c) = -7458\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\). At the crest \(F'' = -(\pi/L)^2\varepsilon = -9{,}87\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/m, so the left side is \(+73{,}6\) m/s\(^2\) and not zero.
  4. The speed \(V = v = 40\) m/s is the speed with which the band carries its shape. The factor is \(-c^2 = -12\,820\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\), the lowest point of the parabola, and the left side at the crest \(+126{,}5\) m/s\(^2\). The cause: the particles of such a shape have transverse acceleration zero, since each keeps its displacement, but the tension still acts on a curved piece with a force \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) per unit length, which is not balanced. A shape that the band merely carries is therefore not a motion of the string, and of all speeds this one is the farthest from a wave.

The speed \(c\) from the chapter on the string at rest therefore holds only for \(v = 0\). For \(v \ne 0\) the speed of the waves relative to the band is \(c\) and relative to the ends \(c \pm v\).

What happens when \(v\) approaches \(c\)? The speed of the backward wave \(c - v\) falls towards zero, and at \(v = c\) the backward wave is a shape at rest \(G(x + 0\cdot t) = G(x)\). At \(v = c = 113{,}23\) m/s the factor \(c^2 - v^2\) in equation (26.7) is zero, the equation reduces to \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2c\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\), and every shape at rest \(w(x)\) with \(w(0) = w(L) = 0\) satisfies it, because \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\). In figure 26.15 this means that the parabola moves to the right together with its vertex and its left zero \(v - c\) arrives at \(V = 0\): a shape that we do not move becomes a wave. At \(v = 40\) m/s this zero is at \(-73{,}23\) m/s, at \(V = 0\) the factor is \(v^2 - c^2 = -11\,220\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\) and a shape at rest is not a motion of the string. Two forces stand behind this: the particles that run along the curved path at rest need a force per unit length \(\mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (item 1 of lemma 26.5 with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\)), and the tension supplies \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mu c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so at \(v = 40\) m/s \(561{,}6\) N against \(4500\) N. Section 26.4 draws them on a piece of the string. For \(v > c\) we have \(c - v < 0\) and the backward wave too goes in the direction of the band, no wave goes against the band any more. The algebra of lemma 26.6 still holds, but the string model (definition 26.3) is set up for \(v < c\) and for \(v \ge c\) we claim nothing. Section 26.4 shows what happens to the energy at \(v = c\).

Now we can compute what happens to a shape that we release. For a string at rest (section 13.1) d'Alembert's formula (13.11) split a pulse with initial velocity zero into two equal halves. Let us release a pulse on the band.

Example 26.9 A pulse released at rest

Into the band of the example (\(v = 40\) m/s, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, \(L = 1\) m) we release a pulse between the ends: at time \(0\) the displacement is \(w_0(x) = h\,(1 - r^2)^3\) for \(|r| < 1\) and \(0\) elsewhere, \(r = (x - x_0)/s\), \(x_0 = 0{,}4\) m, \(s = 0{,}1\) m, \(h = 0{,}25\) mm, the initial transverse velocity is \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0) = 0\) (as in the top picture). The function \(w_0\) is twice continuously differentiable, because the factor \((1 - r^2)^3\) has zero first and second derivative at \(r = \pm 1\). Its largest slope, at \(r = \pm 1/\sqrt5\), is \(h\cdot 1{,}717/s = 4{,}3\cdot 10^{-3}\), below the limit \(0{,}005\) of definition 26.3.

  1. By lemma 26.6, \(w = F(x - (c + v)t) + G(x + (c - v)t)\). Since \(w\) and its derivatives are continuous up to \(t = 0\) (top figure), as \(t \to 0\) and for \(0 < x < L\) we have \(F(x) + G(x) = w_0(x)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0) = -(c + v)F'(x) + (c - v)G'(x) = 0\) for \(0 < x < L\).
  2. The derivative of the first condition is \(F' + G' = w_0'\). From the second, \(G' = \frac{c + v}{c - v}\,F'\). Inserting: \(F'\big(1 + \frac{c + v}{c - v}\big) = w_0'\), that is \(F' = \frac{c - v}{2c}\,w_0'\) and \(G' = \frac{c + v}{2c}\,w_0'\). These shares of the pulse are the heights of the forward wave and the backward wave relative to \(h\).
  3. Integration gives \(F = \frac{c - v}{2c}\,w_0 + k\) and \(G = \frac{c + v}{2c}\,w_0 - k\) with a constant \(k\). Since in the sum \(F(p) + G(q)\) the constant \(k\) cancels, we take \(k = 0\), and the forward wave is \(F\), the backward wave is \(G\).
  4. Numbers: \(\frac{c - v}{2c} = 0{,}3234\), \(\frac{c + v}{2c} = 0{,}6766\), the sum is \(1\). At \(t = 2\) ms the forward wave has its centre at \(x_0 + (c + v)t = 0{,}7065\) m and height \(0{,}081\) mm, the backward wave has its centre at \(x_0 - (c - v)t = 0{,}2535\) m and height \(0{,}169\) mm. The point of the band that was at \(x_0\) at time \(0\) is at \(x_0 + vt = 0{,}480\) m.
  5. The ends need not be taken into account yet at \(t = 2\) ms. For \(x < (c + v)t\) the argument \(x - (c + v)t\) is negative. There \(F\) is not determined by step 3 but by the boundary condition \(w(0, t') = 0\), that is \(F(-(c + v)t') = -G((c - v)t')\) for \(0 < t' \le t\). Since \((c - v)t' \le 0{,}147\) m and \(G = 0{,}6766\,w_0\) is zero below \(0{,}3\) m, \(F\) is zero there too. In the same way \(G\) is zero at arguments between \(L\) and \(L + (c - v)t\), because \(w_0\) is zero above \(0{,}5\) m.

The speeds \(c + v\) and \(c - v\) of corollary 26.7 are seen in the shifts \(0{,}3065\) m and \(0{,}1465\) m, while the band itself moved only by \(vt = 0{,}080\) m in this time. For \(v = 0\) the shares would be \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12\) (formula (13.11)), as for a string at rest. Now the backward wave is higher. The reason is the initial condition \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) at time \(0\): the transverse velocities of the two waves, \(-(c + v)F'\) and \((c - v)G'\), must cancel at every point. The slower wave has at equal slope a smaller transverse velocity, so it must have a larger slope, in the ratio \((c + v)/(c - v) = 2{,}09\). For \(v \to c\) the share of the forward wave goes to zero and the pulse stays entirely in the backward wave, which stands still, as we saw above.

In its splitting the pulse changed not only in height. At the ends each part turns around and becomes another wave. For this we need the boundary conditions.

Let us first see what an end does to the width. The picture shows the \((x, t)\) plane right next to the end \(x = 0\). The orange band is the backward wave of example 26.9: its front and rear edge are parallel lines that approach the end with speed \(c - v = 73{,}23\) m/s, and the horizontal distance between them is the width of the wave \(\ell = 2s = 0{,}2\) m. The front edge reaches the end at \(4{,}097\) ms and the rear edge at \(6{,}828\) ms, so the end has the wave in front of it for \(\ell/(c - v) = 2{,}73\) ms. For all this time \(w = 0\) must hold there, so for exactly as long the blue band leaves the end, a forward wave with the opposite sign that cancels the orange one at the end. The edges of the blue band move away with speed \(c + v = 153{,}23\) m/s, so the lines are flatter, and in \(2{,}73\) ms the first edge gets ahead of the second by \(153{,}23 \cdot 0{,}00273 = 0{,}418\) m. After the reflection the wave is \(2{,}09\) times wider, because the same time is multiplied by the larger speed.

Lemma 26.10 Reflection at an end (odboj na krajišču)

Let \(0 \le v < c\) and \(w\) a motion of the moving string with fixed ends (definition 26.3), written as \(F(x - (c + v)t) + G(x + (c - v)t)\) (lemma 26.6). Then for every \(t > 0\)

\[F\big(-(c + v)t\big) = -G\big((c - v)t\big) , \qquad F\big(L - (c + v)t\big) = -G\big(L + (c - v)t\big) . \tag{26.9}\]

So a backward wave that arrives at the end \(x = 0\) leaves as a forward wave with the opposite sign, its width multiplied by \((c + v)/(c - v) > 1\). A forward wave that arrives at the end \(x = L\) leaves as a backward wave with the opposite sign, its width multiplied by \((c - v)/(c + v) < 1\). The height does not change at a reflection.

Proof

We must show that \(w(0, t) = 0\) and \(w(L, t) = 0\) link the values of \(F\) and \(G\) at the points that the end requires, and that the width follows from the time that the wave spends at the end.

  1. The arguments \(-(c + v)t\) and \(L - (c + v)t\) lie in the interval of values of \(x - (c + v)t\) on \(S\), which is \((-\infty, L)\), since \(p < L\) on the region \(D\). The arguments \((c - v)t\) and \(L + (c - v)t\) lie in the interval of values of \(x + (c - v)t\), which is \((0, \infty)\), because \(c - v > 0\). The functions \(F\) and \(G\) are continuous, \(w\) is continuous on the closed strip, so \(w(0, t) = F(-(c + v)t) + G((c - v)t)\) and \(w(L, t) = F(L - (c + v)t) + G(L + (c - v)t)\).
  2. Both values are zero, because the end is fixed. This is equation (26.9).
  3. Let the backward wave occupy on the \(q\) axis an interval of length \(\ell\). At the end \(x = 0\) we have \(q = (c - v)t\), so the end sees it for the whole time \(\ell/(c - v)\). The forward wave that leaves must fill the same time, and on the axis \(p = -(c + v)t\) this occupies an interval of length \((c + v)\,\ell/(c - v)\). The same for \(x = L\) with the roles exchanged.

Source: The proof is not from the source. WM1990, PDF p. 5: a forward wave with speed \(1 + v\) is reflected from the right support as a wave with speed \(1 - v\).

The last figure puts everything in one place.

Let us draw everything that we computed in the \((x, t)\) plane next to the last picture. The point \(x_0\) is where the pulse starts. From it go two lines: the blue one with slope \(c + v\) to the right and the orange one with slope \(c - v\) to the left, slower and higher. The dashed line of the band has slope \(v\) and lies between. The blue line reaches the end \(x = L\) at \(t_1 = (L - x_0)/(c + v) = 3{,}916\) ms (marked \(t_1\)) and by lemma 26.10 is reflected as a backward wave with the opposite sign, unchanged height \(0{,}081\) mm and width multiplied by \((c - v)/(c + v) = 0{,}478\), that is with half-width \(0{,}048\) m instead of \(0{,}1\) m. The orange line reaches the end \(x = 0\) at \(t_2 = x_0/(c - v) = 5{,}462\) ms and becomes a forward wave with height \(0{,}169\) mm and half-width \(0{,}1\cdot 2{,}09 = 0{,}209\) m, which is half of the width \(0{,}418\) m that we drew at the lemma. Then the orange line reaches \(x = L\) at \(t_3 = t_2 + L/(c + v) = 11{,}99\) ms and the blue one reaches \(x = 0\) at \(t_4 = t_1 + L/(c - v) = 17{,}57\) ms. Every reflection turns the sign, so the displacement after one reflection is negative and after two positive again.

The next section will compute from these paths the round-trip time and the natural frequencies. Here we have shown that the band has two waves instead of one, that the speeds \(c + v\) and \(c - v\) each belong to their own direction, and that after a reflection the width of a wave changes and the height does not. We have also shown where this model stops being valid: at \(v = c\) the backward wave stands still.

26.3 Modes of the moving string

A steel band for a band saw, 50 mm wide and 0,9 mm thick, runs at 40 m/s through two fixed eyelets (očesci) 1 m apart and is pulled with a stress of 100 MPa. These dimensions are our choice, not data from a source. We pluck the band. What frequency do we hear, and how does it change when the band runs faster? Do all points of the band oscillate together, as on a string at rest? In section 13.2 (chapter 13) we found for the string at rest the standing wave \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), and the chapter promised that for belts this shape is no longer a solution. Here we prove it and find what replaces it.

The model is the moving string of section 26.1: the deflection \(w(x, t)\) of the point of the string that lies at \(x \in [0, L]\) at time \(t\) is transverse, \(x\) is measured from the first eyelet in the direction of motion, and the transport speed \(v\) is constant and positive. The letter \(v\) here is the transport speed in m/s, and the deflection is \(w\) as in chapter 13 (in the chapters on beams \(v\) is a deflection). The string has tension \(T\) and mass per length \(\mu\) as in definition 13.2, \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) is the wave speed of definition 13.4, and everything below holds for subcritical speed \(0 \le v < c\). The equation of motion of theorem 26.4 and the two ends are

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (v^2 - c^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 , \qquad w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0 . \tag{26.10}\]

The first term is the local acceleration at the place \(x\), the second is the Coriolis term, the third is the centripetal term. The second is named after Coriolis because it is the acceleration of a body that moves along a path that itself moves: a particle of the string runs at speed \(v\) along a curve whose slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) changes in time, and the transverse velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the particle therefore changes also through \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The third is centripetal because it is the acceleration of a particle that runs at speed \(v\) along a curve of curvature \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and points to the centre of curvature, as in a car in a bend. Section 26.1 derived both from the chain rule. For \(v = 0\) the wave equation of theorem 13.3 remains.

Where is the difficulty? As for the string at rest, we try a motion in which every point oscillates with the same frequency \(\omega\): \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) with a real function \(\varphi\). The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are then proportional to \(\cos\omega t\), but the mixed derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -\omega\varphi'\sin\omega t\) is proportional to \(\sin\omega t\). The functions \(\cos\omega t\) and \(\sin\omega t\) are not proportional: at \(t = 0\) the first is \(1\) and the second \(0\), at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the other way round. So the part of the equation with each of them must vanish separately. The following lemma shows this, and it is also the proof that was promised.

Lemma 26.11 A standing wave is not a solution (stoječe valovanje ni rešitev)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\), \(0 < v < c\) and \(\omega > 0\), and let \(\varphi : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. If \(w(x, t) = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) solves equation (26.10) for every \(t \ge 0\), then \(\varphi = 0\). In particular \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega t)\) is not a solution for any \(\omega\).

Proof

We must show that the equation forces two different conditions on \(\varphi\) at two times.

  1. For \(w = \varphi\cos\omega t\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2\varphi\cos\omega t\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -\omega\varphi'\sin\omega t\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi''\cos\omega t\) (theorem on derivatives of sine and cosine, 8.13).
  2. At \(t = 0\) we have \(\cos 0 = 1\) and \(\sin 0 = 0\), so equation (26.10) gives \(-\omega^2\varphi + (v^2 - c^2)\varphi'' = 0\). This is the instant of largest deflection, when the string is at rest and its slope is not changing.
  3. At \(t = \pi/(2\omega)\) we have \(\cos = 0\) and \(\sin = 1\), so the equation gives \(-2v\omega\varphi'(x) = 0\) for every \(x\). Since \(v\) and \(\omega\) are positive, \(\varphi' = 0\). This is the instant when the string is straight and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are zero everywhere, while the slope changes fastest: only the Coriolis term is left in the equation and nothing balances it.
  4. A function with zero derivative is constant (corollary 1.86), and \(\varphi(0) = 0\) by the boundary condition, so \(\varphi = 0\). The function \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) is not zero everywhere, so by this it is not a solution.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. WM1990 (PDF p. 4) and CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2) state only the result that the eigenfunctions of the moving string change.

What do we use instead of \(\cos\omega t\)? Every point still oscillates with \(\omega\), but not all at once: the point \(x\) reaches its crest with a delay that depends on \(x\). We say the point \(x\) has amplitude \(|\varphi(x)|\) and phase shift \(\arg\varphi(x)\), and we write this with one complex function, as for systems with one degree of freedom in chapter 9: \(w(x, t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\big)\) (definition 9.33). If \(\varphi = |\varphi|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\), then \(w = |\varphi|\cos(\omega t + \theta)\). The word phase means the stage a point has reached in its oscillation: two points with different \(\theta\) are not at the same stage and do not reach their crests at the same time.

Definition 26.12 Mode of the moving string (način nihanja gibajoče se strune)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\) and \(0 \le v < c\). Let \(\omega > 0\) be a number and \(\varphi : [0, L] \to \mathbb{C}\) a complex function that is not zero everywhere and whose real and imaginary parts are twice continuously differentiable. The pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode (način nihanja) of the string with equation (26.10) if the real function

\[w(x, t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\big) = \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(x)\cos\omega t - \mathrm{Im}\,\varphi(x)\sin\omega t\]

solves equation (26.10) for all \(t \ge 0\), boundary conditions included. The number \(\omega\) is the natural circular frequency (lastna krožna frekvenca), \(\varphi\) is the complex mode shape (kompleksna oblika načina). A point \(x\) with \(\varphi(x) = 0\) is a node (vozel).

Source: WM1990 section 3 (PDF pp. 2-3) and CHEN2005 section 2.2 (PDF pp. 2-3) treat complex eigenfunctions of the moving string. The notation with \(\mathrm{Re}(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) is not from the sources. For \(v = 0\) and real \(\varphi\) this is the mode of definition 13.6.

Which pairs \((\omega, \varphi)\) exist? We look for them in three moves. First we insert \(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) into the equation and get an ordinary equation with complex coefficients. Then we remove the term with the first derivative by writing \(\varphi\) as the product \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\psi\) with a phase \(kx\) that grows with position. The equation of section 13.2 remains. Why a phase? The term with the first derivative carries the factor \(\mathrm{i}\), and multiplying by \(\mathrm{i}\) only turns a pointer, it does not lengthen it (definition 9.33): so this term changes the phase of the points, not their amplitude, and the factor \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\), which has size \(1\), can take it over.

The assumption \(v < c\) enters in the second move, where \(k = v\omega/(c^2 - v^2)\). It is justified here because the band runs at \(40\) m/s while waves run along it at \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s. It fails for \(v \ge c\): there the wave against the motion stands still relative to the eyelets or the band carries it backwards, the number \(k\) is not defined at \(v = c\), and there are no modes of this form (section 26.4). In the result it leaves the factor \(1 - v^2/c^2\), with which all frequencies fall to zero at \(v = c\), for the band this factor is \(0{,}8752\).

Theorem 26.13 Modes of the moving string (načini nihanja gibajoče se strune)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\) and \(0 \le v < c\). The pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the string with equation (26.10) if and only if there are a natural number \(n\) and a complex number \(C \ne 0\) with

\[\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\Big) , \qquad \varphi(x) = C\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} , \qquad k_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{n\pi v}{cL} . \tag{26.11}\]

For \(C = |C|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) the real form of the mode is

\[w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = |C|\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\cos\big(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t + k_{\mathrm{n}} x + \theta\big) . \tag{26.12}\]

For \(v = 0\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi c/L\) and \(\varphi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\), which is theorem 13.7.

Proof

We must show that the condition for a mode is equivalent to an ordinary equation with end conditions, and solve it. We write \(\varphi' = \mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}x\), and derivatives of complex functions are taken by components (lemma 9.35).

  1. For \(w = \mathrm{Re}(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) theorem 9.34, item 3, gives \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = \mathrm{Re}(-\omega^2\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi'\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mathrm{Re}(\varphi''\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\). Equation (26.10) is then \(\mathrm{Re}(P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = 0\) with the complex function \(P = -\omega^2\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}v\omega\varphi' + (v^2 - c^2)\varphi''\).
  2. If \(\mathrm{Re}(P(x)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = 0\) for every \(t \ge 0\), then \(t = 0\) gives \(\mathrm{Re}\,P = 0\) and \(t = \pi/(2\omega)\) gives \(\mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}P) = -\mathrm{Im}\,P = 0\). So \(P = 0\), that is
    \[(c^2 - v^2)\,\varphi'' - 2\mathrm{i}v\omega\,\varphi' + \omega^2\varphi = 0 . \tag{26.13}\]
    Conversely \(P = 0\) gives the equation for every \(t\). The same argument (at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\)) shows that the boundary conditions hold if and only if \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\).
  3. Let \(k = v\omega/(c^2 - v^2)\) (a defined number, since \(v < c\)) and \(\psi(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}kx}\varphi(x)\). By the rules for complex functions (lemma 9.35, item 1) and the derivative \((\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx})' = \mathrm{i}k\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) we get \(\varphi' = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}(\psi' + \mathrm{i}k\psi)\) and \(\varphi'' = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}(\psi'' + 2\mathrm{i}k\psi' - k^2\psi)\).
  4. We insert into (26.13) and divide by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx} \ne 0\) (theorem 9.34, item 2). The coefficient of \(\psi'\) is \(2\mathrm{i}k(c^2 - v^2) - 2\mathrm{i}v\omega = 0\) by the choice of \(k\). The coefficient of \(\psi\) is
    \[-(c^2 - v^2)k^2 + 2v\omega k + \omega^2 = \frac{-v^2\omega^2 + 2v^2\omega^2}{c^2 - v^2} + \omega^2 = \frac{\omega^2 c^2}{c^2 - v^2} .\]
    What remains is \((c^2 - v^2)\psi'' + \dfrac{\omega^2c^2}{c^2 - v^2}\psi = 0\), that is \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with \(\kappa = \omega c/(c^2 - v^2) > 0\). The boundary conditions are \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx} \ne 0\).
  5. The real and imaginary parts of \(\psi\) are real, twice continuously differentiable, and each solves \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with zeros at \(0\) and \(L\) (the coefficient \(-\kappa^2\) is real). Since \(\psi\) is not zero everywhere, at least one of them is not.
