For that part steps 3 to 5 of the proof of theorem 13.7 hold, with \(\kappa\) in place of the number \(k = \omega/c\) used there: \(\sin\kappa L = 0\), so \(\kappa L = n\pi\) with a natural number \(n\), and the part is a multiple of \(\sin\kappa x\). The same holds for the other part if it is not zero, so \(\psi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with a complex \(C \ne 0\).
  6. From \(\kappa = n\pi/L\) we get \(\omega = \kappa(c^2 - v^2)/c = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(k = v\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(c^2 - v^2) = n\pi v/(cL) = k_{\mathrm{n}}\). So \(\varphi = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\psi = C\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\). This is the direction "only if".
  7. Conversely, let \(\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\varphi\) from (26.11). Then \(\kappa = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} c/(c^2 - v^2) = n\pi/L\) and \(\psi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\) solves \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with zeros at \(0\) and \(L\). Steps 4 and 3 in reverse give (26.13), and step 2 shows that \(w\) is a solution with the boundary conditions.
  8. The real part: \(\mathrm{Re}\big(|C|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t}\big) = |C|\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta)\), because \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha} = \cos\alpha + \mathrm{i}\sin\alpha\) (definition 9.33) and \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) is real. The first factor is the envelope, the cosine with the phase \(k_{\mathrm{n}}x\) gives the shape in the right column.

Source: WM1990 (27a) and (27b) (PDF p. 4): \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi(1 - \nu^2)\) and the eigenfunction with components \(\sin(n\pi x)\cos(n\pi\nu x)\) and \(\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi\nu x)\) in dimensionless quantities, where \(\nu = v/c\) and not Poisson's ratio. CHEN2005 (5) (PDF p. 2): \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = (n\pi/l)(1 - \rho c^2/P)\sqrt{P/\rho}\), where \(c\) means the transport speed. The proof by removing the first derivative with the phase \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) is not from the sources, it is checked with SymPy (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 1 and 2).

The theorem is short, its meaning is in the shape, and figure 26.19 builds it. We draw first the two eyelets in each row, with the string of length \(L\) between them, and the horizontal position of the string at rest. Each row is one time in the oscillation, from top to bottom \(\omega t = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\). Into it we put the shape of the string at time \(\omega t = 0\) and the grey dashed envelope \(\pm\sin(\pi x/L)\), which is the largest deflection a point reaches. The left column is the string at rest, \(v = 0\): at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is straight, at \(\omega t = \pi\) it is inverted, and at every time the shape is symmetric about the middle. In the right column \(v/c = \tfrac12\) and \(k_1 = \pi/(2L)\): at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is not straight, because the factor \(\cos(\omega t + k_1x)\) differs from point to point, and at none of the four times is the shape symmetric. The place of largest deflection, the orange dot, is at \(0{,}39\,L\) at \(\omega t = 0\), at \(0{,}61\,L\) at \(\pi/2\), at \(0{,}39\,L\) again at \(\pi\) and at \(0{,}61\,L\) at \(3\pi/2\) (computed in outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 5). The envelope and the eyelets stay as they were.

Corollary 26.14 Nodes and amplitudes of the mode (vozli in amplitude načina)

Let \((\omega_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a mode from theorem 26.13. The amplitude of the point \(x\) is \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x)| = |C|\,|\sin(n\pi x/L)|\), as for the string at rest. Mode \(n\) has \(n - 1\) nodes in the interior, at the points \(x = jL/n\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n - 1\). For \(v > 0\) there is no time at which the string is straight everywhere.

Proof

We must show three claims. The theorem gives the amplitude and the nodes, straightness needs one more argument.

  1. By theorem 9.34, item 2, \(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}| = 1\), so \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}| = |C|\,|\sin(n\pi x/L)|\). This is the envelope, the same in the left and the right column.
  2. A node is a point with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = 0\), that is \(\sin(n\pi x/L) = 0\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x} \ne 0\) and \(C \ne 0\). The zeros of the sine are the multiples of \(\pi\) (step 5 of the proof of theorem 13.7), so \(x = jL/n\), and the condition \(0 < x < L\) gives \(j = 1, \dots, n - 1\).
  3. At time \(t\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = |C|\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta)\). For \(x \in (0, L)\) the first factor is nonzero except at the nodes, and the second is zero only where \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi/2\). For \(v > 0\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\) and the argument grows with \(x\) by \(k_{\mathrm{n}}L > 0\), so the cosine has at most finitely many zeros on \((0, L)\). Hence \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(\cdot, t)\) is not zero everywhere. In the right column at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the factor \(\cos(\pi/2 + \pi x/(2L)) = -\sin(\pi x/(2L))\) has no zero between the eyelets, so the shape lies wholly below the axis, while in the left column it is straight at the same time.

Source: WM1990 (PDF p. 4): the nodes are the same as for the string at rest, but the axial motion distorts the shapes strongly (figure 2, PDF p. 4). The proof is not from the sources.

So every point has its own phase. Where this phase comes from is shown by a second view: the mode as two travelling waves.

By the addition formulas (corollary 8.16) the product \(\sin A\cos B\) is half the sum \(\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)\). With \(A = n\pi x/L\) and \(B = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x\) from mode \(n\) we get the sum of two waves of the kind that lemma 26.6 of section 26.2 knows.

Corollary 26.15 A mode as a sum of two travelling waves (način kot vsota dveh potujočih valov)

Let \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\) be from equation (26.12) with \(\theta = 0\) and \(|C| = 1\). Then

\[w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = \tfrac12\sin\!\Big(\frac{n\pi(c - v)}{cL}\,x - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\Big) + \tfrac12\sin\!\Big(\frac{n\pi(c + v)}{cL}\,x + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\Big) . \tag{26.14}\]

The first wave has the form \(F(x - (c + v)t)\) and moves in the direction of motion with speed \(c + v\). The second has the form \(G(x + (c - v)t)\) and moves against the direction of motion with speed \(c - v\). Both speeds are measured relative to the fixed eyelets. The waves have the same frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and wavelengths \(2Lc/(n(c - v))\) and \(2Lc/(n(c + v))\).

Proof

We must show the equality and, for each wave, its speed and wavelength.

  1. By the addition formulas (corollary 8.16), \(\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2\sin A\cos B\). With \(A = n\pi x/L\) and \(B = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x\) we have \(\sin A\cos B = \tfrac12\sin(A + B) + \tfrac12\sin(A - B)\), where \(A + B = (n\pi/L + k_{\mathrm{n}})x + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\) and \(A - B = (n\pi/L - k_{\mathrm{n}})x - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\). Since \(n\pi/L \pm k_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi(c \pm v)/(cL)\), this is (26.14).
  2. The first term is \(\tfrac12\sin(q(x - st))\) with \(q = n\pi(c - v)/(cL)\) and \(s = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/q = (c^2 - v^2)/(c - v) = c + v\). This is the form \(F(x - (c + v)t)\), the blue wave. The wavelength is \(2\pi/q = 2Lc/(n(c - v))\).
  3. The second term is \(\tfrac12\sin(q'(x + s't))\) with \(q' = n\pi(c + v)/(cL)\) and \(s' = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/q' = c - v\), wavelength \(2\pi/q' = 2Lc/(n(c + v))\). This is the orange wave, whose half wavelength for \(n = 1\) and \(v/c = \tfrac12\) is \(\tfrac23 L\).

Source: CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2): Skutch determined the natural frequencies by superposing two waves in opposite directions. The derivation from the mode is not from the sources, it is checked in outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 2.

Figure 26.20 builds this for the first mode at \(v/c = \tfrac12\) at \(\omega t = \pi/3\). In each row there are the two eyelets a distance \(L\) apart and between them the horizontal position of the string at rest. Then we draw the first row, the wave \(\tfrac12\sin(\pi x/(2L) - \omega_1t)\), which the arrow \(c + v\) moves in the direction of motion. Its wavelength is \(4L\), four times the length of the string, so the length \(L\) holds exactly a quarter of the wave. The second row is the wave \(\tfrac12\sin(3\pi x/(2L) + \omega_1t)\) with speed \(c - v\) against the motion, wavelength \(\tfrac43 L\): from crest to trough, the orange dots, is half a wavelength, \(\tfrac23 L\). In the third row is the sum, which is the shape of figure 26.19. For \(v = 0\) the waves have the same wavelength and are mirror images, so the sum is a standing wave. For \(v > 0\) the string carries both waves along at speed \(v\), so the first runs at \(c + v\) and the second at \(c - v\). At the same frequency they therefore have different wavelengths, they are no longer mirror images, and the sum is not a standing wave.

The two waves traverse the length of the string and are reflected at the eyelet. How long does it take for the motion to repeat? Figure 26.21 follows one place of the wave, a crest for example, in the plane of position and time, with the numbers of the band of example 26.17 at \(v = 40\) m/s. We draw the axes: position \(x\) horizontally, time \(t\) vertically upwards. The eyelets are at rest, so they are the vertical lines at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and the arrow \(v\) shows where the band runs. The crest of the wave in the direction of motion travels at speed \(c + v\) along the blue line and reaches the second eyelet after the time \(L/(c + v) = 6{,}526\) ms. There it is reflected and returns against the motion at speed \(c - v\) along the orange line, which is steeper because the slower wave needs more time for the same distance: \(L/(c - v) = 13{,}656\) ms. Together this is the round-trip time \(\tau = 20{,}182\) ms. The grey dashed path is the same round trip at \(v = 0\), symmetric and \(2L/c = 17{,}664\) ms long. The motion of the band lengthens the round trip by \(2{,}518\) ms: the way forward becomes shorter by \(2{,}306\) ms, but the way back becomes longer by \(4{,}824\) ms, because the band holds the slower wave back for longer than it carries the faster one. The ratio of the two round trips is \(1/(1 - v^2/c^2) = 1{,}1426\), and a longer round trip means a lower frequency: this is where the factor \(1 - v^2/c^2\) of theorem 26.13 comes from.

Why does the motion repeat after one round trip? The eyelet holds the string, so the deflection there is zero at all times. When a wave arrives at the eyelet, the wave that leaves it must cancel the arriving one exactly at that place, so it leaves with the opposite sign: a crest returns as a trough (lemma 26.10). These are the dots marked \(\cdot(-1)\). One round trip has two reflections and \((-1)\cdot(-1) = 1\): the crest is a crest again, at the same place and travelling in the same direction as at the start. By the same lemma the width of the wave is multiplied by \((c - v)/(c + v)\) at the first reflection and by \((c + v)/(c - v)\) at the second, together by \(1\). This holds for every place of the wave, so after the time \(\tau\) the whole string is in the same state as at the start, and the same state under the same equation gives the same continuation. The theorem gives the same number without this picture.

Corollary 26.16 Period and round-trip time (perioda in čas obhoda)

The period of the first mode equals the round-trip time,

\[\tau = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_1} = \frac{L}{c + v} + \frac{L}{c - v} = \frac{2Lc}{c^2 - v^2} , \tag{26.15}\]

and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau = 2\pi n\), so every mode is periodic with period \(\tau\).

Proof

We must show the equality of the three expressions and the multiple.

  1. \(\omega_1 = (\pi c/L)(1 - v^2/c^2) = \pi(c^2 - v^2)/(cL)\) by equation (26.11), so \(2\pi/\omega_1 = 2cL/(c^2 - v^2)\). This is \(\tau\).
  2. The time of the leg in the direction of motion is \(L/(c + v)\), the time of the leg back is \(L/(c - v)\). With the same denominator, \(L/(c + v) + L/(c - v) = L\big((c - v) + (c + v)\big)/(c^2 - v^2) = 2Lc/(c^2 - v^2)\).
  3. \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\omega_1\), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau = 2\pi n\), and \(k_{\mathrm{n}}\) does not depend on time, so \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t + \tau) = w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t)\).

Source: CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2): Skutch's route by two waves. The calculation is not from the sources. The reflection at a fixed end is treated in more detail in section 26.2.

Example 26.17 Frequencies of the band at different speeds (frekvence traku pri različnih hitrostih)

The band from the start of the section has \(c = \sqrt{\sigma/\rho} = 113{,}23\) m/s with \(\sigma = 100\) MPa and \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ (steel from BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100, as in section 26.1). By theorem 26.13 we have \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(2\pi) = n\,\dfrac{c}{2L}\,(1 - v^2/c^2)\), so:

\(v\) (m/s) \(v/c\) \(f_1\) (Hz) \(f_2\) (Hz) \(f_3\) (Hz) \(k_1\) (1/m)
0 0 56,61 113,23 169,84 0
20 0,177 54,85 109,69 164,54 0,555
40 0,353 49,55 99,10 148,65 1,110
80 0,707 28,35 56,70 85,06 2,220

At \(v = 40\) m/s the two wavelengths of the first mode by corollary 26.15 are \(2Lc/(c - v) = 3{,}092\) m and \(2Lc/(c + v) = 1{,}478\) m. The round-trip time by corollary 26.16 is \(6{,}526\) \(+\) \(13{,}656\) \(=\) \(20{,}182\) ms, equal to \(1/f_1 = 1/49{,}55\) s. For the string at rest \(2L/c = 17{,}664\) ms.

Source: The numbers are our calculation (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 4). The choice of band and speed is not from a source, WM1990 (PDF p. 1) names band saws only as an example of an axially moving material.

Figure 26.22 shows these numbers on curves. We draw the axes: speed \(v\) horizontally, frequency \(f\) vertically, and on them the ticks every 20 m/s, with the speed \(c\) marked separately. The curve of the first mode is \(f_1\), which falls from 56,61 Hz to zero at \(v = c\). The orange dots are the values of the table. The curves \(f_2\) and \(f_3\) have the same shape, twice and three times as high, since \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = n f_1\) at every speed: the ratio \(1 : 2 : 3\) of section 13.2 stays. At \(v = 40\) m/s the frequency \(f_1\) is \(1 - 0{,}8752 = 12{,}5\,\%\) lower than at \(v = 0\), it falls from \(56{,}61\) Hz to \(49{,}55\) Hz, because \(v^2/c^2 = 0{,}125\). \(f_3\) loses the same share, from \(169{,}84\) Hz to \(148{,}65\) Hz, because the factor \(1 - v^2/c^2\) is the same for all modes: it is the longer round trip of figure 26.21. At \(v/c = 0{,}1\), which is 11,3 m/s, the decrease would be only \(1\,\%\).

One more step: we show in numbers that the standing wave of section 13.2 is indeed not a solution, and why. Lemma 26.11 says that there is no real standing mode, but not how large the imbalance is. We take \(\sin(\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_1t)\) with the correct frequency \(\omega_1\) of the band and look at the eyelet.

Example 26.18 The standing wave at the first eyelet (stoječe valovanje na prvem očescu)

At \(x = 0\) we have \(w = 0\) at every time, so \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = 0\) there. For \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\cos\omega_1t\) also \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w = 0\) at \(x = 0\). The mixed derivative, however, is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -(\pi/L)\omega_1\sin\omega_1t\), equal to \(-\pi\omega_1/L\) at \(\omega_1t = \pi/2\). The left side of equation (26.10), which should be zero, is then \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -2\pi v\omega_1/L\). At \(v = 40\) m/s and \(\omega_1 = 311{,}32\) 1/s this is \(-78\,244\) m/s² per unit amplitude. As a scale we take the tension term \(c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in the middle of the string at \(\omega_1 t = 0\), where it is largest: \(c^2(\pi/L)^2 = 126\,533\) m/s² per unit amplitude. The imbalance is thus \(2g(1 - g^2) = 62\,\%\) of this size, with \(g = v/c = 0{,}353\). For small \(v\) it is about \(2g\), that is linear in the speed.

Source: The calculation is ours (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, line 3). WM1990 (PDF p. 4) says only that the axial motion distorts the shapes.

Why is it so? Figure 26.23 shows what happens to a particle that runs through the eyelet. We draw the eyelet and the taut string on the left. The shape of the string at \(\omega t = 0\) has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \pi A/L\) at the eyelet (\(A\) is the drawn deflection in the middle), at \(\omega t = \pi\) the opposite one, and at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is straight. The particle running through the eyelet has a velocity along the tangent, that is the horizontal component \(v\) and the transverse component \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The velocity vectors differ at the three times: the transverse component goes from \(v\pi A/L\) through zero to \(-v\pi A/L\). The transverse velocity of the particles running through the eyelet thus changes in time. The transverse acceleration of a particle is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by equation (26.2), and since \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are zero at the eyelet, the Coriolis term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) remains. By Newton's law something must act on it. The transverse force per unit mass is by equation (26.10) equal to \(c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and for the standing wave it is zero at the eyelet. An acceleration without a force is a contradiction, so the standing wave cannot be a motion of the string at the eyelet.

Having found the modes, we ask whether they are enough: can every free motion of the string be written as a sum of modes? Section 26.6 treats this with the orthogonality of complex modes. First, however, the real limit demands attention, the critical speed \(v = c\), at which all \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) vanish: section 26.4.

26.4 Critical speed and a conserved quantity

In section 26.3 we found the frequencies of the modes of the moving string, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \dfrac{n\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\Big)\) (theorem 26.13). With a higher transport speed \(v\) they all fall, and at \(v = c\) they are all zero. For our band of example A (steel, \(L = 1\) m, \(\sigma = 100\) MPa, \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, \(T = 4500\) N, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s) the first frequency is \(56{,}61\) Hz at \(v = 0\), \(49{,}55\) Hz at \(v = 40\) m/s and \(0\) at \(v = c\). Why exactly at \(c\), and what does it mean for a band that runs so fast? This is the first question of the section. The second is about energy. For the strings of section 13.1 the sum of kinetic and elastic energy stays constant during the motion. Does this hold here too, where the material runs through the eyelets? And if not, does any quantity exist that is conserved and that tells us in the end that the motion stays small?

From history

Archibald and Emslie modelled a belt running from an eccentric pulley to a smooth pulley as a string running through eyelets and excited by the harmonic motion of an eyelet. They found that the natural frequencies decrease with the transport speed and that the moving string, at a sufficiently high speed, becomes unstable by divergence (divergence instability, divergenčna nestabilnost) (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, a work of 1958 by the reference list on PDF p. 21). Why their belt matters to us: the span between two pulleys is our moving string, and their finding is exactly what this section shows, the frequencies of section 26.3 and the speed at which they fail. Swope and Ames investigated with the method of characteristics how a disturbance spreads along such a string when it is excited at an end. They predicted irregular behaviour of the string near the critical speed, that is the speed of waves in the material (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, a work of 1963 by the reference list on PDF p. 21), which for us is \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4).

The story tells two things: at the speed \(c\) something jumps, and this speed is the same number as the wave speed in a string at rest. Let us see why. We stay with the model of section 26.1: the moving string (definition 26.3) of length \(L\), mass \(\mu\) per unit length, tension \(T\) and transport speed \(v > 0\) in the eyelets, which stand at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), with the equation

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} \tag{26.16}\]

from theorem 26.4. By idealization 4 the slope is small, \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\). In this section the letter \(T\) is always the tension force, not the kinetic energy of chapters 8 and 9, and \(v\) is the transport speed, not the deflection.

26.4.1 When the tension is just enough

Let us look first at the simplest possible motion: a string whose shape does not change. Like water in a steady channel: the shape of the channel rests and the material flows along it. Can this be a motion of the moving string? The answer is given by the force on a piece of material, so we build figure 26.25.

In the left panel we take the axis \(x\) and on it the string, held in the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). We have given it a resting shape \(w(x) = h\sin(\pi x/L)\), where \(h\) is the largest deflection. The string runs through the eyelets with speed \(v\), which in the left panel is half of \(c\), so the arrow is half of the one in the right panel. Take the piece of material that is at this moment over the interval from \(a\) to \(b\), that is the same material points that we follow as they run (section 26.1). What acts on it? The neighbouring parts of the string pull the piece with the force \(T\) along the tangent, each force starting at the point where it acts. The horizontal components of these two forces are opposite and cancel, the vertical ones add up to one force \(T\sigma\) with \(\sigma = w_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\). Here idealization 4 enters. The vertical component of the force \(T\) along the tangent is \(T\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle of the tangent to the axis \(x\), and we write \(T w_{\mathrm{x}} = T\tan\theta\). At a slope of \(0{,}005\) the numbers \(\tan\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) differ by \(0{,}00125\) %, so we may. At a slope of \(0{,}1\) the difference would already be \(0{,}5\) % and the force \(T\sigma\) wrong by that much. The number \(\sigma\) is negative, because the slope decreases along the piece (the string bulges upwards), so this force points down. What is it equal to? By Newton's second law the sum of forces on a body is mass times acceleration, which for a piece of material is written by equation (26.4) of section 26.1. Since the shape does not change, \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), and by lemma 26.1 the acceleration of each material point is only the centripetal one, \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\): the point runs along a curved curve with speed \(v\) and something must pull it towards the centre of curvature. The sum of these accelerations along the piece, multiplied by the mass, is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \mu v^2\sigma\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55). This is the orange arrow, also pointing down. We draw the two arrows from two different points of the piece, so that they do not overlap.

Each arrow has its role. The blue one is what the piece gets from the neighbouring parts, the orange one what the piece needs to stay on the steady curve. In the left panel the blue is four times the orange. So the piece would get more than it needs: the surplus \(T\sigma - \mu v^2\sigma = (T - \mu v^2)\sigma\) would pull it towards the straight line and the shape would not stay. On the band of example A and a piece from \(0{,}3\) to \(0{,}7\) m with \(h = 1{,}5\) mm the blue arrow is the same at every speed, \(T\sigma = -24{,}93\) N, while the orange one \(\mu v^2\sigma\) grows with the square of the speed:

\(v\) (m/s) \(v/c\) \(T\sigma\) (N) \(\mu v^2\sigma\) (N) surplus \((T - \mu v^2)\sigma\) (N)
\(40\) \(0{,}353\) \(-24{,}93\) \(-3{,}11\) \(-21{,}82\)
\(56{,}61\) (left panel) \(0{,}5\) \(-24{,}93\) \(-6{,}23\) \(-18{,}70\)
\(101{,}90\) \(0{,}9\) \(-24{,}93\) \(-20{,}19\) \(-4{,}74\)
\(113{,}23\) (right panel) \(1\) \(-24{,}93\) \(-24{,}93\) \(0\)

As \(v\) grows towards \(c\) the surplus falls to zero. In the right panel the string runs with speed \(v = c\) (the longer arrow \(v\)), the same piece feels the same tension forces and their sum \(T\sigma\), and the needed force is \(\mu c^2\sigma = T\sigma\), because \(\mu c^2 = T\) (definition 13.4). The two arrows are equal: the tension is exactly enough for the material points to run along the curve, and there is no surplus that would straighten the shape. Is this shape special? It is not: the other shapes below the right panel have the same property. The lemma below states this exactly.

Lemma 26.19 Arbitrary steady shape at the speed \(c\) (poljubna stalna oblika pri hitrosti \(c\))

Let \(v = c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) and let \(f : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a twice continuously differentiable function with \(f(0) = f(L) = 0\). Then every such shape \(w(x, t) = f(x)\) is a moving string (definition 26.3). For \(v \ne c\) the only steady shape \(w(x, t) = f(x)\) that is a moving string is \(f = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the function satisfies equation (26.16) exactly when \((T - \mu v^2) f'' = 0\), and that the claim follows from this.

  1. For the steady shape \(w = f(x)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), hence also \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tx}} = 0\). The derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = f'\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = f''\) are continuous, as definition 26.3 requires, and the boundary conditions \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) are satisfied.
  2. For \(w = f(x)\) equation (26.16) is rewritten as \(\mu v^2 f'' = T f''\), so \((T - \mu v^2)\,f'' = 0\). For the piece over \([a, b]\) this is the comparison of the blue and the orange arrow: the integral of \(T f''\) along the piece is \(T\sigma\), the integral of \(\mu v^2 f''\) is \(\mu v^2\sigma\).
  3. If \(v = c\), then \(T - \mu v^2 = T - \mu c^2 = 0\) by definition 13.4, and the two arrows are equally long on every piece of every shape. The equation holds for every \(f\), because the connection with the equation of the piece (26.4) is an equivalence by theorem 26.4.
  4. If \(v \ne c\), then \(T - \mu v^2 \ne 0\) (in the left panel the arrows are not equal), so \(f'' = 0\) everywhere, hence \(f'\) is constant and \(f\) is a straight line (corollary 1.86 twice). From \(f(0) = f(L) = 0\) it follows that \(f = 0\).

Source: WM1990, appendix, section 1 (PDF p. 6): every natural frequency of the travelling string is zero at \(v = 1\) (dimensionless, that is \(v = c\)), the critical speed is \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 1\). The claim about an arbitrary steady shape and its proof are ours.

What does the claim say? At \(v = c\) we have infinitely many resting equilibria, each with its own shape. At \(v \neq c\) a string at rest is only straight. So the moving string at \(v = c\) loses a property that the string without flow has: the string of section 13.1 always has, after we displace it, a force that returns it towards the straight line. This restoring is measured by \(T - \mu v^2\), as we saw in the surplus of the blue arrow over the orange one. Let us test it on the band. At \(v = 40\) m/s and \(w(x) = 1{,}5\text{ mm}\cdot\sin(\pi x/L)\) the residual of the equation \((\mu v^2 - T)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) has the largest value \(58{,}31\) N/m, at \(v = 0{,}9c\) only \(12{,}66\) N/m, at \(v = c\) it is zero (recomputed in num-04.out).

Definition 26.20 Critical speed of the moving string (kritična hitrost gibajoče se strune)

The critical speed (kritična hitrost) of a moving string with mass \(\mu\) per unit length and tension \(T\) is the number

\[v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = c , \tag{26.17}\]

in m/s, that is the wave speed of definition 13.4. The transport speed \(v > 0\) is subcritical (podkritična) for \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\), critical for \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) and supercritical (nadkritična) for \(v > v_{\mathrm{c}}\).

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2 and appendix, section 1, PDF p. 6 (string: \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 1\) in dimensionless form), CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (Swope and Ames: the critical speed is the characteristic wave speed in the material). The form as a definition is ours.

The word critical comes from the Greek krisis, which means decision or break. The name fits, because at this speed the behaviour of the string jumps: below it every resting shape except the straight line has a surplus of force, at it none, above it \(T - \mu v^2\) is negative. On the piece of the table the orange arrow would at \(v = 1{,}2c\) be \(1{,}44\) times as long as the blue one: the flow needs \(-35{,}90\) N, the tension gives \(-24{,}93\) N, and the shortfall of \(10{,}97\) N points away from the straight line. What follows from this at a supercritical speed we do not claim here, because the model with two fixed eyelets is no longer good for \(v > c\). The reason is the two waves of section 26.2. Every motion is a sum \(F\big(x - (c + v)t\big) + G\big(x + (c - v)t\big)\) (lemma 26.6, which holds for every \(v \ge 0\)). For \(v < c\) the second wave runs against the flow with speed \(c - v\) and carries into the span what the eyelet at \(x = L\) determines. For \(v > c\) the number \(c - v\) is negative: the flow carries this wave forward too, with speed \(v - c\), like a swimmer who swims slower than the river runs. Nothing then returns into the span from the eyelet at \(x = L\). The deflection at \(x = L\) is already determined by what arrives from the left, so the condition \(w(L, t) = 0\) can no longer be prescribed. On the band of example A at \(v = 1{,}2c\) both waves would run forward, with speeds \(249{,}1\) and \(22{,}6\) m/s. WM1990 (PDF p. 2) also requires the speed to be subcritical, as will we in the theorems that require \(v < c\). The critical speed of the band of example A is \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c = 113{,}23\) m/s. Above it this model does not describe the band.

From history

Archibald and Emslie found the divergence instability at a sufficiently high speed in the story above, and WM1990 (PDF p. 6, appendix) shows that at \(v = c\) every natural frequency of the string vanishes. At a zero frequency the difference between oscillation and static deformation is lost, and this is the lemma above: the string stays in every shape. Hence divergence (divergence): the deflection does not oscillate but stays.

The story showed where the name divergence comes from. Let us return to the model and to the second question: energy.

26.4.2 The conserved quantity

For the strings of section 13.1 the sum \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \tfrac12 T\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) is constant during the motion: the first half is the kinetic, the second the elastic energy. Let us try the same here. The kinetic energy of the material is no longer only \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\), because the material runs. In figure 26.26 the top shows a piece of string and on it a material point. The string itself moves up with the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the point also slides along it with the speed \(v\) over the slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which lifts it with the velocity \(v w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The transverse velocity of the point is the sum of the two, \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (lemma 26.1), so the kinetic energy per unit length is \(\tfrac12\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\). When we expand the square we get three parts, shown at the bottom: the square with side \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) splits into the square \(w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\), two rectangles \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\,v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the square \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\). Summed over the span, they are called by chapter 8 (theorem 8.97) \(T_2\), \(T_1\) and \(T_0\):

\[T_2 = \tfrac12\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad T_1 = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad T_0 = \tfrac12\mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.18}\]

where \(T_2\) is the part quadratic in \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_1\) the mixed part, linear in \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), and \(T_0\) the part without the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\). The elastic energy is \(V = \tfrac12 T\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). Why this expansion at all? Because the energy integral \(\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 + V\) of chapter 8 (theorem 8.124) warns us that with time-dependent constraints it is this combination that is conserved, not \(T + V\). Does this hold here too? Theorem 8.124 is proved for a system with finitely many coordinates, and strings have infinitely many, so we do not use it but check the same idea directly. The test is simple: \(\mathcal{E}^*\) should be a conserved quantity (definition 8.119).

From history

Chubachi was the first to discuss the periodicity of energy transfer in a moving string (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, a work of 1958 by PDF p. 21). Miranker discussed the energy of the moving string and from the equation without excitation derived an expression for the rate of change of energy, which is usually not zero (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, year 1960 by PDF p. 21). Wickert and Mote pointed out that this expression describes only the local rate of change, since it does not account for the flow of energy through the supports (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, a work of 1989 by PDF p. 22). Miranker also showed that there is another functional that is constant for the moving string (CHEN2005, PDF p. 7), while the energy of the span changes. We shall check all this: first the constant functional, then the expression for the energy.

The story showed two things: the energy of the span is not constant, something else is. Now we prove it.

Theorem 26.21 Conserved quantity of the moving string (ohranjena količina gibajoče strune)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3) and

\[\mathcal{E}^*(t) = \tfrac12\int_0^L\Big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, t)^2 + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(x, t)^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = T_2 - T_0 + V . \tag{26.19}\]

Then \(\mathcal{E}^*(t)\) is constant for every \(t \ge 0\).

Proof

We must show that the derivative \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime}(t)\) is zero, that is, that the line is horizontal. We differentiate under the integral. The term with \(w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is transformed by integration by parts so that it can be compared with the equation of motion. What then remains of the Coriolis term is a derivative in \(x\) and vanishes at the eyelets.

  1. Since \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) are continuous, by lemma 4.19 we differentiate under the integral: \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime}(t) = \int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. Since \(w(0, t) = 0\) for every \(t\), we have \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(0, t) = 0\), and likewise \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\): the eyelets stand still.
  3. By theorem 1.131 \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = w_{\mathrm{tx}}\), and integration by parts (corollary 3.56) with \(f = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(g = w_{\mathrm{t}}\) gives \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\big]_0^L - \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), because the eyelets make the square bracket zero by step 2.
  4. Steps 1 and 3 give \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  5. Equation (26.16) is equivalent to \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). Insert into step 4: \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = -2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\mu v\int_0^L \big(w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big)_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \((w_{\mathrm{t}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}} = 2 w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\).
  6. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55) the last integral is \(\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\) by step 2. So \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\), and by corollary 1.86 \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is constant. On the band this is the horizontal blue line in figure 26.28.

Source: CHEN2005 (33), PDF p. 7 (Miranker): \(S_{\mathrm{E}}[V] = \int_0^L \tfrac12\big[\rho V_{\mathrm{T}}^2 + (P - \rho c^2)V_{\mathrm{X}}^2\big]\mathrm{d}X\) is constant for the moving string. The proof by steps and the connection with theorem 8.124 are not from the source.

What does the theorem say? The mixed term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) in the equation of motion (the Coriolis one, section 26.1) turns out in step 5 to be the \(x\)-derivative of the square of \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), which is zero at the eyelets. The velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at the eyelets because they stand still (idealization 6). The power of the Coriolis force on the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(-2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), is therefore zero, and a force without power does not change \(\mathcal{E}^*\). The connection with \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) tells what happened to \(T_0\): the kinetic energy of the flow, \(\tfrac12\mu v^2\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), reduces the stiffness by \(\mu v^2\). Since \(T_0\) has no velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), it acts as a negative elastic energy. Why? \(V\) and \(T_0\) are multiples of the same integral, \(V = \tfrac12 T\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(T_0 = \tfrac12\mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), so in \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) they merge into \(\tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). This is the elastic energy of a string with the tension \(T - \mu v^2\) in place of \(T\). On the band this is \(3938{,}4\) N of \(4500\) N at \(v = 40\) m/s (\(12{,}5\) % less), and only \(855{,}0\) N at \(v = 0{,}9c\) (\(81\) % less). This is the surplus of figure 26.25: the tension must spend a part of its force on making the material points run along a curved path, and only \(T - \mu v^2 = \mu(c^2 - v^2)\) is left for the return towards the straight line.

Let us test the conserved quantity on the band. For the first mode, \(w = a\sin(\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_1 t + k_1 x)\) with amplitude \(a = 1{,}5\) mm, \(\omega_1 = 311{,}32\) 1/s and \(k_1 = \pi v/(cL)\), at \(v = 40\) m/s (theorem 26.13) the largest slope \(a\pi/L = 4{,}71\cdot 10^{-3}\) matches the limit of idealization 4. A computation with NumPy gives \(\mathcal{E}^* = 21{,}86\) mJ at each of \(200001\) times spread evenly over one period (period \(\tau = 2\pi/\omega_1 = 20{,}18\) ms), the difference between the largest and the smallest value is below \(10^{-12}\) mJ. The residual of the equation of motion for this mode is below \(3\cdot 10^{-14}\) N/m.

Corollary 26.22 Boundedness of the motion below the critical speed (omejenost gibanja pod kritično hitrostjo)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3) with \(0 < v < c\), initial displacement \(w_0(x) = w(x, 0)\) and initial velocity \(w_1(x) = w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0)\). Then for every \(t \ge 0\) the bounds hold

\[\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le \int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \frac{\mu}{T - \mu v^2}\int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le \frac{T - \mu v^2}{\mu}\int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.20}\]

and for every \(x \in [0, L]\) we have \(|w(x, t)| \le \sqrt{L}\,\Big(\int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \dfrac{\mu}{T - \mu v^2}\int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x\Big)^{1/2}\).

Proof

We must show that from the constancy of \(\mathcal{E}^*\) and from both of its terms being nonnegative each of the three inequalities follows. The displacement is obtained from the slope by the fundamental theorem and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

  1. By theorem 26.21 \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is constant, so \(\mathcal{E}^*(t) = \mathcal{E}^*(0) = \tfrac12\mu\int w_1^2 + \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_0'^2\).
  2. Since \(v < c\), we have \(T - \mu v^2 > 0\), so both terms in (26.19) are nonnegative: the curve lies above zero. Hence each of them is at most \(\mathcal{E}^*(0)\): \(\tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 \le \mathcal{E}^*(0)\) and \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 \le \mathcal{E}^*(0)\).
  3. Division by \(\tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\) or \(\tfrac12\mu\) and insertion of \(\mathcal{E}^*(0)\) from step 1 give the first two inequalities. The right-hand side of the first is the blackwhite line in figure 26.27, the left-hand side the curve below it.
  4. Since \(w(0, t) = 0\) (the string starts at the eyelet at height zero), by the fundamental theorem the deflection at \(x\) is the sum of the slopes from the eyelet: \(w(x, t) = \int_0^x w_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t)\,\mathrm{d}s\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (lemma 6.19) for the product of the functions \(1\) and \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}|\) we have \(|w(x, t)| \le \sqrt{x}\,\big(\int_0^x w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)^{1/2} \le \sqrt{L}\,\big(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)^{1/2}\), and the first inequality gives the third.

Source: The claim is ours, the idea is the same Dirichlet criterion as in chapter 8 (theorem 8.131): a conserved quantity that is positive definite bounds the motion. WM1990 (PDF p. 2) requires a subcritical speed, because then the stiffness operator is positive definite.

What do the inequalities say? The motion stays bounded in energy: the initial data determine a bound that it never exceeds. On the band with \(a = 1{,}5\) mm and \(v = 40\) m/s (\(T - \mu v^2 = 3938{,}4\) N) figure 26.27 shows this for the first mode. The horizontal axis is time up to the period \(\tau = 20{,}18\) ms, the vertical one \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) in \(10^{-6}\) m. The orange curve is this integral during the motion. It starts at \(\int w_0'^2 = 8{,}24\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, which is the first term of the bound. The second term of the bound is \(\mu\int w_1^2/(T - \mu v^2) = 2{,}87\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, and the sum of the two is the blackwhite line at \(1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m. The curve comes close to it twice in one period, at most up to \(1{,}072\cdot 10^{-5}\) m, and does not reach it: the difference is \(0{,}38\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, the bound is \(3{,}5\) % too high.

The bound for the displacement is \(3{,}33\) mm at an amplitude of \(1{,}5\) mm. At \(v = 0{,}9c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = 855{,}0\) N, so the coefficient of the second term is \(5{,}26\) times larger than at \(v = 0\) (\(1/(1 - 0{,}81)\)), and the sum of the bound is again \(1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m (for the first mode with amplitude \(a\) the bound is \(a^2\pi^2/(2L)\) at every speed \(v < c\), that is \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) of the resting shape \(a\sin(\pi x/L)\), recomputed with SymPy), the real maximum \(1{,}066\cdot 10^{-5}\) m. The bound does not say that the slope is small everywhere, because \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) bounds the average and not the largest values, so idealization 4 still has to be checked on the solution.

Where does the bound fail? Look back at lemma 26.19. At \(v = c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = 0\), and \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is zero for every resting shape \(w = f(x)\), even if \(f \neq 0\): the case \(f = 1{,}5\text{ mm}\cdot\sin(\pi x/L)\), the shape in the right panel of figure 26.25, has \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m and \(\mathcal{E}^* = 0\). The conserved quantity then tells nothing about the slope, and the bound (26.20) has a zero in the denominator. For \(v > c\) it is worse. The same shape gives \(\mathcal{E}^* = \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 < 0\), at \(v = 1{,}2c\) it is \(-10{,}99\) mJ (the model is here outside the limit of the subcritical speed, the number only shows that \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is no longer nonnegative). The theorem still holds, since its proof does not require \(v < c\), but the corollary does not.

26.4.3 The energy of the span is not conserved

What remains is the second question: what about the sum of kinetic and elastic energy of the span, that is what everyone would expect? Let us call it

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \tfrac12\int_0^L\Big(\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\big)^2 + T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = T_2 + T_1 + T_0 + V . \tag{26.21}\]

Here we have left out the constant part \(\tfrac12\mu v^2 L\) of the kinetic energy of the flow along the axis, which does not show in the derivative. Comparison with (26.19) tells that \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^* = T_1 + 2T_0\), which is the difference between \(T + V\) and \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) of theorem 8.124. If \(T_1 + 2T_0\) changes during the motion, \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) cannot be constant. On the band of example A at \(v = 40\) m/s and \(a = 1{,}5\) mm we draw figure 26.28 as follows: the axis \(t\) runs to the period of the first mode \(\tau\) \(= 20{,}18\) ms and the vertical axis shows energy in mJ. The blue line is \(\mathcal{E}^* = 21{,}9\) mJ, which is constant, and the orange curve is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\), which oscillates between \(25{,}6\) and \(30{,}6\) mJ, the ratio of the largest and the smallest value is \(1{,}197\). Two cycles per period \(\tau\) arise because \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) contains squares of \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which repeat after half an oscillation.

Why does \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) change? The answer is given by the work of forces, which we draw in figure 26.29. The span is not closed: material runs through it and the neighbouring parts of the string pull it at the eyelets. We take the string of the first mode of the band at \(t = 0\) (\(a = 1{,}5\) mm, \(v = 40\) m/s, slope strongly exaggerated) between the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). Let us look first at the piece of material that is at this moment over \([0, L]\). At its ends the neighbours pull it with the force \(T\) along the tangent, forward at \(x = L\) and backward at \(x = 0\), and the power of a force is force times the velocity of the point in its direction. At an eyelet \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) and the material point has the transverse velocity \(v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (lemma 26.1), these are the blue arrows at \(x = 0\) and at \(x = L\). The transverse component of the force is \(T w_{\mathrm{x}}\), the thin vertical arrow next to each force. In the model of small slopes the lengthwise component of the force, \(T\), and the lengthwise velocity, \(v\), are the same at both eyelets, so the lengthwise parts of the power, \(T v\) at \(x = L\) and \(-T v\) at \(x = 0\), cancel and the transverse ones remain. At \(x = L\) the transverse force and the transverse velocity point the same way, the power is \(T v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)^2\), on the band \(+0{,}791\) W. At \(x = 0\) the force is reversed, the power is \(-T v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t)^2\), on the band \(-3{,}997\) W. The energy of the piece of material changes by the theorem on work and energy with the sum \(T v\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L\). But the span is not this piece: in a short time \(h\) the piece moves by \(v h\) along \(x\), at the left end of the span material enters with energy per unit length \(\hat e(0, t)\), at the right end it leaves with \(\hat e(L, t)\). At an eyelet \(\hat e = \tfrac12(\mu v^2 + T)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \tfrac12\mu v^2\), since \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\). The energy of the span therefore changes by the work of forces minus the energy that the material carries away: \(v\,\hat e\) at the right end and brings in at the left. The constant \(\tfrac12\mu v^2\) cancels, and without it the material on the band brings in \(2{,}248\) W and carries away \(0{,}445\) W. What remains is stated by the next lemma.

Lemma 26.23 Rate of change of the energy of the span (sprememba energije razpona)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3). Then \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) of (26.21) is differentiable and

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'(t) = \frac{v}{2}\,\big(T - \mu v^2\big)\,\Big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)^2 - w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t)^2\Big) . \tag{26.22}\]
Proof

We must show that the difference \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^*\) differentiates into the right-hand side, because \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\) by theorem 26.21.

  1. By expanding the square in (26.21), \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^* = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. By lemma 4.19, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{tt}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. The last integral is \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\) by the fundamental theorem and by step 2 of the proof of theorem 26.21 (the eyelets stand still).
  4. From equation (26.16), \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Hence \(\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{tt}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the last integral is \(\tfrac12\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\) by the fundamental theorem, the difference of the squared slopes at the eyelets, because \((w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}} = 2 w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  5. The derivative of step 1 is by steps 2 to 4 equal to \(v\Big(-2\mu v\int w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} + \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\Big) + 2\mu v^2\int w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). The terms with the integral cancel (\(-2\mu v^2 + 2\mu v^2 = 0\)), what remains is \(\tfrac{v}{2}(T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\). Since \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\), this is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'\). It depends only on the slopes at the eyelets, and on the band at \(t = 0\) it is the blue bar.

Source: CHEN2005 (32), PDF p. 7 (Renshaw and others, a work of 1998 by the reference list on PDF p. 22): \(\mathrm{d}E_{\mathrm{E}}/\mathrm{d}T = \tfrac12 c(P - \rho c^2)\,(V_{\mathrm{X}})^2\big|_0^L\), and (28), PDF p. 6 (Lagrangian piece of material): \(\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}T = P c\,(V_{\mathrm{X}})^2\big|_0^L\). The proof by steps is ours, a similar explanation with the flow of energy through the eyelets is in CHEN2005, PDF p. 6.

Let us check on numbers. If we add the work of forces and the flow of energy, as described before the lemma, we get the same as the right-hand side of (26.22). On the band with \(a = 1{,}5\) mm and \(v = 40\) m/s at time \(t = 0\) the slopes are \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(0) = 4{,}712\cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(L) = -2{,}096\cdot 10^{-3}\). In the lower part of figure 26.29 we measure downwards from the zero line. The power of the tension forces is \(T v\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = 0{,}791 - 3{,}997 = -3{,}206\) W, the grey bar. The energy carried out minus carried in is \(v\,\tfrac12(T + \mu v^2)\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = 0{,}445 - 2{,}248 = -1{,}803\) W, the orange bar. The difference is \(-1{,}403\) W, the blue bar between the ends of the first two, and \(\tfrac{v}{2}(T - \mu v^2)\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = -1{,}403\) W, and the numerical derivative \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'\) from a central difference \(-1{,}403\) W. At \(t = 2{,}523\) ms we have \(-1{,}592 - (-0{,}896) = -0{,}697\) W and the right-hand side \(-0{,}697\) W. At \(v = 0{,}9c\) at \(t = 0\) we have \(-0{,}972 - (-0{,}880) = -0{,}092\) W, and the right-hand side and the derivative are equal to it. So the energy of the span changes although there is no damping: material runs through the eyelets and the flow of energy is not zero, because the squares of the slopes at the ends differ: the flow would vanish only for \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(0)^2 = w_{\mathrm{x}}(L)^2\), which does not hold for the band in general. CHEN2005 (PDF p. 6) says the same: the moving string is nonconservative in this sense, although the equation has no dissipative term, and Hamilton's principle holds because the forces are potential.

What does this section show and what returns? The critical speed \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\) is not an ansatz but the point where we have infinitely many resting shapes, where the conserved quantity loses positive definiteness and where all frequencies vanish (lemma 26.19, theorem 26.21, corollary 26.22, theorem 26.13). Below it the motion is bounded in energy. The energy of the span is not conserved (lemma 26.23), because material carries energy at the eyelets and because the tension force does work on the moving material. The mixed part \(T_1\) of (26.18) is not zero, yet it is absent from the constant functional: the force \(-2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) it brings does no work over the span, as the Coriolis force in a rotating frame. Its name, the matrix that writes it and the eigenvalues of the discrete system we shall meet in section 26.5. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) we claim nothing, nor whether the motion dies out in time, because the model has no damping (chapter 20).

26.5 Gyroscopic systems

We found the exact modes of the moving string in section 26.3 with an ansatz containing a phase factor. For a belt with bending stiffness (section 26.7), with finite elements (section 26.8) and in rotating machines (chapter 24) there is no such closed formula, but we do have finitely many coordinates. So in this section we look at what system of ordinary equations we get from the moving string if we describe it with finitely many sines, and at what we can prove about such a system. First we put the sines into the equation and obtain three matrices. One of them is skew-symmetric and is called gyroscopic (žiroskopska). Then we show that gyroscopic forces do no work, that for a positive definite stiffness matrix every eigenvalue is purely imaginary, and, on an example, where this condition fails. We finish with numbers for the band of example A and with the question of why the sines converge poorly at high speed (figures 26.30 to 26.38).

26.5.1 Sines in the equation of the moving string

Take the string of section 26.1: length between the eyelets \(L\), mass per length \(\mu\), tension \(T\), axial speed \(v\), transverse displacement \(w(x, t)\), and the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) fixed in space (the ends of the rest lines in figure 26.30 below). By theorem 26.4, \(\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). We move the term \(\mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) to the right-hand side and obtain

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - S\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 , \qquad S = T - \mu v^2 . \tag{26.23}\]

The letter \(S\) is in this section only an abbreviation for a force in newtons. Since \(S/\mu = c^2 - v^2\) with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4), it is positive for \(v < c\). We take only \(v < c\). Why we may: the band of example A runs at \(v = 40\) m/s with \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, far below \(c\). When not: at \(v = c\), \(S = 0\) and the string has no transverse stiffness left (section 26.4). What the assumption does to the result: because \(S > 0\) the stiffness matrix below is positive definite, and point 2 of theorem 26.27 rests on this.

We look for the solution in a family we already know. The sines \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(x) = \sin(j\pi x/L)\) are zero at both eyelets, and by corollary 13.13 there are enough of them to approximate uniformly any smooth shape that is zero at the eyelets, and we take the first \(N\) of them (figure 26.30). We try

\[w(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(x) , \tag{26.24}\]

where \(q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\) are unknown functions of time in metres. Such a sum does not satisfy equation (26.23) exactly. What a finite \(N\) costs is shown by the numbers at the end of the section: with one sine the first frequency of the band of example A is \(6{,}89\,\%\) too high, with eight it is \(0{,}01\,\%\) too high (the blackwhite curve in figure 26.38). So we use the same requirement as the Galerkin method (definition 6.42): the residual of the equation, that is the left-hand side \(r\) of equation (26.23), must at every instant be orthogonal to every function \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(i = 1, \dots, N\), which means \(\int_0^L r\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). In the static problem the definition applied this requirement to a bilinear form, here we apply it to the residual of the dynamic equation. By lemma 6.43 it suffices to write it for the \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) alone, because the residual is linear in \(w\).

What will be in the equation we get? Figure 26.30 shows what we shall need. We draw the first four shapes \(\varphi_1\) to \(\varphi_4\), each with its own rest line between the eyelets. In between we draw a dashed midpoint \(L/2\). The shapes with odd \(j\) (blue) are mirror images of themselves about the midpoint, the shapes with even \(j\) (orange) are mirrored about the midpoint and change sign. For our computation what matters is what happens to the derivative: the slope of a mirror-symmetric curve has opposite signs on the two sides of the midpoint, so the derivative of an even function is an odd function and conversely.

Lemma 26.24 Galerkin system of the moving string (Galerkinov sistem gibajoče strune)

Let the string be that of theorem 26.4 with the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and let \(v < c\). Let \(w\) be as in equation (26.24) with the sine shapes \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \sin(j\pi x/L)\), and the entries \(G_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the values of the matrix below. The residual of equation (26.23) is orthogonal to \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{N}}\) at every instant exactly when

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0 , \tag{26.25}\]

where \(\vek q = (q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{N}})^\T\) and

\[M_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\mu L}{2}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad K_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{S\,j^2\pi^2}{2L}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int_0^L \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \begin{cases} \dfrac{4\mu v\,i\,j}{i^2 - j^2} & i + j \text{ odd} , \\[1ex] 0 & i + j \text{ even} . \end{cases} \tag{26.26}\]
Proof

We must show what each term of the residual becomes after integration with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\).

  1. The residual is \(r = \mu w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - S\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (equation (26.23)). From equation (26.24), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \ddot q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}''\), since the sine shapes \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) are differentiable and the sum is finite.
  2. For the shapes the product of sines is \(\sin a\,\sin b = \tfrac12\big(\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)\big)\). For \(a = i\pi x/L\) and \(b = j\pi x/L\) the integral \(\int_0^L\cos(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is zero for integer \(m \ne 0\) (the integral of a cosine over whole half-periods). Hence \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{L}{2}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'' = -(j\pi/L)^2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) also \(-\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}''\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = (j\pi/L)^2\,\tfrac L2\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. For the term with the mixed derivative (the curve \(\varphi_2\varphi_1'\) is an example), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}' = (j\pi/L)\cos(j\pi x/L)\). We use \(\sin a\,\cos b = \tfrac12\big(\sin(a + b) + \sin(a - b)\big)\) and \(\int_0^L\sin(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{L}{m\pi}\big(1 - (-1)^m\big)\) for an integer \(m \ne 0\), which is \(2L/(m\pi)\) for odd and zero for even \(m\).
  4. For \(i + j\) even, \(i + j\) and \(i - j\) are both even (or \(i - j = 0\), where \(\sin 0 = 0\)), so \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). For \(i = 1\), \(j = 3\) figure 26.31 shows it: the areas above the line and below it cancel. For \(i + j\) odd both are odd and \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{j\pi}{L}\cdot\tfrac12\Big(\tfrac{2L}{(i + j)\pi} + \tfrac{2L}{(i - j)\pi}\Big) = j\Big(\tfrac{1}{i + j} + \tfrac{1}{i - j}\Big) = \dfrac{2ij}{i^2 - j^2}\). For \(i = 2\), \(j = 1\) this is \(4/3\), the sum of two equal areas in figure 26.31.
  5. Row \(i\) of the condition \(\int_0^L r\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) is, by steps 2 to 4, equal to \(\mu\tfrac L2\,\ddot q_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} G_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} + S\,i^2\pi^2/(2L)\,q_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). This is equation (26.25), in which the entries \(G_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are the values of row \(i\) of the matrix. The converse holds because the steps are equalities.

Source: The procedure is ours: the sines after section 13.2, the residual requirement after definition 6.42. WM1990 (PDF p. 6) mentions the choice of the eigenfunctions of the string at rest as expansion functions for moving systems. The numbers in equation (26.26) are checked by quadrature in num-05.py.

The reason \(\mat G\) has entries only for \(i + j\) odd is shown by figures 26.30 and 26.31. The integrand \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) is the product of the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the slope \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\), and the slope has the opposite symmetry to the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\). We draw the product \(\varphi_1\varphi_3'\) between the eyelets, a case of equal parity. Across the midpoint the curve is mirrored and changes sign: the areas \(+0{,}19\) and \(+1{,}69\) above the line have their twins \(-1{,}69\) and \(-0{,}19\) below the line on the other side of the midpoint, so the integral is zero. Below it we draw the product \(\varphi_2\varphi_1'\), a case of different parity. This curve is its own mirror image about the midpoint, the areas \(+0{,}67\) on the left and on the right add up to \(4/3\), which is the value \(2ij/(i^2 - j^2)\) of step 4 for \(i = 2\), \(j = 1\). So the first shape does not couple to itself but couples to the second. Physically: motion in the first shape produces, through the term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), a force in the second shape, because the slope of the first shape (the derivative of an even shape is odd) has the same symmetry as the second shape.

Figure 26.32 shows all the values for \(N = 4\). We draw the frame of the matrix with row \(i\) and column \(j\) and write in the values \(4ij/(i^2 - j^2)\) from equation (26.26). The cells with zeros are where \(i + j\) is even, so a checkerboard. On the diagonal are only zeros, because \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,[\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^2]_0^L = 0\) (the eyelet is fixed). Every element below the diagonal is the negative of its mirror element above it: \(G_{21} = 2\mu v \cdot 4/3 = +2{,}67\,\mu v\) (the area \(4/3\) of figure 26.31) and \(G_{12} = -2{,}67\,\mu v\). This is no accident, since integration by parts with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}(0) = \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}(L) = 0\) gives \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}'\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and swapping \(i\) and \(j\) changes the sign. It is exactly this property of the matrix that carries the rest of the section.

26.5.2 The gyroscopic matrix and the gyroscopic system

System (26.25) has the same structure as the system of GR (example 1.8, PDF p. 54 to 56), where a mass on springs in a wheel turning with constant angular velocity is described in the coordinates of the wheel. GR writes there that the equation of motion acquires a term \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\), that this term belongs to the Coriolis or gyroscopic forces, and that these are apparent forces, because they arise only from the description in a moving frame (GR PDF p. 47 and 56, remark 1.1). The name gyroscopic comes from the gyroscope, a device with a spinning wheel (Greek gyros, circle), since such forces show up precisely in spinning bodies. Why GR uses it is not written, so this is the name in use and not our conclusion. In our string nothing spins. The term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is the one that section 26.1 calls Coriolis, because in the acceleration of a particle it arises from the simultaneous motion along the string with speed \(v\) and the changing slope. In the coordinates \(q_{\mathrm{j}}\) it has the same property as for the wheel: it is linear in the velocities \(\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\) and has skew-symmetric coefficients. So we keep the same name for the matrix that is skew-symmetric, as figure 26.32 shows.

Definition 26.25 Gyroscopic matrix and gyroscopic system (žiroskopska matrika in žiroskopski sistem)

Let \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) be real symmetric \(n \times n\) matrices with \(\mat M\) positive definite (definition 6.27). A real \(n \times n\) matrix \(\mat G\) is gyroscopic (skew-symmetric, poševno simetrična) if \(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\), that is \(G_{\mathrm{ji}} = -G_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (a pair of values across the diagonal) and \(G_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\) (the diagonal). The system of ordinary differential equations for \(\vek q : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^n\),

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0 , \tag{26.27}\]

is a (linear conservative) gyroscopic system. The matrix \(\mat G\) is called the gyroscopic matrix and the vector \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) the gyroscopic forces.

Source: GR (2.242), PDF p. 137, and (1.39), (1.40), PDF p. 47, where the coefficients of the gyroscopic forces are skew-symmetric. The matrix \(\mat G\) has nothing to do with the shear modulus \(G\) (a scalar), which it does not meet.

By lemma 26.24 the Galerkin system of the moving string is a gyroscopic system: \(\mat M\) is a positive definite matrix with the number \(\mu L/2\) on the diagonal, \(\mat K\) is positive definite because \(S > 0\) for \(v < c\), and \(\mat G\) is skew-symmetric by figure 26.32.

Lemma 26.26 Gyroscopic forces do no work (žiroskopske sile ne opravijo dela)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable solution of the gyroscopic system (26.27). Then the power of the gyroscopic forces (the scalar product of force and velocity) \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) is zero at every instant and the quantity

\[E = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\,\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q \tag{26.28}\]

is constant.

Proof

We must show that the scalar \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\) is zero and that the derivative of \(E\) is zero.

  1. For every column \(\vek x\), \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\) is a number, hence equal to its transpose: \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x = (\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x)^\T = \vek x^\T\mat G^\T\vek x = -\,\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\). A number equal to its own negative is zero. For \(\vek x = \dot{\vek q}\) the first claim follows. With two coordinates this is figure 26.33: the force is perpendicular to the velocity.
  2. Because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat K\,\vek q = \dot{\vek q}^\T(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q)\).
  3. By equation (26.27), \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = -\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\), so \(\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = -\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} = 0\) by step 1.

Source: GR (2.243), PDF p. 137: gyroscopic forces neither add nor remove energy, they only transfer it between coordinates. The proof follows GR.

With two coordinates the lemma can be seen by eye (figure 26.33). We draw the plane of the coordinates \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) and in it the path along which the state point \((q_1, q_2)\) moves. At the chosen instant the point has the velocity \(\dot{\vek q} = (2, 1)\), tangent to the path (we choose the units so that the numbers are simple). Every skew-symmetric \(2 \times 2\) matrix has the form \(\mat G = g\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\). For \(g = 1\) the gyroscopic force is \(-\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} = (-\dot q_2, \dot q_1) = (-1, 2)\): the components of the velocity swap places and one gets a minus, which is a turn by a right angle. The scalar product of the force and the velocity is \((-1) \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1 = 0\). A force perpendicular to the velocity bends the path but does not change the size of the velocity. This is how a string pulls a stone that we whirl in a circle: it pulls towards the hand, yet the stone comes no closer to the hand, so the string does no work (work is force times the path in the direction of the force). This view adds what the calculation of step 1 does not show: the gyroscopic force turns the motion. With more than two coordinates the plane cannot be drawn, but the conclusion \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x = 0\) remains.

What is \(E\) for our string? From step 2 of the proof of lemma 26.24, \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac L2\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) and \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac L2\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (j\pi/L)^2 q_{\mathrm{j}}^2\), so \(E = \tfrac12\int_0^L\big(\mu w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + S\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\). This is the functional of theorem 26.21, and lemma 26.26 says that it is conserved already in the Galerkin system (checked on a random state with five sines and the band of example A, both sides equal to six places). It is also the energy integral \(\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 + V\) of theorem 8.124. The kinetic energy of the transverse motion of the string is \(\tfrac12\mu\int_0^L (w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (the velocity of a particle from lemma 26.1, the axial part \(\tfrac12\mu v^2 L\) is constant and does not enter the equations), so by theorem 8.97 it splits into \(T_2 = \tfrac12\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), \(T_1 = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(T_0 = \tfrac12\mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), the potential energy is \(V = \tfrac12 T\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(T_2 - T_0 + V = E\). The term \(T_1\) is linear in the velocities. From the definition of \(G_{\mathrm{ij}}\), \(T_1 = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\vek q\), and in Lagrange's equations \(\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\tfrac{\partial T_1}{\partial\dot{\vek q}} - \tfrac{\partial T_1}{\partial\vek q} = \tfrac12\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} - \tfrac12\mat G^\T\dot{\vek q} = \mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\). The gyroscopic force is thus the part of the equations that \(T_1\) brings (GR (1.39), (1.40), PDF p. 47), and it does not change the energy by itself, as the skew-symmetry of the matrix in figure 26.32 shows.

26.5.3 Eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system

The trial \(\vek q = \vek x\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) solves equation (26.27), because the derivative of a complex exponential is a product with \(\lambda\) (theorem 9.34), if \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\) with \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) from \(\mathbb{C}^n\). For \(\mat G = \mat 0\), \(\mat K\,\vek x = -\lambda^2\mat M\,\vek x\), so by lemma 10.26 \(-\lambda^2\) is real and, for positive definite \(\mat K\), positive, and \(\lambda\) is purely imaginary. Does it stay so when \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\)? The answer depends on the stiffness matrix, as figure 26.36 shows.

Theorem 26.27 Eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system (lastne vrednosti žiroskopskega sistema)

Let \((\mat M, \mat G, \mat K)\) be a gyroscopic system (definition 26.25) and let \(\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\) (one of the points of figure 26.36) with \(\vek x \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{\vek 0\}\) solve \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\). Denote \(m = \bar{\vek x}^\T\mat M\,\vek x\), \(k = \bar{\vek x}^\T\mat K\,\vek x\) and \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \mathrm{i}g\). Then \(m > 0\), \(k\) and \(g\) are real numbers, and

  1. \(\lambda\) is purely imaginary exactly when \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\). Then \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with \(\omega = \big(-g \pm \sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\big)/(2m)\).
  2. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, \(k > 0\), and so every eigenvalue is purely imaginary and different from zero. The system then has no solution that grows exponentially.
  3. If \(g^2 + 4mk < 0\), \(\lambda\) has a nonzero real part and the system is not stable (it has a solution that grows exponentially).
Proof

We must show that the equation with the eigenvector reduces to a quadratic equation for \(\lambda\) with real coefficients.

  1. Write \(\vek x = \vek a + \mathrm{i}\vek b\). For a real symmetric \(\mat A\), \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat A\,\vek x = \vek a^\T\mat A\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat A\,\vek b + \mathrm{i}\,(\vek a^\T\mat A\,\vek b - \vek b^\T\mat A\,\vek a)\) and the remainder is zero (lemma 10.26). Hence \(m\) and \(k\) are real, and \(m > 0\), because \(\mat M\) is positive definite and \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\).
  2. For \(\mat G\), \(\overline{(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x)} = \vek x^\T\mat G\,\bar{\vek x}\), which is a number equal to its transpose \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G^\T\vek x = -\,\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x\). A number equal to the negative of its conjugate is purely imaginary: \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \mathrm{i}g\) with real \(g\).
  3. We multiply the equation \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\): \(m\lambda^2 + \mathrm{i}g\,\lambda + k = 0\). The solutions are \(\lambda = \big(-\mathrm{i}g \pm \sqrt{-(g^2 + 4mk)}\big)/(2m)\).
  4. For \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\) the root is \(\mathrm{i}\sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\), so \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\,\big(-g \pm \sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\big)/(2m)\) is purely imaginary, like the points on the imaginary axis in the example of figure 26.36. For \(g^2 + 4mk < 0\) the root is real and nonzero, so \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = \pm\sqrt{|g^2 + 4mk|}/(2m) \ne 0\), like the points on the circle off the imaginary axis. This is point 1.
  5. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, \(k = \vek a^\T\mat K\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat K\,\vek b > 0\) by step 1, so \(g^2 + 4mk > 0\) and by step 4 \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\). The product of the solutions \(\omega\) is \(-k/m < 0\), so \(\omega\) and the other root have different signs and \(\omega \ne 0\). No solution grows either: by lemma 26.26, \(\tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q \le E(0)\) for every \(t\), and since \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u \ge \kappa\,\vek u^\T\vek u\) with \(\kappa > 0\), the smallest value of \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u\) at \(\vek u^\T\vek u = 1\) (it exists by the extreme value theorem), we get \(\vek q^\T\vek q \le 2E(0)/\kappa\). This is point 2.
  6. The determinant \(\Delta(\lambda) = \det(\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\) equals the determinant of the transposed matrix, \(\det(\lambda^2\mat M - \lambda\mat G + \mat K) = \Delta(-\lambda)\), because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric and \(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\) (GR (2.246), PDF p. 138). If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue, so is \(-\lambda\): the dots in figure 26.36 lie in pairs, mirrored through the origin. For \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \ne 0\) one of the values \(\lambda\), \(-\lambda\) therefore has \(a = \mathrm{Re} > 0\) and an eigenvector \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\). The real part \(\vek q(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\vek y\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\big)\) is a solution, because the system is real. It is not zero: for \(\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda = 0\), \(\vek q = \mathrm{e}^{at}\,\mathrm{Re}\,\vek y\) and we may take \(\vek y\) real (the kernel of a real matrix is closed under real and imaginary parts), and for \(\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda = \beta \ne 0\), at \(\beta t = 0\) and \(\beta t = \pi/2\) the values of \(\mathrm{e}^{-at}\vek q\) are \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek y\) and \(-\mathrm{Im}\,\vek y\), at least one of which is nonzero. The solution grows as \(\mathrm{e}^{at}\). This is point 3.

Source: GR (2.244) to (2.247), PDF p. 137 to 138: the eigenvalues are real pairs or purely imaginary pairs, and a real eigenvalue is possible only if the effective stiffness matrix is not positive definite. The notation with \(m\), \(g\), \(k\) and the condition \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\) is ours.

How many eigenvalues does the system have for positive definite \(\mat K\)? The polynomial \(\Delta(\lambda)\) has degree \(2n\), because \(\mat M\) is positive definite, so there are \(2n\) eigenvalues (with multiplicity), all \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\). The eigenvalues \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) lie on the imaginary axis of figure 26.36. The eigenvector for \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the conjugate of the eigenvector for \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), because the system is real. For \(\mat G = \mat 0\) the eigenvector can be real. For \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\) it is in general complex, as in the stabilization example below with \(\vek x = (1, \pm\mathrm{i})^\T\). This is the mathematical form of what we saw in the moving string as the phase factor \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) in theorem 26.13: the shapes are no longer standing, the waves travel. We prove the orthogonality of these modes in section 26.6.

As a special case take \(N = 1\). Then \(\mat G = (0)\), because \(G_{11} = 0\), and \(\omega_1^2 = K_{11}/M_{11} = S\,\pi^2/(\mu L^2)\), so \(\omega_1 = (\pi/L)\sqrt{c^2 - v^2}\). For the band of example A (0,9 × 50 mm, \(L = 1\) m, tension 100 MPa, steel \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, the dimensions and speed are our choice) at \(v = 40\) m/s this is \(f_1 = 52{,}963\) Hz, while the exact value from theorem 26.13 is \(49{,}548\) Hz: the approximation is \(6{,}89\,\%\) too high (the first dot of the blackwhite curve in figure 26.38). What is missing? A single shape cannot represent the coupling between the shapes \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) that \(G_{12} \ne 0\) brings. Take \(N = 2, 4, 8\): \(f_1 = 49{,}783\) (\(+0{,}47\,\%\)), \(49{,}584\) (\(+0{,}07\,\%\)) and \(49{,}554\) Hz (\(+0{,}01\,\%\)), the next three dots of the same curve. For \(N = 2\), \(f_2 = 112{,}695\) Hz against the exact \(99{,}097\) Hz. The error decreases at our \(v/c = 0{,}353\), but not uniformly over the frequencies: the second frequency needs more shapes than the first (figure 26.38).

26.5.4 Gyroscopic stabilization

Theorem 26.27 requires a positive definite \(\mat K\). What if it is not? For \(\mat G = \mat 0\), theorem 8.135 says that the equilibrium is unstable if there is a \(\vek u\) with \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u < 0\). Does the same hold when \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\)? Let us look first at the example from GR, then at an example that we can compute to the end by hand and that is drawn in figure 26.36.

Example 26.28 Inertia wheel: stability when positive definiteness is lost (kolo z maso: stabilnost ob izgubi pozitivne definitnosti)

GR (example 2.9, PDF p. 139 to 141) takes a mass \(m = 1\) on springs of stiffness \(k_1 = 50\) and \(k_2 = 98\) in a wheel turning with constant angular velocity \(\Omega\) (the numbers are GR's). The matrices are \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat G = 2m\Omega\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat K^* = \mathrm{diag}(k_1 - \Omega^2 m,\ k_2 - \Omega^2 m)\) (GR PDF p. 140). The matrix \(\mat K^*\) is positive definite for \(\Omega < \omega_1 = \sqrt{50} = 7{,}0711\). The eigenvalues for three speeds (computed in num-05.py):

\(\Omega\) \(\mat K^*\) \(\det\mat K^*\) eigenvalues \(\lambda\)
\(5\) \(\mathrm{diag}(25, 73)\) \(1825\) \(\pm 3{,}1131\,\mathrm{i}\), \(\pm 13{,}7226\,\mathrm{i}\)
\(8\) \(\mathrm{diag}(-14, 34)\) \(-476\) \(\pm 1{,}3092\), \(\pm 16{,}6648\,\mathrm{i}\)
\(12\) \(\mathrm{diag}(-94, -46)\) \(4324\) \(\pm 3{,}1865\,\mathrm{i}\), \(\pm 20{,}636\,\mathrm{i}\)

For \(\Omega = 5\) theorem 26.27 applies, everything is purely imaginary. For \(\Omega = 8\), \(\mat K^*\) has one negative eigenvalue, \(\det\mat K^* < 0\), and we get the real pair \(\pm 1{,}3092\), so instability, as theorem 26.27 (point 3) allows. For \(\Omega = 12\) both eigenvalues of \(\mat K^*\) are negative, \(\mat K^*\) is negative definite and \(\det\mat K^* > 0\), yet all eigenvalues are again purely imaginary: the system is stable although \(\mat K^*\) is not positive definite.
