GR PDF p. 141 ascribes this precisely to the gyroscopic forces.

Theorem 8.135 assumes \(\mat G = \mat 0\), and the example shows that the conclusion fails for \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\). The next example shows the mechanism in its simplest form, with one number \(g\) (figure 26.36).

We take a dimensionless system with two coordinates, unit mass \(\mat M = \mat I\), negative definite stiffness matrix \(\mat K = -\mat I\) and \(\mat G = g\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) with a number \(g > 0\). Without the gyroscopic term (\(g = 0\)), \(\lambda^2 = 1\) and \(\lambda = \pm 1\) twice: the system is unstable, as theorem 8.135 says. In the figure the axes show the real and imaginary parts of \(\lambda\). At \(g = 0\) the eigenvalues are on the real axis at \(\pm 1\). The characteristic equation is

\[\det\begin{pmatrix}\lambda^2 - 1 & g\lambda\\ -g\lambda & \lambda^2 - 1\end{pmatrix} = (\lambda^2 - 1)^2 + g^2\lambda^2 = \lambda^4 + (g^2 - 2)\,\lambda^2 + 1 = 0 . \tag{26.29}\]

For \(\nu = \lambda^2\), \(\nu^2 + (g^2 - 2)\nu + 1 = 0\) with discriminant \((g^2 - 2)^2 - 4 = g^2(g^2 - 4)\).

  • For \(g < 2\) the discriminant is negative, \(\nu\) is not real and so \(\lambda\) is neither real nor purely imaginary. Since the product of the roots \(\nu\) is \(1\), \(|\nu| = 1\) and \(|\lambda| = 1\): the eigenvalues lie on a circle of radius \(1\). At \(g = 1\), \(\lambda = \pm 0{,}866 \pm 0{,}5\,\mathrm{i}\) (num-05.py), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = 0{,}866 > 0\) and the solution grows as \(\mathrm{e}^{0{,}866\,t}\) (theorem 26.27, point 3).
  • At \(g = 2\) the discriminant is zero, \(\nu = -1\) doubly and \(\lambda = \pm\mathrm{i}\) doubly: the eigenvalues arrive at the imaginary axis.
  • For \(g > 2\) the discriminant is positive, the sum of the roots is \(-(g^2 - 2) < 0\) and the product \(1 > 0\), so both \(\nu\) are real and negative, hence all four eigenvalues are purely imaginary. At \(g = 3\), \(\nu^2 + 7\nu + 1 = 0\), \(\nu = (-7 \pm \sqrt{45})/2 = -0{,}1459\) and \(-6{,}854\), \(\lambda = \pm 0{,}382\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(\pm 2{,}618\,\mathrm{i}\). Computing the eigenvalues of the state matrix gives the same.

Why the gyroscopic term holds the system can be seen in the plane of the coordinates (figure 26.37). The stiffness \(\mat K = -\mat I\) means a force \(-\mat K\,\vek q = +\vek q\) that pushes the state point away from the origin, the harder the farther it is, like a ball off the top of a dome. The gyroscopic force is perpendicular to the velocity (figure 26.33) and bends the path. Let us ask whether the point can circle. We draw a circle of radius \(r = 1\) and on it a point circling anticlockwise with angular velocity \(\omega\), so with the velocity \(\omega r\) along the tangent. On it act the outward force of size \(r\) and the gyroscopic force of size \(g\,\omega r\), which points to the centre because it is perpendicular to the tangent. The circling \(\vek q = r\,(\cos\omega t, \sin\omega t)^\T\) has the acceleration \(\ddot{\vek q} = -\omega^2\vek q\), so of size \(\omega^2 r\) towards the centre, and with unit mass the surplus of force towards the centre must supply it: \(g\,\omega r - r = \omega^2 r\), which is

\[\omega^2 - g\,\omega + 1 = 0 , \qquad \omega = \frac{g \pm \sqrt{g^2 - 4}}{2} . \tag{26.30}\]

A real \(\omega\) exists exactly for \(g \ge 2\). This is the same limit as from the discriminant above, this time from the three forces in the figure. At \(g = 3\), \(\omega = 0{,}382\) or \(2{,}618\), the sizes of the eigenvalues \(\pm 0{,}382\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(\pm 2{,}618\,\mathrm{i}\). The slower circling is drawn: the gyroscopic force is \(3 \cdot 0{,}382 = 1{,}146\), the outward force \(1\), and the surplus \(0{,}146\) is exactly \(\omega^2 r = 0{,}382^2\). For \(g < 2\) there is no such \(\omega\), because \(\omega^2 - g\,\omega + 1 > 0\) for every \(\omega\): at every speed of circling the gyroscopic force \(g\,\omega r\) is smaller than the sum \(r + \omega^2 r\) that it would have to supply, and the point does not stay on the circle.

Panel (b) of figure 26.37 shows, in the plane \(q_1\), \(q_2\), what happens when we release the point from rest at \((1, 0)\). Without the gyroscopic term it goes straight away and at \(t = 2\) it is at \(\cosh 2 = 3{,}76\). At \(g = 1\) the gyroscopic force bends the path, but too little: at \(t = 2\) the point is \(3{,}32\) from the origin and moves away along a spiral. At \(g = 3\) the force turns it back before it escapes, and the path stays between the circles of radii \(1\) and \(1{,}34\). The motion there is the sum of the two circlings of equation (26.30) with the shares \(1{,}171\) and \(-0{,}171\) (from the initial conditions), so the largest distance is \(1{,}171 + 0{,}171 = 1{,}342\) and the smallest \(1{,}171 - 0{,}171 = 1\).

The matrix \(\mat K = -\mat I\) is negative definite, yet at \(g \ge 2\) the system stays bounded: this is gyroscopic stabilization (žiroskopska stabilizacija). The reason is in the condition of theorem 26.27: for the eigenvector \(\vek x = (1, \pm\mathrm{i})^\T/\sqrt2\), \(m = 1\), \(k = -1\) and \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \pm\mathrm{i}g\), so \(g^2 + 4mk = g^2 - 4\), which is nonnegative exactly for \(g \ge 2\) (then the points lie on the imaginary axis, for \(g < 2\) off it) (the labels \(m\), \(k\), \(g\) are those of the theorem). The gyroscopic term must be large enough that the discriminant of the quadratic equation from step 3 of the proof is not negative. Positive definiteness is therefore a sufficient, but not a necessary condition for purely imaginary eigenvalues. We shall meet the same structure in the moving beam: in section 26.7, for \(T L^2/EI = 100\) the system is stable between \(v = 11{,}811\) and \(v = 12{,}177\) (dimensionless), although \(\mat K\) is not positive definite there.

26.5.5 Convergence of the Galerkin frequencies

How well does the Galerkin system predict the frequencies of the moving string, where we know the exact value? Take \(L = c = \mu = 1\) (dimensionless) and the ratios \(v/c = 0{,}5\) and \(0{,}9\). The exact frequencies are \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi\,(1 - v^2/c^2)\) (theorem 26.13): \(\omega_1 = 2{,}35619\) and \(\omega_2 = 4{,}71239\) at \(0{,}5\), \(\omega_1 = 0{,}59690\) and \(\omega_2 = 1{,}19381\) at \(0{,}9\). We write system (26.25) as a first-order system of dimension \(2N\) with the state vector \((\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) (GR §2.11.3, PDF p. 139) and the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}\mat 0 & \mat I\\ -\mat M^{-1}\mat K & -\mat M^{-1}\mat G\end{pmatrix}\), whose eigenvalues are \(\lambda\), and solve it with \(N = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\) sines. The largest absolute real part of the eigenvalues is everywhere below \(4 \cdot 10^{-15}\), as theorem 26.27 demands. The relative errors \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) of the first and second frequency are shown in figure 26.38.

We draw the axes: the number of sines \(N\) from \(1\) to \(32\) and the error \(\varepsilon\) from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{1}\), both logarithmic, so that the powers have the same length. First the blue curve: at \(v/c = 0{,}5\), \(\varepsilon_1 = 1{,}37 \cdot 10^{-2}\) at \(N = 2\) and \(3{,}95 \cdot 10^{-6}\) at \(N = 32\), \(\varepsilon_2 = 0{,}315\) at \(N = 2\) and \(1{,}51 \cdot 10^{-5}\) at \(N = 32\). Then the orange curve at \(v/c = 0{,}9\): \(\varepsilon_1 = 0{,}111\) and \(1{,}34 \cdot 10^{-5}\), \(\varepsilon_2 = 3{,}74\) (frequency \(5{,}65\) against the exact \(1{,}19\)) and \(5{,}38 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The blackwhite curve is the band of example A at \(v/c = 0{,}353\), from \(6{,}89 \cdot 10^{-2}\) with one sine to \(1{,}93 \cdot 10^{-6}\) with \(32\). The labels say which colour is which speed. At both speeds the error decreases about eightfold with every doubling of \(N\) (for example \(\varepsilon_1\) at \(0{,}5\): \(1{,}73 \cdot 10^{-3} \to 2{,}31 \cdot 10^{-4} \to 3{,}06 \cdot 10^{-5} \to 3{,}95 \cdot 10^{-6}\)), but at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) more shapes are needed to get onto this path: \(\varepsilon_2\) at \(N = 4\) is \(0{,}120\) at \(0{,}9\) and \(6 \cdot 10^{-3}\) at \(0{,}5\). All computed errors are positive, so the approximations are above the exact values. This is an observation on the computed cases, not a proof: Ritz's upper-bound theorem (theorem 10.59) requires \(\mat G = \mat 0\), and for gyroscopic systems we do not prove an upper bound.

Why so poor at \(v/c = 0{,}9\)? Take the shape of mode \(n = 1\) from theorem 26.13, that is \(\psi_1(x) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_1x}\sin(\pi x/L)\) with \(k_1 = \pi v/(cL)\) (the theorem calls it \(\varphi\), here it is \(\psi_1\), since \(\varphi_1\) is the first sine in this section). Its real and imaginary parts are the shapes of the string at two instants, a quarter of a period apart, figure 26.39. The string moves as \(w = \mathrm{Re}(\psi_1\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_1 t})\), so at \(t = 0\) the shape is \(\mathrm{Re}\,\psi_1\), and a quarter of a period earlier, at \(\omega_1 t = -\pi/2\), it is \(\mathrm{Re}(-\mathrm{i}\,\psi_1) = \mathrm{Im}\,\psi_1\).

We draw the rest line between the eyelets, a distance \(L\) apart, and above it the shape at rest \(\sin(\pi x/L)\), which is the first sine. Over it we lay the real part of the mode: the factor \(\cos(0{,}9\,\pi x/L)\) falls at \(x = 0{,}5\,L\) to \(0{,}156\) (at \(v/c = 0{,}5\) it would be \(0{,}707\)), so at this instant the middle of the string is nearly on the rest line and the crest moves towards the left eyelet. Next we draw the imaginary part, which is the shape of the string a quarter of a period earlier and has its crest towards the right eyelet. Since neither of these shapes resembles a single sine, the first sine \(\sin(\pi x/L)\) captures only the fraction \(0{,}083\) of the squared norm of the real part and \(0{,}968\) of the imaginary part (the squared norm over \(x \in [0, L]\)), and at \(v/c = 0{,}5\) it captures \(0{,}922\) of both. The first two sines together capture at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) \(0{,}998\) of the real and \(0{,}975\) of the imaginary part (recomputed in num-05.py), so the real part lies almost wholly in the second sine. So the first mode at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) needs at least two sines, and the higher modes more. WM1990 (PDF p. 6) writes the same: at high transport speed the eigenfunctions of the string at rest, which it calls solutions with constant phase, are a poor approximation of the motion and many of them are needed for a sufficiently accurate computation. For the string we avoid this because the complex modes are known (section 26.3). For systems that have no closed formula, for example finite elements (section 26.8), we must take enough shapes, and we use the eigenfunctions of the moving string for orthogonality in section 26.6.

Let us summarize what we showed and how. With the sines and the residual requirement (lemma 26.24) we reduced the moving string to the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with a matrix \(\mat G\) that is skew-symmetric because of the fixed eyelets, and, because of the parity of the shapes (figure 26.30), nonzero only for \(i + j\) odd. From the skew-symmetry we derived that gyroscopic forces do no work (lemma 26.26) and that for positive definite \(\mat K\) all eigenvalues are purely imaginary (theorem 26.27). Positive definiteness is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one: example 26.28 has a negative definite \(\mat K\) and a stable system. For our string \(\mat K\) is positive definite exactly when \(S = T - \mu v^2 > 0\), that is for \(v < c\) (section 26.4). In the computed cases the frequencies lie above the exact ones and converge, more slowly at high speed, because the sines are not adapted to the travelling waves.

26.6 Orthogonality and expansion in modes

In section 26.3 we found the exact modes (načini) of the moving string, the complex functions \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (theorem 26.13). For the string at rest we expanded the initial shape and the initial velocity in modes (theorem 13.11), and the coefficients came from the orthogonality of the modes (theorem 13.70). The question is whether the same holds for a string that runs through its two eyelets with speed \(v\). The answer has two parts. Ordinary orthogonality in the mass fails, but orthogonality survives in another product, which has to be found first. This section finds it, proves the orthogonality and derives the coefficients of the expansion from it.

From history

Methods for axially moving materials date to the nineteenth century, and the eigenfunctions of the moving string and beam had been calculated before. Wickert and Mote (1990) state that orthogonality relations among the eigenfunctions had not been derived until then (WM1990, PDF p. 1). The generalized coordinates in an expansion in eigenfunctions therefore remained coupled, and the classical modal analysis and the Green's function method, which had been applied to the stationary string and beam, were not applicable to axially moving materials. The response was known only for special excitations, for example a constant transverse point force (Chonan, 1986) or harmonic motion of a support (Miranker, 1960) (WM1990, PDF p. 1). For discrete systems Meirovitch (1974, 1975) had studied the matrix eigenvalue problem of gyroscopic systems and derived a corresponding modal analysis, in which a transformation of the generalized coordinates and momenta decouples the equations (WM1990, PDF p. 2). Wickert and Mote wrote the equations of the moving string and beam in first-order form with one symmetric and one skew-symmetric differential operator and showed that the eigenfunctions are orthogonal with respect to both (WM1990, PDF p. 1 and 2).

The moving string that we last looked at in section 26.3 therefore has exact modes, but we have not been able to compute the coefficients of an expansion in them. The story showed two things: the difficulty is not in the eigenfunctions but in the product with respect to which they are orthogonal, and the way to that product is to write the equation in first-order form. We do it here on the string we already know, and prove everything with lemma 6.13.

26.6.1 State and first-order form

The string equation of theorem 26.4 is of second order in time, so the shape \(w(\cdot, t)\) alone does not suffice to continue the motion from time \(t\). Newton's second law connects the force with the acceleration, that is with the second derivative in time, so the motion is determined only when the displacement and the velocity of all particles at one time are known, as for the pendulum with one degree of freedom (chapter 9). Whoever sees only the shape of the string does not know whether a particle is on its way up or down, because this is shown only by the velocity. The displacement and the velocity together we call the state (stanje), because all later motion follows from them, as for the damped systems of section 20.8. We draw it on the string of mode 1 from the example of section 26.3. We choose units so that \(L = \mu = T = 1\), hence \(c = 1\), and take \(v = 1/2\) (the ratio \(v/c\) as in section 26.3). Then \(\omega_1 = \pi\,(1 - v^2/c^2) = 2{,}356\).

We build figure 26.40 as one draws it on the board. First we draw the axis \(x\) along which the string is stretched, and on it the two eyelets at \(0\) and \(L\), which are fixed in space (the idealization of section 26.1). Then we draw the shape \(w\) that the string has in mode 1 at time \(t = 0\), that is \(w(x, 0) = \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi_1(x) = \sin(\pi x)\cos(\pi x/2)\). Last, at four particles we add the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\): the particle at \(x\) has at this time the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{Re}\,(\mathrm{i}\omega_1\varphi_1) = -\omega_1\,\mathrm{Im}\,\varphi_1(x)\). At \(x = 0{,}6\) this gives \(w = 0{,}559\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = -2{,}356\cdot 0{,}769 = -1{,}813\), the third arrow from the left. The velocity is not in the outline of the string, so we write the state as a pair of functions.

We use the pair \((w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) for a second purpose: we write the string equation as a pair of first-order equations, because this separates a symmetric part from a skew-symmetric one, which we did not need for the string at rest. The equation is (section 26.1)

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + \mathcal G\,w_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal K\,w = 0 , \qquad \mathcal G f = 2\mu v\,f' , \qquad \mathcal K f = -\kappa\,f'' , \qquad \kappa = T - \mu v^2 = \mu\,(c^2 - v^2) , \tag{26.31}\]

since \(\mu(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The operator \(\mathcal G\) comes from the Coriolis term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) (named in section 26.1), the operator \(\mathcal K\) from the tension reduced by the centripetal term \(\mu v^2\). For \(v < c\) we have \(\kappa > 0\). We need this condition in lemma 26.30. In this section the letters \(\mathcal G\) and \(\mathcal K\) mean operators, not the matrices of section 26.5 (the matrices \(\mat G\) and \(\mat K\) arise from them by the Galerkin method).

Definition 26.29 State and first-order form (stanje in oblika prvega reda)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and eyelets fixed in space (section 26.1) have mass per length \(\mu\) and tension \(T\) on \([0, L]\). The state space \(S\) is the set of pairs \(\vek z = (p, w)\) of complex functions \(p, w\colon [0, L] \to \mathbb C\) that are twice continuously differentiable and have \(p(0) = p(L) = w(0) = w(L) = 0\). The state product (produkt stanj) of two states is the complex number

\[\langle \vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \int_0^L \big(p_1\,\bar p_2 + w_1\,\bar w_2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.32}\]

where the bar means the complex conjugate. The operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) act on a state \(\vek z = (p, w)\) as

\[\mathcal A\,\vek z = \begin{pmatrix} \mu\,p \\ \mathcal K\,w \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mathcal B\,\vek z = \begin{pmatrix} \mathcal G\,p + \mathcal K\,w \\ -\mathcal K\,p \end{pmatrix} , \tag{26.33}\]

with \(\mathcal G\) and \(\mathcal K\) from equation (26.31). The state of the moving string at time \(t\) is \(\vek z(t) = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\).

Source: WM1990 (8a), (8c), (11) (PDF p. 2). The notation with \(\mu\), \(\kappa\) and dimensions is ours, in WM1990 the quantities are dimensionless (\(\mathcal M = I\)).

The conjugation in the product is needed so that \(\langle \vek z, \vek z\rangle = \int (|p|^2 + |w|^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is real and nonnegative also for the complex states that we shall obtain as eigenstates. The function \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at both eyelets at every time, because \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) for all \(t\), so \((w_{\mathrm{t}}, w) \in S\) if \(w\) is smooth enough. That equation (26.31) is equivalent to the first-order form is shown by the following computation: for \(\vek z = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) we have \(\mathcal A\,\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal B\,\vek z = (\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + \mathcal G\,w_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal K\,w,\ \mathcal K\,w_{\mathrm{t}} - \mathcal K\,w_{\mathrm{t}})\). The second component is zero without any assumption, the first is the left side of equation (26.31). The string therefore moves by equation (26.31) exactly when

\[\mathcal A\,\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal B\,\vek z = \vek 0 . \tag{26.34}\]

The second row is there so that the operators get the properties that follow: without it the first row would be equation (26.31), but the operators would be neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric.

What should symmetry and skew symmetry mean for an operator? For a matrix, \(\mat A^{\mathsf T} = \mat A\) means \(\vek u^{\mathsf T}\mat A\,\vek v = \vek v^{\mathsf T}\mat A\,\vek u\), that is the product does not depend on the order (chapter 10). We ask the same of an operator with respect to the state product (26.32), and for skew symmetry the swap of order changes the sign (opposite areas in figure 26.41), as for the matrix \(\mat B^{\mathsf T} = -\mat B\).

Both properties come from one single step, integration by parts (lemma 6.13). Let us first draw it on two functions that we know how to integrate.

In figure 26.41 we take, above the axis \(x\) with \(L = 1\), the function \(f = \sin(\pi x)\) and the function \(g = \sin(2\pi x)\). Both are zero at the eyelets, like the displacement and the velocity of the string in the space \(S\). Their product \(f\,g\) is therefore zero at both eyelets. Below, above the second axis, we draw the derivative of the product, the curve \((f\,g)' = f'g + f\,g'\). The area under a derivative is the change of the function from one eyelet to the other, here \(f(L)\,g(L) - f(0)\,g(0) = 0 - 0 = 0\). The derivative of the product has two parts, the part \(f'g\) with area \(4/3 = 1{,}333\) and the part \(f\,g'\) with area \(-1{,}333\). Since the area of the sum is zero, the areas of the parts are opposite:

\[\int_0^L f'\,g\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L f\,g'\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{26.35}\]

We moved the derivative from \(f\) to \(g\) and paid with the sign. The operator of the first derivative is therefore skew-symmetric. If we move the derivative twice, the sign changes twice and returns, so the second derivative is symmetric.

The step uses one assumption, the fixed eyelets. Without it the product is not zero at the eyelets and a boundary term remains. For \(f = g = x\) on \([0, 1]\), which are not zero at the right end, \(\int_0^1 f'g\,\mathrm{d}x = 1/2\) and \(-\int_0^1 f\,g'\,\mathrm{d}x = -1/2\), and the difference is the boundary term \(f(1)\,g(1) = 1\). For a string whose support moves (the case in the story above), equation (26.35) therefore does not hold and the boundary term stays in the calculation. In this section the eyelets are fixed (definition 26.29) and the boundary term is always zero, as at the eyelets of figure 26.41.

Lemma 26.30 Symmetry of \(\mathcal A\) and skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\) (simetrija operatorja \(\mathcal A\) in poševna simetrija operatorja \(\mathcal B\))

Let \(\vek z_1, \vek z_2 \in S\) be states of definition 26.29. Then, as for the transfer of a derivative,

\[\langle \mathcal A\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \langle \vek z_1, \mathcal A\vek z_2\rangle , \qquad \langle \mathcal B\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = -\,\langle \vek z_1, \mathcal B\vek z_2\rangle . \tag{26.36}\]

For every nonzero state \(\vek z = (p, w) \in S\)

\[\langle \mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle = \int_0^L \big(\mu\,|p|^2 + \kappa\,|w'|^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x > 0 , \tag{26.37}\]

and the number \(\langle \mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle\) is purely imaginary.

Idea

The operator \(\mathcal K\) is symmetric by lemma 6.13, like the second derivative in lemma 13.69, and the operator \(\mathcal G\), a first derivative, is skew-symmetric for the same reason: in integration by parts a derivative moves from one function to the other and changes sign (the opposite areas in figure 26.41). This is also the real reason why the Coriolis force does no work: its power \(\int p\,\mathcal G p\,\mathrm{d}x\) equals \(\mu v\,[p^2]_0^L = 0\) for real \(p\).

Proof

We must show three equalities, each with one transfer of a derivative. We start with \(\mathcal K\) and \(\mathcal G\).

  1. For functions \(f, g\) of \(S\) (twice continuously differentiable, zero at the eyelets) we have \(\int_0^L (\mathcal K f)\,\bar g\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\int_0^L f'\,\bar g'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By lemma 6.13, \(-\kappa\int f''\,\bar g = -\kappa\,[f'\,\bar g]_0^L + \kappa\int f'\,\bar g'\), and the boundary term is zero because \(\bar g(0) = \bar g(L) = 0\) (the eyelets in figure 26.41, here for the product \(f'\,\bar g\)). The right side is symmetric in \(f\) and \(g\) up to conjugation, because \(\kappa\) is real: \(\int (\mathcal K f)\,\bar g = \int f\,\overline{\mathcal K g}\).
  2. For \(\mathcal G\) the same: \(\int (\mathcal G f)\,\bar g = 2\mu v\int f'\,\bar g = 2\mu v\,[f\,\bar g]_0^L - 2\mu v\int f\,\bar g' = -\int f\,\overline{\mathcal G g}\), the boundary term is zero. This is equation (26.35) multiplied by \(2\mu v\), with the opposite areas of figure 26.41.
  3. Symmetry of \(\mathcal A\). By definition \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \int \mu\,p_1\,\bar p_2 + \int (\mathcal K w_1)\,\bar w_2\). By step 1 the second term equals \(\int w_1\,\overline{\mathcal K w_2}\), and the first equals \(\int p_1\,\overline{\mu p_2}\). Together this is \(\langle\vek z_1, \mathcal A\vek z_2\rangle\).
  4. Skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\). The sum \(\langle\mathcal B\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle + \langle\vek z_1, \mathcal B\vek z_2\rangle\) has four terms with \(\mathcal K\) and two with \(\mathcal G\). By step 2 the two terms with \(\mathcal G\) cancel (opposite areas): \(\int (\mathcal G p_1)\,\bar p_2 + \int p_1\,\overline{\mathcal G p_2} = 0\). The four terms with \(\mathcal K\) are \(\int (\mathcal K w_1)\,\bar p_2 - \int w_1\,\overline{\mathcal K p_2} + \int p_1\,\overline{\mathcal K w_2} - \int (\mathcal K p_1)\,\bar w_2\), and by step 1 the first cancels the second and the third the fourth. The sum is zero.
  5. Positivity. For \(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2 = \vek z\) step 1 gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle = \mu\int |p|^2 + \kappa\int |w'|^2\), which is equation (26.37). For \(\mu > 0\) and \(\kappa > 0\) (that is \(v < c\)) the sum is nonnegative. If it is zero, then \(p = 0\) and \(w' = 0\), so \(w\) is constant, and because \(w(0) = 0\) we get \(w = 0\), hence \(\vek z = \vek 0\).
  6. By step 4 for \(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2 = \vek z\) we have \(\langle\mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle = -\langle\vek z, \mathcal B\vek z\rangle = -\overline{\langle\mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle}\), since \(\langle\vek a, \vek b\rangle = \overline{\langle\vek b, \vek a\rangle}\). A number equal to minus its own conjugate is purely imaginary.

Source: WM1990 (12) (PDF p. 2): symmetry of \(\mathcal A\) and skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\), positive definiteness of \(\mathcal A\) for \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) in the Appendix (PDF p. 2 and 7). The proof by integration by parts is ours.

Lemma 26.30 shows what happens at \(v = c\): then \(\kappa = 0\), the product \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle\) is zero for \(\vek z = (0, w)\) with \(w \neq 0\), and \(\mathcal A\) is no longer positive (figure 26.42). This is exactly the critical speed of section 26.4 in another dress: with the positivity of \(\mathcal A\) the theorem that follows disappears, and with it everything that follows from it.

We build figure 26.42 as follows. First we draw the axes, \(v/c\) horizontally and \(\kappa/T\) vertically. Then the curve \(\kappa/T = 1 - v^2/c^2\), which equals \(1\) at \(v = 0\), as for the string at rest. For our example the point at \(v/c = 1/2\) gives \(\kappa/T = 3/4\). At \(v = c\) the curve falls to zero. The region under the curve to its left, where \(\kappa > 0\), is the region where \(\mathcal A\) is positive and the theorem holds.

Eigenstates are states that change only in size and phase (an example is mode 1 at two times, figure 26.45) when we write the time part as \(\vek z = \mathrm{Re}\,(\vek\zeta\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t})\). We insert this ansatz in equation (26.34) and obtain (since \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) do not differentiate in time) the eigenvalue problem

\[\lambda\,\mathcal A\,\vek\zeta + \mathcal B\,\vek\zeta = \vek 0 , \qquad \vek\zeta \in S , \ \vek\zeta \neq \vek 0 , \tag{26.38}\]

with eigenvalue \(\lambda \in \mathbb C\). The pair \((\lambda, \vek\zeta)\) we call an eigenpair (lasten par) of the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\). The connection with the modes of section 26.3 is simple.

Lemma 26.31 Eigenstates and modes of the moving string (lastna stanja in načini gibajoče se strune)

A pair \((\lambda, \vek\zeta)\) with \(\vek\zeta = (q, \varphi)\) is an eigenpair of (26.38) exactly when \(q = \lambda\varphi\) and \(\varphi \neq 0\) solves

\[\lambda^2\mu\,\varphi + \lambda\,\mathcal G\varphi + \mathcal K\varphi = 0 , \qquad \varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0 . \tag{26.39}\]

For \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) this is the equation \(\mu\,(-\omega^2\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}\omega v\,\varphi' + v^2\varphi'') = T\varphi''\), so the pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the moving string (definition 26.12) and \(\vek\zeta = (\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi, \varphi)\).

Proof

We must show that the second row of equation (26.38) gives \(q = \lambda\varphi\) and the first row equation (26.39).

  1. The second row is \(\lambda\,\mathcal K\varphi - \mathcal K q = 0\), so \(\mathcal K(\lambda\varphi - q) = -\kappa\,(\lambda\varphi - q)'' = 0\). The function \(y = \lambda\varphi - q\) therefore has \(y'' = 0\), that is \(y = a + bx\), a straight line. Since it is zero at both eyelets (\(y(0) = y(L) = 0\)), it is the axis, \(y = 0\), which is \(q = \lambda\varphi\).
  2. The first row is \(\lambda\mu\,q + \mathcal G q + \mathcal K\varphi = 0\). With \(q = \lambda\varphi\) this is equation (26.39). Conversely, if \(\varphi\) solves (26.39), both rows are satisfied.
  3. For \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) we insert \(\mathcal G\varphi = 2\mu v\,\varphi'\) and \(\mathcal K\varphi = -(T - \mu v^2)\,\varphi''\): \(-\omega^2\mu\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}\omega\mu v\,\varphi' - (T - \mu v^2)\,\varphi'' = 0\), which is the equation in the statement.

The equation in the statement is the one that the ansatz \(w = \mathrm{Re}\,(\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) solved in theorem 26.13. The eigenpairs with \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) are therefore exactly the states \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) with the modes \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) of that theorem.

26.6.2 Orthogonality of the complex modes

For the matrices of section 26.5 we did the same computation with \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\) and \(\mat K\) (theorem 26.27): the eigenvalues are purely imaginary because \(\mat G\) is skew and \(\mat K\) is positive definite. Here the same proof runs on operators. Its idea: with the eigenvalue equation (26.38) we rewrite \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\) twice, once from the left argument and once from the right, and the skew symmetry says that the two forms differ by the factor \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\).

What it means that an eigenvalue is purely imaginary, and where this comes from, we first draw with the numbers of mode 1 (\(L = \mu = T = 1\), \(v/c = 1/2\)).

In figure 26.43 we draw the real and the imaginary axis of the complex plane. For the eigenstate \(\vek\zeta_1\) of mode 1 we compute (numerically, with the trapezoidal rule on 20001 points) the number \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = 7{,}402\). It lies on the positive real axis, because by equation (26.37) it is an integral of two squares. The number \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = -17{,}441\,\mathrm{i}\) lies on the imaginary axis, because \(\mathcal B\) is skew-symmetric (lemma 26.30). The quotient of a number on the imaginary axis and a number on the real axis is again on the imaginary axis: \(\lambda_1 = 17{,}441\,\mathrm{i}/7{,}402 = 2{,}356\,\mathrm{i}\), which is \(\mathrm{i}\omega_1\). This is the idea of item 1 of the theorem that follows. The position on the imaginary axis tells how the state moves: the time part \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) has absolute value \(1\), so the vibration neither grows nor dies out. An eigenvalue with real part \(a \neq 0\) would give \(|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}| = \mathrm{e}^{at}\), that is growth or decay. On the same axis lie the conjugate value \(\bar\lambda_1 = -2{,}356\,\mathrm{i}\), which we will meet with the real states, and the eigenvalue of mode 2, \(\lambda_2 = 4{,}712\,\mathrm{i}\). Item 2 of the theorem speaks about pairs of different points on this axis.

Theorem 26.32 Orthogonality of the complex modes of the moving string (ortogonalnost kompleksnih načinov gibajoče se strune)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and fixed eyelets be given (definition 26.29). Then, as figure 26.43 shows:

  1. Every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of (26.38) is purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with real \(\omega\), and for an eigenpair \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle > 0\) and \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = -\lambda\,\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\).
  2. If \((\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}})\) are eigenpairs with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\), then
    \[\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0 . \tag{26.40}\]
Idea

For the string at rest the proof of theorem 13.70 subtracts two equations. Here we subtract in the same way, but in the state space, where the eigenvalue equation connects \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\). The purely imaginary eigenvalues come from the positivity of \(\mathcal A\) and the skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\) (lemma 26.30).

Proof

We show first item 1 and then the difference \((\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{m}})\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\).

  1. We multiply the eigenvalue equation (26.38) in the state product (26.32) by \(\vek\zeta\), which is linear in the first argument. We obtain the number \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) times \(\lambda\) plus the number \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\), together zero: \(\lambda\,\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle + \langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = 0\).
  2. By lemma 26.30, \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is real and greater than zero, and \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is purely imaginary. From step 1, \(\lambda = -\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle/\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is therefore a purely imaginary number. This is item 1.
  3. For two eigenpairs we write \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\) (the eigenvalue equation for \(n\), multiplied by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\)). By skew symmetry (lemma 26.30), \(-\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\).
  4. The eigenvalue equation for \(m\) is \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\), so \(\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\bar\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\,\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\), because the product is conjugate-linear in the second argument.
  5. By item 1, \(\bar\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\), and by the symmetry of \(\mathcal A\), \(\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\). Steps 3 and 4 together give \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\).
  6. For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) (two different points in figure 26.43) this gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\), and by step 3 also \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot 0 = 0\).

Source: WM1990 (14b), (16) (PDF p. 3): the eigenvalues are imaginary, \(\langle\mathcal A\phi_{\mathrm{n}}, \phi_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \delta_{\mathrm{nm}}\) and \(\langle\mathcal B\phi_{\mathrm{n}}, \phi_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\) for \(n \neq m\) (Meirovitch, 1974). Proved here by integration by parts from lemma 26.30, WM1990 does not give the proof.

The theorem gives orthogonality in two products at once, as for matrices (theorem 10.21, definition 10.17) in mass and stiffness. The difference is that the products are no longer the mass and the stiffness but \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\), in which mass and stiffness are mixed, as equation (26.33) shows.

We test the theorem on modes 1 and 2 with \(v/c = 1/2\) and compare it with the ordinary mass product \(\int\mu\,\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x\) of the string at rest. The real and imaginary part of the mode are \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \sin(n\pi x)\cos(n\pi x/2)\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = \sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi x/2)\), therefore

\[\int_0^1\varphi_1^{\mathrm R}\varphi_2^{\mathrm R}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}16168 , \qquad \int_0^1\varphi_1^{\mathrm I}\varphi_2^{\mathrm I}\,\mathrm{d}x = -0{,}06467 , \qquad \mathrm{Re}\int_0^1\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}09701 \neq 0 . \tag{26.41}\]

The mass product of the modes is not zero. For the string at rest theorem 13.70 gave zero because the eigenvalue \(\omega^2\) is only a factor of the mass in the equation \(-T\varphi'' = \omega^2\mu\,\varphi\) (at \(v = 0\) we have \(\kappa = T\)). For the moving string equation (26.39) has the further term \(\lambda\mathcal G\varphi\) and the eigenvalue enters in two powers, so the same computation does not give zero. Zero is, by theorem 26.32, the state product (26.32), in which the mass part is accompanied by a stiffness part:

\[\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_2\rangle = \underbrace{\mu\,\omega_1\omega_2\!\int_0^1\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x}_{= \,1{,}0771 + 1{,}0771\,\mathrm{i}} + \underbrace{\kappa\!\int_0^1\varphi_1'\,\bar\varphi_2'\,\mathrm{d}x}_{= \,-1{,}0771 - 1{,}0771\,\mathrm{i}} = 0 . \tag{26.42}\]

The mass part is \(\omega_1\omega_2\) times the mass product, because \(p_{\mathrm{n}} = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) (lemma 26.31) and \(\mu\,p_1\bar p_2 = \mu\,\omega_1\omega_2\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\), with \(\omega_1\omega_2 = 1{,}125\,\pi^2\). The computation is numerical (trapezoidal rule on 20001 points), the remainder is \(10^{-8}\).

In figure 26.44 we first draw the axis \(x\) between the eyelets. Then the mass part, which has area \(0{,}09701\cdot 1{,}125\,\pi^2 = 1{,}0771\): if we judged orthogonality by it alone, we would reject it. So we add the stiffness part with the opposite area. Last we add the two, the blackwhite curve is their sum: its area is zero, although the sum is not zero at any point except at the ends and at its crossings. This is the orthogonality the theorem claims, and it is not orthogonality point by point.

For the expansion we need real states. Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) is purely imaginary and \(\mathcal A\), \(\mathcal B\) map real states to real states, \(\bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is an eigenstate together with \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\), with eigenvalue \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). We write \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\). By lemma 26.31, \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = (-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = (\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\), since \(\mathrm{i}\omega(\varphi^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\varphi^{\mathrm I}) = -\omega\varphi^{\mathrm I} + \mathrm{i}\omega\varphi^{\mathrm R}\). The real part of the mode in time is then (with \(\omega t\) as the phase) \(w = \mathrm{Re}\,(\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = \varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t - \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\). Let us see what this means for the particles of the string.

We build figure 26.45 over the times. First we draw the first panel with \(\omega t = 0\): the shape is \(\varphi_1^{\mathrm R}\) and it is nowhere zero in the interior. On it we mark three particles at \(0{,}25\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}75\). For the second panel with \(\omega t = \pi/8\) we use \(w = \varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t - \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\): the particle at \(0{,}75\) is now on the axis, because there \(\varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t = \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\). The particle at \(x\) passes its rest position at \(\omega t = \pi/2 - k_1 x\), which with \(k_1 = \pi/2\) for \(x = 0{,}75\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}25\) is exactly \(\pi/8\), \(\pi/4\) and \(3\pi/8\), as the third panel and the fourth panel show. The particles of the string therefore do not pass through their rest positions together. For the string at rest \(\varphi^{\mathrm I} = 0\) and they all pass together at \(\omega t = \pi/2\). Wickert and Mote point out that the complex eigenfunctions give a response with varying phase, so the particles do not pass their rest positions simultaneously (WM1990, PDF p. 3). They pass at \(0{,}0625\), \(0{,}125\) and \(0{,}1875\) of the period \(\tau_1 = 2\pi/\omega_1 = 2{,}667\).

Corollary 26.33 Real pairs of modes (realni pari načinov)

Let \((\mathrm{i}\omega, \vek\zeta)\) be an eigenpair with \(\omega > 0\) and \(\vek\zeta = \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\), where \(\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\) are real states. With the real product \((\vek a, \vek b) = \int (a_1b_1 + a_2b_2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) we have:

  1. \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} = \omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\) and \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} = -\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\),
  2. \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = \tfrac12\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) (half of the number) and \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = 0\),
  3. for two eigenpairs with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) (both positive) all four products \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\) and \((\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\), \(a, b \in \{\mathrm R, \mathrm I\}\), are zero.
Proof

We must show that the real and imaginary part of theorem 26.32 separate.

  1. The eigenvalue equation with \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) is \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta = -\mathrm{i}\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta\). Since \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) do not mix real and imaginary parts (they have real coefficients), \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} = \omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} - \mathrm{i}\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\). Comparing real and imaginary parts gives item 1.
  2. The conjugate state \(\bar{\vek\zeta}\) is an eigenstate with \(-\mathrm{i}\omega \neq \mathrm{i}\omega\) (for \(\omega > 0\)). Theorem 26.32 gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \bar{\vek\zeta}\rangle = \int(\mathcal A\vek\zeta)^{\mathsf T}\vek\zeta\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). Written out in real and imaginary part this is \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) - (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) + 2\mathrm{i}\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = 0\), because \(\mathcal A\) is symmetric also for the real product. The real and imaginary part give the first two equalities, and the sum \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) + (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I})\) gives the half.
  3. For \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) the numbers \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) are different. Theorem 26.32 for the pairs \((\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}})\) and \((\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{m}})\) gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\) and \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\). The real and imaginary parts of both give four equations: \((R, R) + (I, I) = 0\), \((I, R) - (R, I) = 0\), \((R, R) - (I, I) = 0\) and \((I, R) + (R, I) = 0\), where \((a, b)\) means \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\). All four are zero. The same for \(\mathcal B\).

Source: WM1990 (15), (16) (PDF p. 3): the structure \(\phi_{\mathrm{n}} = \phi_{\mathrm{n}}^R + \mathrm{i}\phi_{\mathrm{n}}^I\) and the orthogonality. Items 1 to 3 are our proof.

For mode 1 the same numerical computation gives \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}) = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}) = 3{,}70110\) and \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}) = -10^{-8}\), which is zero up to the error of the rule and is item 2 of the corollary. Together \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = 7{,}40220\), \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = -17{,}44103\,\mathrm{i}\) and so \(-\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle/\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = 2{,}35619\,\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{i}\omega_1\), which is item 1 of the theorem for this mode. These are the numbers of figure 26.43 with two more decimals.

26.6.3 Expansion in modes

The goal is to solve the initial value problem: at \(t = 0\) the string has shape \(w_0\) and velocity \(w_1\), so the state \(\vek z_0 = (w_1, w_0)\). Which motion follows? For the string at rest (theorem 13.11) we wrote the motion as a sum of modes with coefficients from orthogonality. Here there are two coordinates per mode, \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\), because each mode has two real parts. We write

\[\vek z(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^\infty\Big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(t)\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(t)\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\Big) . \tag{26.43}\]

The theorem that follows says which coefficients this must have. We do not prove the completeness of the expansion, that is that every state of \(S\) is such a sum: Wickert and Mote assume it (WM1990, PDF p. 3, "it is assumed that the expansion is complete"). For the string at rest theorem 13.11 proves it from Fourier series, for the moving string the proof remains open and we mark it as cited, not proved.

Theorem 26.34 Modal coordinates of the moving string (modalne koordinate gibajoče se strune)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and fixed eyelets be given, \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) its modes with distinct \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\) (theorem 26.13) and \(N_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\). Let \(\vek z(t) = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) be a motion that the sum (26.43) represents at every time \(t\) so that the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\), the derivative in time and the integral may be applied term by term. Then the point \((\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\) turns on a circle with angular velocity \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\):

\[\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} , \qquad \dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} , \tag{26.44}\]

so \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(t) = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(t) = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t - \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), with the initial values

\[\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) = \frac{(\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})}{N_{\mathrm{n}}} , \qquad \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0) = \frac{(\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})}{N_{\mathrm{n}}} . \tag{26.45}\]
Idea

We insert the sum in equation (26.34) and multiply it by one of the real states. Because of theorem 26.32 and corollary 26.33 one term remains, and the equation for the coefficient is the equation of an oscillator.

Proof

We must show that multiplication by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\) gives (26.44) and that the initial condition gives (26.45).

  1. Equation (26.34) for the sum (26.43) gives \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\big) = \vek 0\). By corollary 26.33 (item 1) \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\) and \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\), so the sum reads \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big((\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + (\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\big) = \vek 0\).
  2. We multiply this by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\). By corollary 26.33 (items 2 and 3) the mixed products are zero and only the term with \(n = m\) and with \(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\) remains of the sum, and gives \(N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R} - \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}) = 0\). Multiplying by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\) leaves \(N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I} + \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) = 0\), because \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}) = N_{\mathrm{m}} > 0\). This gives (26.44).
  3. From (26.44), \(\ddot\xi^{\mathrm R}_{\mathrm{n}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\,\xi^{\mathrm R}_{\mathrm{n}}\), so \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = a\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + b\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\) (theorem 9.41), and \(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\) gives \(b = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\). The same for \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\).
  4. Initial condition: \(\vek z(0) = \vek z_0\), so \((\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R})\big) = N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\) by items 2 and 3 of corollary 26.33. The same for \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\). This is (26.45).

Source: WM1990 (19), (20), (21b) (PDF p. 3): modal coordinates and their initial values (Meirovitch, 1975). The proof and the choice of \(N_{\mathrm{n}}\) are ours, the completeness of the expansion is assumed (WM1990, PDF p. 3) and not proved.

Let us see whether this works on an example. We take the string with \(L = \mu = T = 1\) and \(v/c = 1/2\) from the previous examples and give it \(w_0 = \sin\pi x\), \(w_1 = 0\), so the state \(\vek z_0 = (0, \sin\pi x)\) (the initial shape is the first sine of chapter 13, not a mode of the moving string, since \(\varphi_1^{\mathrm R} = \sin\pi x\cos(\pi x/2)\)). By equation (26.45) the coefficients are

\[\xi_1^{\mathrm R}(0) = \xi_1^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0{,}67906 , \quad \xi_2^{\mathrm R}(0) = 0{,}125 , \ \xi_2^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0 , \quad \xi_3^{\mathrm R}(0) = -\xi_3^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0{,}02646 , \ \ldots \tag{26.46}\]

and the sum of the first \(N\) terms at \(t = 0\) gives the displacement \(w_0\) and velocity zero with the following errors (largest deviation over \(x\)):

\(N\) 1 2 4 8 12
\(\max\lvert w - w_0\rvert\) \(0{,}0850\) \(0{,}0397\) \(0{,}0036\) \(0{,}00042\) \(0{,}00012\)
\(\max\lvert w_{\mathrm{t}}\rvert\) \(0{,}616\) \(0{,}323\) \(0{,}036\) \(0{,}010\) \(0{,}005\)

We draw the first column of the table at the top of figure 26.46. Above the axis \(x\) with the eyelets we draw, grey and dashed, the initial shape \(w_0 = \sin\pi x\), which the expansion must hit. Over it we draw the sum of the first pair, \(0{,}67906\,(\varphi_1^{\mathrm R} + \varphi_1^{\mathrm I})\). The largest gap between them is \(0{,}0850\) at \(x = 0{,}189\). With every added pair the orange curve comes closer to the grey one, at \(N = 12\) the gap is \(0{,}00012\), in the figure less than the thickness of a line.

The error falls with \(N\), which is observed, not proved: the convergence of the expansion is not proved, as said above. The motion at later times is obtained by rotating the pair \((\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\) with angular velocity \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) by equation (26.44). Below left in figure 26.46 this is drawn for mode 1. In the plane with the coordinates \(\xi_1^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\xi_1^{\mathrm I}\) the starting point is \((0{,}679,\ 0{,}679)\). At \(t = 0\) we have \(\dot\xi_1^{\mathrm R} = \omega_1\xi_1^{\mathrm I} > 0\) and \(\dot\xi_1^{\mathrm I} = -\omega_1\xi_1^{\mathrm R} < 0\), so the point goes to the right and down, clockwise. After the time \(t\) it is turned by the angle \(\omega_1 t\) (drawn for \(\omega_1 t = \pi/3\)). It stays all the time on the circle of radius \(\sqrt 2\cdot 0{,}67906 = 0{,}960\), because the solution in theorem 26.34 gives \((\xi_1^{\mathrm R})^2 + (\xi_1^{\mathrm I})^2 = \xi_1^{\mathrm R}(0)^2 + \xi_1^{\mathrm I}(0)^2\) for every \(t\).

The circle shows a second meaning of orthogonality, which the curves of figure 26.44 do not show: orthogonality tells how the modes share the conserved quantity. By theorem 26.21 the quantity \(\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12\int_0^L(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \kappa\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is constant during the motion, and by equation (26.37) it is half the product of the state with itself, \(\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12(\mathcal A\vek z, \vek z)\). The sum of the first \(N\) pairs is itself a motion of the string. We write out its product term by term. The mixed terms between different modes and between the real and the imaginary part of the same mode are zero by corollary 26.33, so what remains is

\[\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^{N} N_{\mathrm{n}}\Big(\big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\big)^2 + \big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\big)^2\Big) . \tag{26.47}\]

Every mode carries its own share, set by the radius of its circle. Since the point stays on the circle, the share does not change during the motion: the modes do not exchange the conserved quantity. Without orthogonality mixed terms would remain in the sum and the share of one mode could not be told. In the example the initial state has \(\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12\kappa\int_0^1\pi^2\cos^2(\pi x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 3\pi^2/16 = 1{,}8506\). Mode 1 carries \(\tfrac12\cdot 3{,}70110\cdot 0{,}960^2 = 1{,}7067\), that is \(92{,}2\,\%\), mode 2 \(6{,}25\,\%\), and modes 3 and 4 \(1{,}26\,\%\) and \(0{,}24\,\%\), together \(99{,}97\,\%\). The sum of the shares approaches \(100\,\%\), which is one more observation in favour of the completeness of the expansion, not a proof.

For the steel band of section 26.1 (dimensions, tension and speeds are our choice) the frequency of the first mode at \(v = c/2 = 56{,}6\) m/s is \(f_1 = (1 - v^2/c^2)\cdot 56{,}61 = 0{,}75\cdot 56{,}61 = 42{,}5\) Hz, where \(56{,}61\) Hz is the frequency of the first mode at \(v = 0\) (section 26.3), and this expansion would write any initial displacement of the band as a sum of sines of these frequencies with shifted phases.

Let us also look at the way back to the string at rest (section 26.1 has \(v = 0\) as a special case). For \(v = 0\) we have \(\mathcal G = 0\), \(k_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = 0\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = (0, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\), \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = (\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, 0)\). Equation (26.45) gives for the initial point \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) \propto \int\kappa\,w_0'\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\,(\pi n/L)^2\int w_0\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) (by lemma 6.13) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0) \propto \mu\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\int w_1\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). These are the coefficients from the initial displacement and the initial velocity, as the expansion in modes of the string at rest gives them (theorem 13.11).

What has this section given us? The orthogonality of the moving string does not go by the mass product but by the state product (26.32) with the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) (theorem 26.32), which we showed by integration by parts and the eigenvalue equation. The expansion in modes (theorem 26.34) writes the response to an initial condition with the same steps as for the string at rest, and orthogonality tells that every mode carries a constant share of the conserved quantity \(\mathcal E^*\) (equation (26.47)). We already met a first-order form for damping (section 20.8), there with two symmetric matrices, here with one symmetric and one skew-symmetric operator. Later we shall need the two operators and the state product for the beam in section 26.7, where the second order is replaced by the fourth. The completeness of the expansion and the convergence in the example remain unproved. We do not yet treat the Green's function, which WM1990 derives from the same orthogonality (PDF p. 3 and 4), nor the response to a moving force, which WM1990 computes for a monocable aerial tramway with a payload (enovrvna žičnica, PDF p. 4 and 5).

26.7 The moving beam

The string of sections 26.1 to 26.5 has no bending stiffness. A real band or saw blade has a thickness and bends only if we bend it, like a ruler. This section asks three questions. How does the equation of the moving string change if the band has bending stiffness? How large is the change for the steel band of example A, that is, is the string a good model of the band? And what happens to the critical speed of section 26.4? The last question leads to a kinship: the critical speed of the beam is the critical force of the column of chapter 8, converted into a speed.

26.7.1 Model and equation

We draw the band as before (figure 26.47, top). It is held in two supports, fixed in space at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and slides through them with speed \(v\) towards increasing \(x\), drawn as the velocity arrow. The shape of the band is the graph of the deflection \(w(x, t)\) over the \(x\) axis, with the deflection \(w\) upwards, strongly enlarged for clarity. The particles of the band that lie between \(a + vt\) and \(b + vt\) at time \(t\) we call the piece: it is the same material all the time, moving together along \(x\) with speed \(v\) (section 26.1, lemma 26.1). Below we draw the piece in a separate picture and enter the forces that act on it.

We draw the forces on the piece in the bottom picture one by one. The piece is curved along the band like the band. At each end its neighbour pulls it with the tension force \(T\) along the tangent: the right part in the direction of increasing \(x\), the left part in the opposite direction. Each pull starts at the end of the piece on which it acts. The tension along the tangent gives the vertical component \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\): the tangent has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), so the vertical part of the pull is \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) times the horizontal part, and for a slope up to \(0{,}01\) the horizontal part differs from \(T\) by less than \(0{,}005\) %. Because the band has bending stiffness, the neighbour does not act only along the tangent: the part to the right of \(b + vt\) also acts on the piece with the vertical shear force \(V(b + vt, t)\) upwards and the part to the left of \(a + vt\) with \(-V(a + vt, t)\), drawn as the force \(V(a + vt, t)\) downwards, by the law of action and reaction, as for the beam in chapter 13 (lemma 13.38). Finally the right part also acts with a bending moment \(M(b + vt, t)\) counterclockwise and the left part with \(-M(a + vt, t)\), drawn as \(M(a + vt, t)\) clockwise.

A band with bending stiffness is thus a moving string with one more force. We write the model with all idealizations named.

Definition 26.35 Axially moving beam (gibajoči nosilec)

An axially moving beam is a band of length \(L\) between two supports fixed in space at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), which moves through them with constant transport speed \(v > 0\) in the direction of increasing \(x\). Its deflection \(w(x, t)\) is a real function of two variables with continuous partial derivatives up to the fourth order. The idealizations of the moving string of definition 26.3 hold (constant mass \(\mu\) per unit length, constant tension \(T\), \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}01\), the transport speed \(v\) the same for all particles), except the idealization of zero bending stiffness, which is replaced by two new ones, (i) and (ii):

(i) The band has constant bending stiffness \(EI\) and in every cross-section the moment \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as the beam in chapter 13 (theorem 13.37). (ii) The rotary inertia of the cross-sections, that is the kinetic energy of the rotation of the cross-sections owing to the turn \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), is neglected, as for that beam.

The supports are either simple (členkasta), where \(w = 0\) and \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), or fixed (vpeta), where \(w = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), at both ends and at every time.

Source: Model: WM1990 §2.2 (PDF p. 2), which extends the moving string by bending stiffness, and Mote 1965 (cited there, not in the books). The naming of the idealizations and the bounds are ours.

The idealization (ii) has a measure. We estimate it for the steel band of example A (band \(0{,}9 \times 50\) mm, \(L = 1\) m, stress \(100\) MPa, \(T = 4500\) N, \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, the dimensions and speeds are our choice, we have no data of real belts). Figure 26.48 shows what we neglect. The straight band of thickness \(h\) has its cross-section upright (grey, dashed). In the bent band the same cross-section is perpendicular to the centre line, as for the beam in chapter 13, so in bending it turns by the slope angle \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The cross-section moves with the band at the speed \(v\), so its angular velocity is the time derivative of \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) following a particle that moves with speed \(v\), that is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (chain rule as in lemma 26.1), and the transverse velocity of a particle is \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The kinetic energy of rotation per unit length is \(\tfrac12\,\rho I\,(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}})^2\), and the kinetic energy of the transverse motion is \(\tfrac12\,\rho A\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\). The angular velocity is the derivative of the transverse velocity with respect to \(x\), so for a mode with wave number \(k\) it is of the order \(k\) times the transverse velocity, and the ratio is of the order \((I/A)\,k^2\) with \(I/A = h^2/12\) for a rectangle of thickness \(h\). For \(h = 0{,}9\) mm this is \(6{,}75\cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 9{,}87\ \text{m}^{-2} = 6{,}7\cdot 10^{-7}\) for the first mode (\(k = \pi/L\)). The estimate is an order of magnitude, not a calculation. What does the idealization do to the result? For \(v = 0\) and simple supports the sine stays the shape of the vibration also with rotary inertia. For the same shape the kinetic energy is larger by the factor \(1 + (I/A)\,k^2\), the elastic energy is the same, and in a vibration the largest kinetic energy equals the largest elastic energy, so \(\omega^2\) is smaller by the same factor. The frequency is lower by half the ratio, \(3{,}3\cdot 10^{-7}\) of \(56{,}651\) Hz, that is \(0{,}00002\) Hz. When does the idealization stop holding? The ratio reaches \(1\) % when \(k^2 = 0{,}12/h^2\), that is at the wavelength \(2\pi/k = 18\,h = 16\) mm (mode \(j = 122\)). For waves only a few tens of thicknesses long the rotation of the cross-sections would have to be kept, for the first modes of the band it need not.

Now we derive the equation. The way is that of section 26.1: the momentum of a piece made of the same particles, then the vanishing of the integrand. The band is the same as for the string, and the shear force joins the forces at the ends of the piece.

Theorem 26.36 Equation of motion of the axially moving beam (gibalna enačba gibajočega nosilca)

Let \(w\) be the deflection of an axially moving beam by definition 26.35 without external load, and let the law of momentum hold for every piece of particles: the derivative of the momentum of a piece is the sum of the transverse forces that the two neighbouring parts exert on it. Then for every \(x \in [0, L]\) and every \(t\)

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} , \tag{26.48}\]

that is

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big) + \big(\mu v^2 - T\big)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = 0 . \tag{26.49}\]
Proof

We must show that the piece has the momentum \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) with \(g(s, t) = w(s + vt, t)\), that its derivative equals the difference of the forces at the ends of the piece, and that the equation at a point follows from the integral over the piece.

  1. A particle that is at \(x = s + vt\) at time \(t\) has the deflection \(g(s, t) = w(s + vt, t)\). So for every \(t\) the piece has the particles \(s \in [a, b]\), the variable \(s\) is their label and the limits are constant. By lemma 26.1 the velocity of the particle is \(g_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the acceleration \(g_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), evaluated at \((s + vt, t)\) (chain rule, lemma 8.30).
  2. The momentum of the piece is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}s\). The limits are constant and \(g_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is continuous, so its derivative in time is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) by lemma 4.19.
  3. The transverse force with which the right part acts on the piece at \(x = b + vt\) is the sum of the component of the tension \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (derivation 13.1, the tangent has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\)) and of the shear force \(V = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\) (balance of moments of the piece, lemma 13.38, item 1, step 2, with rotary inertia neglected by idealization (ii)). The reason lies in the moments at the ends of the piece: on a short piece they differ by about \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) times the length of the piece (exactly in the lemma), the pull \(T\) along the tangent does not turn the piece, there is no rotary inertia, so this difference is balanced only by the pair of shear forces with the length of the piece as arm, hence \(V = -M_{\mathrm{x}} = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\). The left part acts at \(x = a + vt\) with the opposite value (law of action and reaction). The force is \(F = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\), so the sum of the forces on the piece is \(F(b + vt, t) - F(a + vt, t)\).
  4. The law of momentum from steps 2 and 3 (the difference of the forces at the ends of the piece) is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}s = F(b + vt, t) - F(a + vt, t)\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55, item 1, antiderivative \(F\) in \(x\)) the right-hand side is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{vt}}^{b+vt} F_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and by the shift \(x = s + vt\) it is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b F_{\mathrm{x}}(s + vt, t)\,\mathrm{d}s\) with \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\).
  5. From steps 1 and 4, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r(s + vt, t)\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) with \(r = \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}) - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\), a continuous function. At time \(t\) every interval \([x_1, x_2] \subset [0, L]\) is a piece with \(a = x_1 - vt\) and \(b = x_2 - vt\). So \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} r(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every such interval.
  6. Let \(x_1 \in [0, L)\), the left end of the piece. By step 5 the function \(x \mapsto \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x} r\,\mathrm{d}s\) is identically zero, by the fundamental theorem (item 2) its derivative is \(r(x, t)\), so \(r(x, t) = 0\). For \(x = L\) we take the intervals \([x_1, L]\) and continuity. Thus equation (26.48) is proved, and equation (26.49) follows by rearranging the terms.

Source: WM1990 (5) (PDF p. 2): \(\rho(U_{\mathrm{TT}} + 2VU_{\mathrm{XT}} + V^2 U_{\mathrm{XX}}) - P U_{\mathrm{XX}} + EI\,U_{\mathrm{XXXX}} = F\), the same equation with \(F = 0\) (\(\rho \to \mu\), \(P \to T\)). The source cites Mote 1965 and does not derive it. The proof with a piece of particles is not from the source, the way is as for theorem 26.4.

We test the equation on two limiting cases. For \(EI = 0\) what remains is \(\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the equation of the moving string (theorem 26.4). For \(v = 0\) what remains is \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), a beam with an axial force. For the band of example A the sine is still a solution: \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\cos\omega t\) satisfies the equation exactly when \(\mu\,\omega^2 = T\,(\pi/L)^2 + EI\,(\pi/L)^4\), because \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2 w\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = (\pi/L)^4 w\). The first term gives \(T\,(\pi/L)^2 = 44\,413\) N/m², the second \(EI\,(\pi/L)^4 = 58{,}0\) N/m², so \(f_1 = 56{,}651\) Hz. The string has \(f_1 = c/(2L) = 56{,}614\) Hz: the bending stiffness raises the frequency by \(0{,}065\) %, which is half the ratio of the second and the first term, \(\tfrac12\cdot 0{,}1306\ \% = 0{,}0653\ \%\).

For \(v \ne 0\) the sine is no longer a solution. The term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) (the material flows with speed \(v\)) contains \(-2v\,(\pi/L)\,\omega\cos(\pi x/L)\sin\omega t\), and the cosine occurs in no other term. This is the same reason as for the string (section 26.3): the oscillation is no longer standing. We therefore find the natural oscillations by the Galerkin method with the sines of section 26.5. With \(w = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\sin(j\pi x/L)\) and \(k_{\mathrm{j}} = j\pi/L\) we get \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with

\[M_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,\mu L , \qquad K_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,L\,\big(EI\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^4 - (\mu v^2 - T)\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^2\big) , \qquad G_{\mathrm{jk}} = \frac{4\mu v\,j\,k}{j^2 - k^2}\ \ (j + k\ \text{odd}) , \tag{26.50}\]

all other entries are zero. The last value follows from \(G_{\mathrm{jk}} = 2\mu v\,k_{\mathrm{k}} \int_0^L \sin k_{\mathrm{j}} x\,\cos k_{\mathrm{k}} x\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\sin a\cos b = \tfrac12(\sin(a + b) + \sin(a - b))\), where \(\int_0^L \sin(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = 2L/(m\pi)\) for odd \(m\) and \(0\) for even \(m\). The matrix \(\mat G\) is skew (\(G_{\mathrm{kj}} = -G_{\mathrm{jk}}\)). For example A and \(N = 24\) sines we get the first frequency \(f_1\) as follows (the string by the equation \(f_1 = (c/2L)(1 - v^2/c^2)\)):

\(v\) (m/s) 0 20 40 80
\(f_1\) of the beam (Hz) 56,651 54,891 49,613 28,504
\(f_1\) of the string (Hz) 56,614 54,847 49,548 28,352
difference 0,065 % 0,080 % 0,130 % 0,535 %

The difference grows with the speed. The reason is that the motion reduces the tension that is left for bending: \(T - \mu v^2\) is \(2254\) N out of \(4500\) N at \(80\) m/s, while the bending part \(EI\,k_1^2 = 5{,}9\) N stays the same and so has a larger share. How much exactly is told only by the calculation in the table. At \(v = 80\) m/s the difference is still below \(0{,}6\) %. In this range the band is therefore a string and the model of sections 26.1 to 26.5 suffices. When does the bending stiffness overcome the tension? The term \(EI\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^4\) exceeds \(T\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) when \(j^2 > T L^2/(\pi^2 EI) = 766\), that is from \(j = 28\) on. The wavelength is then \(2L/28 = 71\) mm, which is \(79\) times the thickness of the band.

The critical speed remains. There the bending stiffness changes not only the numbers but the content of the theorem.

26.7.2 Critical speed of the beam

Let us see what equation (26.49) says if the band rests in shape and only the material moves. Let \(w\) not depend on time. The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) drop out and what remains is

\[EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + \big(\mu v^2 - T\big)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.51}\]

This is the equation of the column of chapter 8, \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), with the force

\[P = \mu v^2 - T . \tag{26.52}\]

We know the reason from figure 26.25 in section 26.4: a piece of material that runs at the speed \(v\) along a curve at rest needs the force \(\mu v^2\sigma\), and the tension gives it \(T\sigma\), where \(\sigma\) is the change of slope along the piece. Here we look at the same thing from the side of the column (figure 26.49). At the top left is the band in a fixed shape, which the tension \(T\) pulls at its ends and through which the material runs at the speed \(v\). Every second the mass \(\mu v\) passes through each cross-section with the velocity \(v\), so the momentum \(\mu v^2\): at \(80\) m/s this is \(28{,}08\) kg/s times \(80\) m/s, which is \(2246\) N. On a curve the direction of this momentum turns, and the force that turns it is \(\mu v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) per unit length (the acceleration \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of lemma 26.1). A pull \(T\) along the tangent gives the curved band exactly such a force, \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The band must give the force \(\mu v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) to the material, so that much less of the tension is left to it: the flow of material acts as a compression \(\mu v^2\) along the band. The pull \(T\) and the compression \(\mu v^2\) together are the compressive force \(P = \mu v^2 - T\) on a column of the same shape at the top right. While \(P\) is negative the band is still in tension, only with the smaller force \(T - \mu v^2\). When \(P\) is positive the band is a column in compression. What this view adds to the earlier one is that we may use for the band everything we already know about the column.

Figure 26.50 shows this for the band of example A. The left graph is the force \(P(v) = \mu v^2 - T\) from \(-T = -4500\) N at \(v = 0\) to \(1900\) N at \(v = 135\) m/s: a parabola that passes from tension (\(P < 0\)) to compression (\(P > 0\)) at the speed of the string \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s. At \(80\) m/s the tension left is still \(2254\) N, half of \(4500\) N, which we used at the table of frequencies. The critical forces of the column, that is the forces at which a straight column can stay bent, are \(\pi^2 EI/L^2 = 5{,}876\) N and \(4\pi^2 EI/L^2 = 23{,}503\) N, which at the scale of \(4500\) N is less than the thickness of a line. So we draw a magnification of the neighbourhood of the point \(P = 0\) and get the right graph: on it the two critical forces are horizontal lines, \(5{,}876\) N and \(23{,}503\) N, that the parabola crosses at \(113{,}30\) m/s and \(113{,}52\) m/s, which are \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) for simple and for fixed supports.

We name the speed at which this happens and estimate it. For the string we called critical in section 26.4 the speed at which the behaviour changes. For the beam the same holds.

Theorem 26.37 Critical speed of the axially moving beam (kritična hitrost gibajočega nosilca)

Let the axially moving beam be as in definition 26.35 with simple supports (case a) or with fixed supports (case b). Let \(P = \mu v^2 - T\), \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/L^2\) in case a and \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 4\pi^2 EI/L^2\) in case b, and

\[v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\frac{T + P_{\mathrm{cr}}}{\mu}} . \tag{26.53}\]

For \(\mathcal Q(\eta) = \int_0^L \big(EI\,\eta''^2 - P\,\eta'^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\) it holds:

  1. For every solution \(w\) (band) of equation (26.49), \(\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12\int_0^L \mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \tfrac12\,\mathcal Q(w(\cdot, t))\) is constant in time.
  2. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\), \(\mathcal Q(\eta) > 0\) for every twice continuously differentiable \(\eta \ne 0\) with the support conditions, equation (26.51) with the same conditions has only the solution \(w = 0\), and with \(\theta = 1 - \max(P, 0)/P_{\mathrm{cr}} > 0\) we have \(\theta\,EI\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le 2\,\mathcal E^*\) at every time.
  3. For \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\), equation (26.51) has a nonzero solution: \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\) in case a and \(w = 1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\) in case b, and \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\) for it.
Proof

We must show the conservation of the functional in time, the positivity of the form \(\mathcal Q\) below the limit by the theorems on the column, and the solution at the limit. Below, \(w\) has continuous derivatives up to the fourth order and satisfies the support conditions at every time.

  1. We multiply equation (26.49) by \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). By lemma 4.19, \(\int \mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12\int\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. The term with \(2v\) is \(2\mu v\int w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \mu v\,\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\), because \(w = 0\) at both supports at every time, so also \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\). The term of the gyroscopic force thus does no work, which is a property of the force (lemma 26.26).
  3. By integration by parts (corollary 3.56), \(\int P\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[P\,w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\big]_0^L - P\int w_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12 P\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) at the supports.
  4. Twice by parts: \(\int EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = EI\big[w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}} - w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big]_0^L + EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The first term is zero (\(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)). The second is zero for simple supports (\(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\)) and for fixed supports (\(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\), because \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at every time). What remains is \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12\,EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  5. The sum of steps 1 to 4 is \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\big(\tfrac12\int\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \tfrac12\int (EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 - P\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\big) = 0\). This is item 1.
  6. For \(P \le 0\), \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge EI\int\eta''^2\), for \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} > P > 0\) by theorem 8.150 (case a) or 8.151 (case b), step 1 of their proofs, \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge EI\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\int\eta''^2\). So \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge \theta\,EI\int\eta''^2\). If \(\int\eta''^2 = 0\), then \(\eta''= 0\), \(\eta\) is linear and because of \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\) equal to zero. Therefore \(\mathcal Q > 0\) for \(\eta \ne 0\). The condition \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) is \(\mu v^2 < T + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), that is \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\). On the right graph this is the part of the parabola below the dashed line, below \(5{,}876\) N in case a and below \(23{,}503\) N in case b.
  7. The static solution: we multiply equation (26.51) by \(w\) and integrate by parts twice.
