The terms at the ends are zero, because \(w = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) or \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), what remains is \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\), as in the proof of theorem 8.150. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) step 6 gives \(w = 0\). Item 2 follows also from step 5: \(\theta\,EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 \le \mathcal Q(w) \le 2\,\mathcal E^*\).
  8. At \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) we have \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). For \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = (\pi/L)^4 w\), so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \big(EI\,(\pi/L)^4 - (\pi^2 EI/L^2)(\pi/L)^2\big)\,w = 0\). The conditions of simple supports hold (\(w = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at \(0\) and \(L\)). For \(w = 1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\), \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = -(2\pi/L)^4\cos(2\pi x/L)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\pi/L)^2\cos(2\pi x/L)\), so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\pi/L)^2\cos(2\pi x/L)\,\big(-EI\,(2\pi/L)^2 + 4\pi^2 EI/L^2\big) = 0\), and \(w = w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at \(0\) and \(L\). By step 7, therefore, \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\).

Source: WM1990 (13) (PDF p. 2): \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\mu^2 + \pi^2}\) for simple and \(\sqrt{\mu^2 + 4\pi^2}\) for fixed supports, in dimensionless notation \(\mu^2 = P L^2/EI\) from WM1990 (6) (our \(T L^2/EI\)). Appendix A (PDF pp. 6 and 7), (A1) and (A2): the static equation and the positive definiteness of \(\langle u, Ku\rangle\). For fixed supports the source gives the static solution only as \(v^2 - \mu^2 = (2n\pi)^2\). In chapter 8 it is shown for fixed ends that the next zero of the determinant is \(kL = 8{,}987\) (\(\tan(kL/2) = kL/2\)): \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) (the first zero) does not change. The functional \(\mathcal E^*\) for the beam is not from the source, the pattern is CHEN2005 (33) (PDF p. 7) for the string.

What we have shown. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the form \(\mathcal Q\) is positive and the functional \(\mathcal E^*\) bounds \(\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), so the shape of the band cannot grow in time beyond the bound set by the initial state. At \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) there exists an equilibrium shape, at the bottom of figure 26.49: a half-wave of the sine between simple supports or the wave \(1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\) with a horizontal tangent at fixed supports. Each may be enlarged by an arbitrary factor: the band can stay bent at unchanged tension and speed. The name critical speed has the same reason as the critical force of the column: below it the straight position is energetically stable (definition 8.72), at it the question is decided whether a bent shape stays in equilibrium at all. For \(EI \to 0\), \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} \to 0\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}} \to \sqrt{T/\mu} = c\): the critical speed of the string of section 26.4 is the limit of the case without bending stiffness.

Now a number. For the band of example A the ratio \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}/T\) is small: \(5{,}876/4500 = 1/766 = 0{,}001306\) in case a. We denote it by \(\varepsilon\), so that \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\,\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\). Since \((1 + \varepsilon/2)^2 = 1 + \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/4\), the difference is \(1 + \varepsilon/2 - \sqrt{1 + \varepsilon} = (\varepsilon^2/4)/\big(1 + \varepsilon/2 + \sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\big)\) (the difference of the squares divided by the sum). The denominator is larger than \(2\), so the difference is smaller than \(\varepsilon^2/8 = 2{,}1\cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\,(1 + \varepsilon/2)\) holds with a relative error below \(2{,}1\cdot 10^{-7}\). Therefore \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 113{,}23\,(1 + 0{,}000653)\), that is \(113{,}30\) m/s, which is \(0{,}0653\) % above \(c\). For fixed supports \(\varepsilon = 23{,}503/4500 = 0{,}005223\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) is \(113{,}52\) m/s, \(0{,}2608\) % above \(c\). The difference between \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(c\) is \(0{,}07\) m/s out of \(113\) m/s for this band, so the critical speed of the string is a good approximation. It is different for a band without tension: for \(T = 0\), \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = (\pi/L)\sqrt{EI/\mu} = 4{,}09\) m/s (simple supports) or \(8{,}18\) m/s (fixed). A string without tension has \(c = 0\), so critical speed zero, while the beam has it at a few metres per second. There the bending stiffness is not a correction but decides.

26.7.3 Test: a window of stability above the critical speed

Theorem 26.37 is one-sided: below \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is stable. We try to reverse it. For the column of chapter 8 the opposite holds: above \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the straight position is unstable. So it would be natural for the band to be unstable for every \(v > v_{\mathrm{c}}\). We show that this is not true (in the window it is stable), and why. The theorem is thereby tested on an example that it does not survive.

We use the dimensionless notation of WM1990: \(L = 1\), \(EI = 1\), \(\mu = 1\) and \(\bar T = T L^2/EI\) (in the source \(\mu^2\), but \(\mu\) is the mass per length for us, so we do not use it) and \(\bar v = v\sqrt{\mu L^2/EI}\) (in the source \(\nu\), which is Poisson's ratio in the book). Let \(\bar T = 100\) and simple supports. By equation (26.50), \(K_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,\big((j\pi)^4 + (100 - \bar v^2)\,(j\pi)^2\big)\), which is negative exactly for \(\bar v^2 > 100 + j^2\pi^2\). The limits are \(\bar v_1 = 10{,}4819\), \(\bar v_2 = 11{,}8101\) and \(\bar v_3 = 13{,}7414\) (SymPy and NumPy, num-07.out). The first is \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) of theorem 26.37.

Figure 26.51 shows what happens to the eigenvalues of the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with \(N = 24\) sines. On the axes are the speed \(\bar v\) from \(10\) to \(13\) and the largest real part of the eigenvalues \(\lambda\). Zero means that all eigenvalues are purely imaginary and the solutions are bounded oscillations, a positive real part means growth like \(e^{\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda\, t}\). The curve is zero up to \(10{,}48\), then rises to \(4{,}77\) at \(11{,}25\) and falls back to zero at \(11{,}81\). The real part \(4{,}77\) means that the deflection doubles in the time \(\ln 2/4{,}77 = 0{,}145\) (the unit of time is \(L^2\sqrt{\mu/EI}\)). Between \(11{,}81\) and \(12{,}18\) the curve is zero again: all eigenvalues are purely imaginary again. Above \(12{,}177\) the curve rises again and equals \(10{,}3\) at \(13\). The vertical lines mark \(\bar v_1\) and \(\bar v_2\) and the computed end of the window at \(12{,}177\).

The window between \(\bar v_2\) and \(12{,}18\) has an explanation that we prove for the system we use. We look at the first part, above \(\bar v_1\).

The proof runs on two planes of complex numbers (figure 26.52). The eigenvalues \(\lambda\) enter the proof only squared, so we first draw the plane of the number \(s = \lambda^2\). A bounded oscillation has \(\lambda = \pm\mathrm{i}\omega\), so \(s = -\omega^2\) on the negative half-axis. Every other \(s\), positive or complex in a conjugate pair, has square roots in the plane of \(\lambda\) that do not lie on the imaginary axis: \(\pm\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{k}}}\) on the real axis or four points, symmetric about both axes. In both cases at least one root falls into the right half-plane, where the solution grows. The lemma says that a negative determinant of the matrix \(\mat K\) pushes at least one \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) off the negative half-axis.

Lemma 26.38 Instability for a negative determinant of the stiffness (nestabilnost pri negativni determinanti togosti)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric positive definite \(N \times N\) matrix, \(\mat G\) skew and \(\mat K\) symmetric, all with constant real entries. If \(\det\mat K < 0\), the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) has a solution whose size grows like \(e^{\sigma t}\) with \(\sigma > 0\).

Proof

We must show that the polynomial \(p(\lambda) = \det(\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K)\) has a root with nonzero real part, and that this root gives a growing solution.

  1. The matrix \(\mat M\lambda^2 - \mat G\lambda + \mat K\) is the transpose of the matrix \(\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K\) (\(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\)), and the determinant does not change under transposition. So \(p(-\lambda) = p(\lambda)\) and \(p(\lambda) = q(\lambda^2)\) with a polynomial \(q\) of degree \(N\) with leading coefficient \(\det\mat M > 0\) and \(q(0) = p(0) = \det\mat K\).
  2. We write \(q(s) = \det\mat M\,\prod_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{N}(s - s_{\mathrm{k}})\) with complex roots \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\). Then \(\det\mat K = q(0) = \det\mat M\,\prod_{\mathrm{k}}(-s_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  3. If all \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) were real and \(\le 0\), every \(-s_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) and \(\det\mat K \ge 0\). Since \(\det\mat K < 0\), there is an \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) that is not real and \(\le 0\): it lies off the negative half-axis, so it is positive or complex.
  4. Let \(\lambda\) be a square root of such an \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\). If \(\lambda\) were purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\), then \(s_{\mathrm{k}} = \lambda^2 = -\omega^2 \le 0\) would be real. This is a contradiction, so \(\lambda\) has a nonzero real part. Since \(-\lambda\) is also a root, we may take \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = \sigma > 0\), the root in the right half-plane.
  5. For \(\lambda\) there is \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\) with \((\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K)\,\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), so \(\vek z(t) = \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\vek\varphi\) is a solution, with \(|\vek z(t)| = \mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}|\vek\varphi|\). Its real and imaginary parts are real solutions that together give \(|\vek z|^2 = |\mathrm{Re}\,\vek z|^2 + |\mathrm{Im}\,\vek z|^2\), so at least one grows like \(\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}\).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The theorem on the eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system with positive definite stiffness (theorem 26.27) is the converse direction, GR §2.11 (PDF pp. 137 to 141).

The lemma says: if \(\mat K\) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues, the system is unstable even if the Coriolis term \(\mat G\) is not zero. The proof also tells how the solution grows. The polynomial \(q\) has real coefficients, so complex roots come in conjugate pairs and the product \((-s_{\mathrm{k}})(-\bar s_{\mathrm{k}}) = |s_{\mathrm{k}}|^2\) of each pair is positive. A negative product of all \(-s_{\mathrm{k}}\) therefore needs a positive real \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\), and \(\lambda = \sqrt{s_{\mathrm{k}}}\) is real: the solution grows without oscillating, like a column that buckles. Our \(\mat K\) is diagonal, so \(\det\mat K = \prod K_{\mathrm{jj}}\) and the sign is decided by the number of negative entries. Between \(\bar v_1\) and \(\bar v_2\) only \(K_{11}\) is negative (SymPy), so by the lemma the system is unstable for every \(N \ge 1\). This agrees with figure 26.51: at \(\bar v = 10{,}6\) the largest real part is \(2{,}489\), at \(11\) it is \(4{,}508\) and at \(11{,}5\) it is \(4{,}324\) (num-07.out). Above \(\bar v_2\) both \(K_{11}\) and \(K_{22}\) are negative, the determinant is positive again and the lemma says nothing: it proves neither instability nor stability.

The stability in the window is computed, not proved, and we understand it with two sines. Let \(N = 2\) and \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat K = \mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) with \(k_1, k_2 < 0\), \(\mat G = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & g \\ -g & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (by equation (26.50), \(g = G_{12} = -8\bar v/3\)). The determinant of the lemma is

\[p(\lambda) = (m\lambda^2 + k_1)(m\lambda^2 + k_2) + g^2\lambda^2 = m^2\lambda^4 + \big(m\,(k_1 + k_2) + g^2\big)\lambda^2 + k_1 k_2 .\]

Purely imaginary roots require both roots \(\lambda^2\) to be real and negative. We denote \(b = m(k_1 + k_2) + g^2\). Since \(k_1 k_2 > 0\), the roots have the same sign, their sum is \(-b/m^2\), so both are negative and real exactly when \(b > 0\) and the discriminant \(b^2 - 4m^2 k_1 k_2 \ge 0\), that is \(b \ge 2m\sqrt{k_1 k_2}\). With \(|k_{\mathrm{i}}| = -k_{\mathrm{i}}\) this is \(g^2 - m\,(|k_1| + |k_2|) \ge 2m\sqrt{|k_1|\,|k_2|}\), which is the same as \(g^2 \ge m\,\big(\sqrt{|k_1|} + \sqrt{|k_2|}\big)^2\). At \(\bar v = 12\), \(g = -32\), \(g^2 = 1024\), \(k_1 = -168{,}43\), \(k_2 = -89{,}25\) and \(m = 1/2\), so \(m(\sqrt{|k_1|} + \sqrt{|k_2|})^2 = 251{,}4\). The condition is met with a large margin. The term \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) does no work and cannot add energy, but it couples two modes that would each grow alone into an oscillation. We call it gyroscopic stabilization (giroskopska stabilizacija), because \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) has the form of a gyroscopic force (section 26.5).

How a force that does no work stops the growth is shown by figure 26.53, with a motion instead of a polynomial. On the axes are the coefficients of the two sines, \(q_1\) and \(q_2\), and the state of the system is a point in this plane. Since \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) are negative, the elastic energy \(\tfrac12\,(k_1 q_1^2 + k_2 q_2^2)\) is a hill with its top at the origin, the grey ellipses are its contour lines, and the force \(-\mat K\,\vek q\) points down from the top, away from the origin. We release the point from rest at \(q_1 = 1\). Without the term \(\mat G\) it slides straight down the hill: \(q_1 = \cosh(18{,}35\,t)\), and at \(t = 0{,}1\) it is already at \(3{,}21\). With the term \(\mat G\) a further force acts on it, \(-\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\), which is always perpendicular to the velocity \(\dot{\vek q}\): its components are \((-g\,\dot q_2,\ g\,\dot q_1)\) and the scalar product with the velocity \((\dot q_1,\ \dot q_2)\) is \(-g\,\dot q_2\,\dot q_1 + g\,\dot q_1\,\dot q_2 = 0\). A force perpendicular to the velocity does not increase the speed, it only turns it. As soon as the point runs down the hill, this force bends it sideways and then back towards the top, and the path becomes a wreath of arcs around the top. In the time \(1{,}53\) that one round takes, the distance from the top stays between \(1\) and \(1{,}58\). The hill does not hold the point, the turning does. That is why the condition above is a lower bound for \(g^2\): the turning must be strong enough for the steepness of the hill. A spinning top stands in the same way: it is not held upright by its weight, which pulls it off the top, but by its spin.

Two sines do not explain the end of the window. For \(N = 2\) the limit of stability moves to \(13{,}85\), for \(N = 4\) it is \(12{,}181\) and for \(N = 24\) it is \(12{,}177\) (num-07.out): modes 3 and 4, which \(G_{\mathrm{jk}}\) couples with modes 1 and 2 (the sum \(j + k\) is odd), move the end of the window. WM1990 gives the window \(11{,}81 < \bar v < 12{,}18\) (PDF p. 6) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{c}} = 10{,}48\) (figure 4, PDF p. 5), which agrees with our calculation.

What we have got. Theorem 26.37 is correct and says only that below \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is stable, not that above it it is unstable. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is unstable at least as long as \(\mat K\) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues (lemma 26.38), then the Coriolis term decides. For the column of chapter 8 there is no Coriolis force and theorem 8.135 requires \(\mat G = \mat 0\): here it is not applicable. For the band of example A (\(\bar T = 7559\)) we did not compute windows, the numbers are for \(\bar T = 100\) as in the source. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the contribution of the nonlinear terms, which the model does not have, grows with the speed (WM1990 PDF p. 6, Mote 1966, Thurman and Mote 1969): the linear windows are therefore a property of the model, not a prediction.

26.8 Finite elements for the moving string

In section 26.5 we turned the moving string (gibajoča se struna) into a system of ordinary equations with the Galerkin method, where the trial functions were the sines of chapter 13. A sine reaches across the whole string, so every entry of the matrices is an integral over the full length, and at the speed \(v/c = 0{,}9\) two sines gave the second frequency \(5{,}65\) instead of \(1{,}19\). Chapters 7 and 12 showed another way: small pieces that we assemble, where each piece contributes its own matrix, computed once. The question of this section is whether that way also works when the equation is no longer symmetric because of the mixed derivative term \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). The answer has two parts. The matrix of this term is assembled from elements like the mass and stiffness matrices, and its symmetric part cancels at the interior nodes (figure 26.56), so after the two eyelets hold the ends it is antisymmetric. Therefore the system of elements inherits everything that we proved for the system of sines: the eigenvalues are purely imaginary and the energy is conserved.

Take the steel band of section 26.1: \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, tension \(T = 4500\) N, wave speed \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, span \(L = 1\) m. The dimensions of the band, the tension and the speeds are our own choice, no source in the books gives belt data (section 26.1). Let the band run at \(v = c/2 = 56{,}61\) m/s. By theorem 26.13 the lowest natural frequency is \(f_1 = \frac{c}{2L}\left(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\right) = 42{,}46\) Hz. A model of \(n = 4\), \(8\), \(16\) and \(32\) equal elements gives (the numbers are in the table below) \(f_1 = 45{,}32\), \(43{,}16\), \(42{,}64\) and \(42{,}50\) Hz (figure 26.58). All of them are above the true value and approach it. What of this we can prove and what we cannot, the section shows step by step.

The path is as follows, its steps are in figures 26.54, 26.55, 26.56, 26.58 and 26.59. First we show that the true solution satisfies a weak equation in which only first derivatives appear (lemma 26.39), because a trial function made of hat functions has kinks at the nodes and no second derivative. Then we compute the three element matrices (lemma 26.40). We assemble them and show that the total gyroscopic matrix is antisymmetric (corollary 26.41). At the end we try an end that no eyelet holds, and show that the energy is then no longer conserved (lemma 26.42).

26.8.1 The weak form

The model is the same as in section 26.1 (the elements are in figure 26.56): a string of mass \(\mu\) per length and tension \(T\) that moves along a fixed track with constant speed \(v\) through two eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), which are fixed in space and hold the displacement at zero, \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\). The idealizations of section 26.1 apply, the track speed is below critical, \(v < c\) with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4). We write \(w\) for the displacement, as in chapter 13, and the letter \(v\) is always the track speed in this chapter, never the displacement of chapter 7. The nodal displacements of an element are written \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) as there. By theorem 26.4 the equation of motion is

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (\mu v^2 - T)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.54}\]

We build the trial function from hat functions (definition 6.25). Let us draw it (figure 26.54). At the top is the track with nodes \(0\) to \(4\) at spacing \(h\), and the eyelets hold its ends. The trial function \(w_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a broken line through the nodal displacements \(d_1\), \(d_2\), \(d_3\), straight between the nodes. In the middle row is the hat function \(\psi_2\), which equals \(1\) at node \(2\) and \(0\) at all other nodes. It is zero at both eyelets, like each of \(\psi_1\), \(\psi_2\), \(\psi_3\). The bottom row shows the slope \(w_{\mathrm{h}}'\): it is constant on every element, so its graph is a staircase. At a node \(w_{\mathrm{h}}\) has a kink, and there the slope jumps from \((d_2 - d_1)/h\) to \((d_3 - d_2)/h\). The second derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the slope of the slope. On a step it is zero, and at the jump it does not exist, because the slope changes there by a finite amount over zero distance. So we cannot insert \(w_{\mathrm{h}}\) into equation (26.54). The way out is known from chapter 6: we multiply the equation by a test function and integrate by parts, so that one derivative passes to the test function. Then only first derivatives appear, which are staircases, and those we can integrate.

Lemma 26.39 Weak form of the moving string (šibka oblika gibajoče se strune)

Let \(w\) be a twice continuously differentiable solution of equation (26.54) on \([0, L]\) with \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\), and let \(\psi\) be a piecewise continuously differentiable function on \([0, L]\) (a test function, for example a tent function) with \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\). Then for every time \(t\)

\[\mu\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + 2\mu v\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L \psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 . \tag{26.55}\]
Proof

We must show that equation (26.55) follows from equation (26.54) when we multiply it by \(\psi\) and integrate, and that the last term gets a first derivative, the step, instead of a second, which does not exist at a kink.

  1. Multiply equation (26.54) at a chosen time by \(\psi(x)\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). The integral is linear (lemma 6.10), so \(\mu\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (\mu v^2 - T)\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\).
  2. The function \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuously differentiable because \(w\) is twice continuously differentiable, and \(\psi\) is piecewise continuously differentiable, like the hat, which is made of straight pieces. By lemma 6.13 with \(N = \psi\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) in place of \(w\) we have \(\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \psi(L)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) - \psi(0)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t) - \int_0^L \psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. Because \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\) (the test function is zero at both eyelets), both boundary terms are zero and \(\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\int\psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). Insert into step 1: the term \((\mu v^2 - T)\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) becomes \((T - \mu v^2)\int\psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is equation (26.55).

Source: WM1990 (1) (PDF p. 2) for the equation, step 2 is lemma 6.13. We derived the weak form ourselves, WM1990 does not treat elements (PDF p. 6 mentions only global discretizations).

The lemma states only one direction: the true solution satisfies equation (26.55). We do not need the converse. The lemma has two assumptions and each enters in one step. The first, that the true solution \(w\) is twice continuously differentiable, enters in step 2, where we integrate \(\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by parts. It holds for smooth initial shapes. For an initial shape with a kink, for example a string pulled aside at one point, the second derivative does not exist at the kink and the lemma does not hold in this form. This does not affect the matrices, because we compute them from equation (26.55) and not from the lemma. The second, \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\), enters in step 3 and removes the two boundary terms. What remains without it is shown in section 26.8.5. The Galerkin method (definition 6.42) demands that an approximation, not the true solution, satisfies equation (26.55), for every test function from the same family as the trial functions. The term with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is the mass term, the term with \(\psi' w_{\mathrm{x}}\) the stiffness term as in chapter 6, and the term with \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is the one that chapter 7 did not have. Its coefficient \(2\mu v\) is from the lemma on the acceleration of a material particle (lemma 26.1), where the same term arose from the chain rule.

26.8.2 Element matrices

We make the mesh as in chapter 7: \(n\) equal elements of length \(h = L/n\), nodes \(x_{\mathrm{k}} = kh\) for \(k = 0, \dots, n\), on each element the shape functions \(N_1 = (x_{\mathrm{b}} - x)/h\) and \(N_2 = (x - x_{\mathrm{a}})/h\) (definition 7.2). The displacements of nodes \(0\) and \(n\) are zero because of the eyelets, the unknowns are \(d_1(t), \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}-1}(t)\), and the trial function is \(w_{\mathrm{h}}(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n-1} d_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}(x)\), where \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the hat function of node \(j\).

Each term of equation (26.55) gives one of three integrals over the element. We draw the element as in chapter 7 (figure 26.55). First we take the element of length \(h\) between nodes \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\), in one step the horizontal axis and the two vertical lines that the nodes bound. On it we draw the function \(N_1\), which is \(1\) at the left node and \(0\) at the right, and the function \(N_2\), which is the other way round. Under each of them is a triangle with base \(h\) and height \(1\), its area is \(h/2\). We need the area because the integral of the product \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{j}}'\) is exactly the area under \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) times the value of the derivative \(N_{\mathrm{j}}'\), since the derivative is constant on the element: \(N_1' = -1/h\) and \(N_2' = 1/h\).

Lemma 26.40 Element matrices of the moving string (matrike elementa gibajoče se strune)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an element of length \(h\) with nodes \(1\) and \(2\), \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (d_1, d_2)^\T\) the nodal displacements, \(\mu\), \(T\) and \(v\) constant on the element, and \(N_1\), \(N_2\) the shape functions. The integrals of the terms of equation (26.55) over the element are

\[\mat m_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{\mu h}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mat g_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \tag{26.56}\]

where \((\mat m_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = \mu\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), \((\mat g_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = (T - \mu v^2)\int N_{\mathrm{i}}' N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\). Moreover:

  1. The sum \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}} + \mat g_{\mathrm{e}}^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(-2, 2)\) is diagonal, its entry \((1, 1)\) is \(-2\mu v\) and its entry \((2, 2)\) is \(+2\mu v\). These are the contributions of the elements to the diagonal. It does not depend on \(h\).
  2. For nodal displacements \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\,(d_2^2 - d_1^2)\). The squares are the displacements at the ends of the element.
Proof

We must show three integrals, the gyroscopic one is an area times a slope, and two consequences.

  1. By lemma 10.47 with \(\rho A = \mu\) the mass matrix is \(\frac{\mu h}{6}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the integral of the matrix of constant slopes \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat b_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac1{h^2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) times a constant coefficient, which is here \(T - \mu v^2\) instead of \(EA\). The proof of lemma 7.5 (steps 2 and 3) uses only that the coefficient is constant on the element, so \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  3. The derivatives are \(N_1' = -1/h\) and \(N_2' = 1/h\) (lemma 1.82), constant on the element. Hence \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = N_{\mathrm{j}}'\int N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The integral \(\int_0^h (1 - s/h)\,\mathrm{d}s = h - h/2 = h/2\) with \(s = x - x_{\mathrm{a}}\), and equally \(\int_0^h s/h\,\mathrm{d}s = h/2\). These are the areas of the triangles under \(N_1\) and \(N_2\).
  4. So \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac h2 N_{\mathrm{j}}'\), area times slope, which is \(-\tfrac12\) for \(j = 1\) and \(+\tfrac12\) for \(j = 2\), for both rows \(i\). Multiplication by \(2\mu v\) gives \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  5. Item 1: \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}^\T = \mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the sum is \(\mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  6. Item 2: \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\,(-d_1^2 + d_1 d_2 - d_1 d_2 + d_2^2) = \mu v\,(d_2^2 - d_1^2)\).

Source: The mass and stiffness matrices as in lemmas 10.47 and 7.5 (COOK (11.3-4) PDF p. 392, COOK (2.2-1) PDF p. 34). The gyroscopic matrix of the element is our own computation (SymPy, outlines/ch-jermeni/num-08.out A), the sources do not give it.

The proof showed why the matrix \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\) differs from \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\): it contains \(N_{\mathrm{j}}'\) and not \(N_{\mathrm{j}}\) or \(N_{\mathrm{i}}'\), so it is not symmetric. Its two rows are equal because the two shape functions have equal areas \(h/2\) under them. Item 1 is what we need: the symmetric part, which is the one that disturbs us, since in the equation \(\mat m\ddot{\vek d} + \mat g\dot{\vek d} + \mat k\vek d = \vek 0\) it would do work or take energy away, is only on the diagonal, namely \(-\mu v\) at the left and \(+\mu v\) at the right node of the element. Why the symmetric part? The power of the term \(\mat g\dot{\vek d}\) is the number \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat g\,\dot{\vek d}\). A number equals its own transpose, \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat g\,\dot{\vek d} = \dot{\vek d}^\T\mat g^\T\dot{\vek d}\), so it equals half the sum of the two, \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T(\mat g + \mat g^\T)\dot{\vek d}\). Only the symmetric part appears in it, the antisymmetric part gives no power (lemma 26.26). Item 2 says the same in words: the term \(\vek d^\T\mat g\,\vek d = \mu v\,\big(w(x_{\mathrm{b}})^2 - w(x_{\mathrm{a}})^2\big)\) depends only on the displacements at the edges \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\) of the element, nothing comes from the interior. So it equals the integral of a derivative, \(2\mu v\int w\,w_{\mathrm{x}} = \mu v\int (w^2)_{\mathrm{x}}\), which the fundamental theorem computes as a difference of boundary values.

The lemma assumes that \(\mu\), \(T\) and \(v\) are constant on the element. Here this holds exactly, because in the model of section 26.1 they are constant along the whole span. The assumption enters where we take a coefficient out of the integral (steps 1, 2 and 4 of the proof). If the tension varied along the element, its mean over the element would stand in \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) in place of \(T\), because the product \(N_{\mathrm{i}}' N_{\mathrm{j}}'\) is constant, and the form of the matrix would stay the same.

26.8.3 Assembly and antisymmetry

We assemble the elements as theorem 7.13 taught us. Let us see what happens to the diagonal of the gyroscopic matrix (figure 26.56). We draw \(n = 4\) elements with nodes \(0\) to \(4\) along the track. At every node one element reaches in from the right and one from the left. The element on the right of a node has it as its left node and contributes \(-\mu v\) to the diagonal, next to the node stands \(-1\) in units of \(\mu v\). The element on the left has it as its right node and contributes \(+\mu v\). The sum at interior nodes is \(0\), and at the end nodes \(-1\) stays at node \(0\) and \(+1\) at node \(4\). Nodes \(0\) and \(n\) are held by the eyelets, the displacement there is zero and their rows and columns drop out, so the symmetric part drops out of the system of unknowns \(d_1, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}-1}\) too.

Corollary 26.41 The assembled gyroscopic matrix is antisymmetric (skupna žiroskopska matrika je antisimetrična)

Let the string of section 26.8.1 be divided into \(n\) equal elements with nodes \(0, \dots, n\) and let \(v < c\). Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\), \(\mat K\) be matrices of order \(n - 1\) with entries

\[M_{\mathrm{ij}} = \mu\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad G_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad K_{\mathrm{ij}} = (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x \tag{26.57}\]

for \(i, j = 1, \dots, n-1\), and let the Galerkin system be \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek d} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek d} + \mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\) (equation (26.55) with \(\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\)). Then:

  1. The matrices \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\), \(\mat K\) are the sums over the elements of the element matrices of lemma 26.40, placed as in theorem 7.13.
  2. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat G}\) with all nodes \(0, \dots, n\) has \(\tilde{\mat G} + \tilde{\mat G}^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(-2, 0, \dots, 0, 2)\), which is nonzero only in the first and last entry. The matrix \(\mat G\) is antisymmetric, \(G_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{i}+1} = \mu v\), \(G_{\mathrm{i}+1,\mathrm{i}} = -\mu v\) and all other entries are zero.
  3. The matrices \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric and positive definite. The first form is the integral of the square of the trial function, the second the integral of the square of the slope with a positive coefficient.
  4. All eigenvalues of the system are purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with real \(\omega\), and \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek d} + \tfrac12\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d\) is constant.
Proof

We must show that the assembly happens as for the bar, where the diagonal cancels, and then that the properties of section 26.5 apply.

  1. By lemma 6.10 the integrals in equation (26.57) are sums of integrals over the elements. On an element that is not in the row of the connectivity table of node \(i\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\), like the tent outside its two elements (theorem 7.13, step 4), on the others \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the shape function of the element (step 5 of the same theorem). The piece of element \(e\) is therefore the entry of the element matrix of lemma 26.40 at the place that the connectivity table gives, which is item 1.
  2. Element \(e\) lies between nodes \(e - 1\) and \(e\). The diagonal entry \(\tilde G_{\mathrm{kk}}\) receives \(-\mu v\) from element \(k + 1\) (node \(k\) is its first) and \(+\mu v\) from element \(k\) (node \(k\) is its second), for \(k = 1, \dots, n-1\), and the sum is \(0\). Node \(0\) has only element \(1\) and gets \(-\mu v\), node \(n\) has only element \(n\) and gets \(+\mu v\). Off the diagonal, element \(e\) contributes its entry \((1, 2)\) at place \((e-1, e)\) with value \(\mu v\) and its entry \((2, 1)\) at place \((e, e-1)\) with value \(-\mu v\), no place gets two contributions, so \(\tilde{\mat G} + \tilde{\mat G}^\T\) is zero off the diagonal. Deleting rows and columns \(0\) and \(n\), which the eyelets hold, removes the only nonzero entries, and \(\mat G\) is antisymmetric with the stated entries.
  3. By item 2 of theorem 7.13, \(\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), every term is by lemma 10.47 nonnegative and positive for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} \ne \vek 0\). The sum is zero only if every \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), so \(\vek d = \vek 0\). The same theorem gives \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^n (d_{\mathrm{e}} - d_{\mathrm{e}-1})^2\) with \(d_0 = d_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) (equation (7.14)). For \(v < c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = \mu(c^2 - v^2) > 0\), so the sum is zero only if all differences are zero, and so all \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) equal \(d_0 = 0\). Zero differences mean zero slope on every element.
  4. By items 2 and 3 we have real matrices \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) symmetric and positive definite and \(\mat G\) antisymmetric, which are the assumptions of theorem 26.27, giving purely imaginary eigenvalues, and of lemma 26.26, giving the conservation of \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}}\).

Source: Assembly by theorem 7.13, the structure of the system (symmetric \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\), antisymmetric \(\mat G\)) as in GR §2.11 (PDF pp. 137 and 139). Items 1 to 3 are our own proof, the sources do not treat discrete models of moving strings.

The proof showed where the antisymmetry comes from: at every interior node the two neighbours cancel the symmetric part, since the node sees the same entry \(\mu v\) once with a plus and once with a minus sign. The same can be read from the definition: \(G_{\mathrm{ij}} + G_{\mathrm{ji}} = 2\mu v\int (\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}})'\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\mu v\,\big[\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\big]_0^L\), which is zero because all test functions vanish at the ends. For hat functions this means the same as item 2. This computation shows that for the antisymmetry only the eyelets holding the ends matter, not the shape of the elements, so the same holds for other meshes.

A third view is the matrix itself, where the antisymmetry can be seen by eye. For \(n = 4\) the matrix with all nodes \(0\) to \(4\) and the matrix of the system with nodes \(1\) to \(3\) are

\[\tilde{\mat G} = \mu v\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mat G = \mu v\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{26.58}\]

The diagonal of the matrix \(\tilde{\mat G}\) is the row of sums in the figure, \(-1, 0, 0, 0, +1\). Above the diagonal stands \(+1\) and below it \(-1\), which are the entries \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 1)\) of the matrix \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\) that every element puts at its own place. The eyelets delete the first and last row and the first and last column. What remains is \(\mat G\) of order \(3\), which has only zeros on the diagonal, and mirroring it across the diagonal only changes its sign (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-08-teach.out H).

We try the corollary on numbers (figure 26.57). We draw the axes: the speed \(v/c\) horizontally, the coefficient \(1 - v^2/c^2 = (T - \mu v^2)/T\) vertically, and the curve, which starts at \(1\) for \(v = 0\). At \(v/c = 0{,}5\) and \(n = 8\) the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat M\) (\(L = c = \mu = 1\)) is \(0{,}0448\) and of the matrix \(\mat K\) it is \(0{,}913\), at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) the matrix \(\mat K\) is still positive definite with smallest value \(0{,}231\) and at \(v/c = 0{,}99\) with \(0{,}0242\). This shows where the assumption \(v < c\) enters (step 3 of the proof): the coefficient \(T - \mu v^2\) falls towards zero as \(v\) approaches \(c\) (the curve sinks to the axis), and \(\mat K\) becomes almost singular. At \(v = c\) we have \(\mat K = \mat 0\), which is the critical speed of section 26.4. At \(v > c\) the coefficient is negative, \(\mat K\) is no longer positive definite and theorem 26.27 does not hold in this form. The largest absolute real part of the eigenvalues is below \(3 \cdot 10^{-15}\) at all three speeds, so zero up to rounding.

26.8.4 Numbers and convergence

Figure 26.58 shows the error of the frequencies of the element model against the number of elements \(n\). We draw the axes: \(n\) on the horizontal axis with equal spacing per doubling and the frequency error \(\Delta\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{h}} - \omega\) on the vertical axis with decades. For \(v/c = 0{,}5\) the error of the first frequency is \(0{,}1586\), \(0{,}0390\), \(0{,}0097\), \(0{,}0024\) and \(0{,}0006\) at \(n = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\). The error of the second frequency is \(1{,}288\), \(0{,}317\), \(0{,}078\), \(0{,}019\) and \(0{,}005\). Each time we double the elements the error is divided by \(4{,}06\), \(4{,}02\), \(4{,}00\) and \(4{,}00\) (first frequency), so it goes as \(h^2\), which is the dashed line of slope \(-2\). At \(v/c = 0{,}9\) the error of the second frequency is \(1{,}826\) at \(n = 4\) and still \(0{,}242\) at \(n = 8\). At the doublings from \(n = 4\) to \(n = 64\) it is divided by \(7{,}54\), \(4{,}63\), \(4{,}14\) and \(4{,}03\). The order \(h^2\) is the same, but at the higher speed the factor \(4\) settles only with more elements.

The errors are positive in all computed cases: the frequencies of the model are above the true ones. We observed this and did not prove it. In chapter 10 theorem 10.59 gives an upper bound when the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \mat K\vek d = \vek 0\) has no gyroscopic term, but here \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\) and its proof does not apply. We also only measured the order \(h^2\). A proof would need an error estimate for a system with an antisymmetric term, which we did not find in the books that we use.

The table connects the numbers of the errors in the figure with the band from the start of the section (\(v = c/2 = 56{,}61\) m/s, \(L = 1\) m). The angular frequency \(\omega\) computed with \(L = c = \mu = 1\) is in units of \(c/L\), so the frequency of the band is \(f = \omega\,c/(2\pi L)\) with \(c/(2\pi L) = 18{,}02\) Hz:

\(n\) \(f_1\) (Hz) \(f_2\) (Hz)
4 45,32 108,12
8 43,16 90,64
16 42,64 86,33
32 42,50 85,27
exact 42,46 84,92

We also compare with section 26.5 at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) with the same number of unknowns. Two sines give \(\omega_1 = 0{,}663\) and \(\omega_2 = 5{,}655\), three elements (two unknowns) \(\omega_1 = 0{,}851\) and \(\omega_2 = 5{,}393\), the true values are \(0{,}597\) and \(1{,}194\). With two unknowns both families are poor and the elements are no better. For the sines of the stationary string WM1990 (PDF p. 6) says the same: at high speed they describe the motion poorly. The advantage of the elements is that the error falls with the number of elements as figure 26.58 shows.

26.8.5 An end that nothing holds

The antisymmetry of the matrix \(\mat G\) came from the eyelets. We try what happens without the right eyelet. The lower half of figure 26.56 has the same elements, contributions from the right and from the left and sum, only that node \(n\) is not held and its \(+1\) stays. We try it as a model of the mechanism, not as a description of a real end of a belt. A real free end, where the track leaves the span, is not treated in this chapter and the sources do not derive it. Node \(n\) is now an unknown and the test function \(\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\), which equals \(1\) at \(x = L\), is allowed (the dashed half hat \(\psi_4\)). In the derivation of the weak form in lemma 26.39 the boundary term \((\mu v^2 - T)\,\psi(L)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\) remains. If we set it to zero for every \(\psi(L)\) we demand the boundary condition \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\). At \(x = 0\) the eyelet is still there, \(w(0, t) = 0\).

Lemma 26.42 Energy at an unheld end (energija pri koncu, ki ni držan)

Let the model of section 26.8.1 have an eyelet at \(x = 0\) and the boundary condition \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\) at \(x = L\) (a node without an eyelet), let \(v < c\) and let \(w\) be three times continuously differentiable. Let \(\mathcal E^*(t) = \frac12\int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\) be the conserved quantity of section 26.4. Then:

  1. \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal E^*}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2 \le 0\). The energy falls and never grows.
  2. In the Galerkin system with elements, where node \(n\) is an unknown, the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat G\) is \(\mat G + \mat G^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(0, \dots, 0, 2)\), \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek d} = \mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2 \le 0\). The uncancelled term \(+2\mu v\) is the contribution of the last node.
Proof

We must show that the energy is not conserved at an end that nothing holds, and why.

  1. Differentiate in time under the integral (\(w\) is smooth enough): \(\dot{\mathcal E}^* = \int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. From equation (26.54), \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Insert: the integrand is \(-2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\big(w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\).
  3. By the product rule, \(2 w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (w_{\mathrm{t}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\). The fundamental theorem gives \(\dot{\mathcal E}^* = -\mu v\,\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L + (T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\big]_0^L\).
  4. At \(x = 0\) we have \(w = 0\) at all times, so \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(0, t) = 0\) (the left eyelet stays, the right one is gone). At \(x = L\) we have \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\). What remains is \(-\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2\), which is item 1. With an eyelet at \(L\) we would also have \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\) and the quantity would be conserved.
  5. Item 2: the matrix of element \(n\) from lemma 26.40 has its entry \((2, 2)\) equal to \(+\mu v\) at place \((n, n)\), and node \(n\) has no neighbour on the right to cancel it. The other entries cancel as in corollary 26.41. So \(\mat G + \mat G^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(0, \dots, 0, 2)\) and \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek d} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T(\mat G + \mat G^\T)\dot{\vek d} = \mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  6. Multiply the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \mat G\dot{\vek d} + \mat K\vek d = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\): \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \dot{\vek d}^\T\mat K\vek d = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}} = -\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\dot{\vek d} = -\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric.

Source: The derivation is our own. That the energy of the span is not conserved because particles carry energy through the eyelets is in CHEN2005 §2.5 (PDF p. 6) and in equation (32) (PDF p. 7), see lemma 26.23.

The lemma says what would happen: the energy would not be conserved but would fall at the rate \(\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). The term \(-\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2\) is cancelled only by an eyelet that holds \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\).

Let us draw how the energy falls (figure 26.59). The axes: time in units of \(L/c\) horizontally, the energy \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}}\) divided by its initial value vertically. We release the model with \(n = 8\) elements at \(v/c = 0{,}5\) from rest in the shape of one arch, the nodal values of \(\sin(\pi x/L)\), once with both eyelets and once without the right one. With both eyelets the energy stays at \(100\,\%\), in the computation it deviates by less than \(10^{-13}\) of the initial value. Without the right eyelet it falls and never rises. After the time \(2L/c\) there is \(33\,\%\) of it left, \(67\,\%\) is lost, and after the time \(4L/c\) there is \(4\,\%\) left. The curve falls in stages: it is steep when the end moves fast, because the rate of fall is \(\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), and almost horizontal when the end is almost at rest. At \(n = 16\) and \(n = 32\) there is \(40\,\%\) and \(41\,\%\) left after the time \(2L/c\), so the numbers still change with the mesh (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-08-teach.out G).

We also compute the eigenvalues (\(L = c = \mu = 1\), \(v/c = 0{,}5\)). At \(n = 4, 8, 16\) the matrix \(\mat G + \mat G^\T\) has a single nonzero entry, of value \(1\), which is \(2\mu v\). The largest real part of the eigenvalues is \(-0{,}43\), \(-0{,}42\) and \(-0{,}21\), so all eigenvalues are left of the imaginary axis, which is something quite different from less than \(3 \cdot 10^{-15}\) at the held end. These numbers change with the mesh, so we do not conclude a final decay rate from them. Only that the energy does not grow is proved (item 2 of lemma 26.42). That all eigenvalues lie left of the imaginary axis we merely observed.

26.8.6 What we showed and what we did not

We proved three things. First: the weak form of the moving string has three integrals and the element matrices are these three, among them the gyroscopic matrix \(\mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), which does not depend on the length of the element (lemma 26.40). Second: after assembly its symmetric part remains only at the end nodes, the eyelets remove them, so the system of elements is of the same kind as the system of sines and has purely imaginary eigenvalues and a constant energy (corollary 26.41). Third: when an end is not held this fails, because energy flows out through the end (lemma 26.42).

We observed, but did not prove, that the frequencies of the model converge from above with an error of order \(h^2\). We do not know whether this holds for every \(v < c\) and every mesh, and from the sources that we have we cannot check it. We did not treat unequal meshes, higher elements, or the moving beam with bending stiffness. Those need the Hermite elements of chapter 12 and we do not derive them here. The link between eyelets fixed in space and the pulleys that a belt wraps comes in the section on the belt drive.

26.9 Belt drive

So far we had a single moving string stretched between two eyelets (section 26.1), and in the sections up to 26.8 we took it apart into modes, a critical speed and finite elements. A belt in a machine, however, runs over several wheels, which we call pulleys (jermenice) because the belt runs over them. What of the computed results survives when the string is built into such a drive, and what does the model leave out? The section answers the first question with a theorem proved from the earlier sections, and the second by stating what was left out and where it is treated in the literature.

From history

According to the source, the first to treat the belt drive from the point of view of axially moving continua was Aiken, in a paper of 1878 titled "An Account of Some Experiments on Rigidity Produced by Centrifugal Force" (CHEN2005, PDF p. 4 and 21). This is the view of this chapter: every free part of a belt is a moving string. What Aiken's experiments showed is on none of the pages read, so we tell nothing about it. Mahalingam used the moving string in 1957 for the transverse vibration of power transmission chains, excited at both eyelets with the same frequency and a phase difference (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 and 21). WM1990 counts chains and belts in the same class of systems as magnetic tapes, aerial cable tramways and band saws (WM1990, PDF p. 1). Ulsoy and co-workers first treated, in 1985, the coupled vibration of a belt and tensioner system (napenjalnik), modelling the belt as a moving string. A tensioner is a pulley with a moving centre on an arm that turns about a fixed point (CHEN2005, PDF p. 4), and the name says that it keeps the belt tense. They compared their model with measurements on an automotive accessory drive and found four principal mechanisms of transverse belt instability (CHEN2005, PDF p. 15 and 24). We use these four mechanisms at the end of the section to sort out what the chapter has covered and what it has not.

The story showed that a drive is made of spans, each a moving string of its own, and that there are several kinds of instability. We now build the drive from what we already know and say along the way what is an assumption.

We draw it as on a board. First we take two equal pulleys with axes at \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), which stay at rest, and give them a radius \(R\). Round both we stretch a closed band, the belt: on each pulley it embraces half of the circumference, and between the pulleys it lies straight in two spans. A span is the free part of the belt between two pulleys, a piece of belt that touches neither of them. The point where a span leaves a pulley is an eyelet as in section 26.1: there the belt still lies on the pulley and turns with it, so it cannot move transversely. The distance between the eyelets of one span is \(L\), equal to the distance of the axes because the pulleys are equal.

A motor turns the left pulley, so we call it driving (gonilna), the right one is driven (gnana). It turns clockwise, and the belt does not slip on it: a point of the belt has the speed of the rim, \(v = \omega R\) with the angular velocity \(\omega\) of the pulley (definition 8.86). Slip would need a theory of friction, which is in no source of the book, so no slip is an assumption. The top span runs from the driving pulley to the driven one, the bottom span back, both with the transport speed \(v\) of section 26.1.

Each span is a string with its own tension, since the belt has a different span on each side of a pulley. What is the force at the end of a span? A span pulls the belt lying on the pulley with a force that lies on the tangent along the span and starts at the eyelet, like the force of a neighbouring part on a piece of the string (derivation 13.1). On the figure these are the force \(T_1\) in the bottom span and the force \(T_2\) in the top one. Why should they differ? If they were equal, the two forces on the pulley would be parallel, equal in size and in the same direction, one above the axis and one below it at the same distance \(R\). Their moments about the axis would therefore cancel: the belt could then pass nothing from pulley to pulley. We compute the moment of the belt on the pulley from the law of angular momentum for a piece of belt, as we used it for a piece of a beam in section 13.5.3.

Lemma 26.43 Torque of the belt on a pulley (moment jermena na jermenici)

Let a belt run with constant speed \(v\) without slip over the arc of a pulley with centre \(O\) and radius \(R\). The pulley then has the angular velocity \(\omega = v/R\). Let the span arriving on the pulley have the tension force \(T_-\) and the span leaving it \(T_+\). The moment with which the pulley acts on the belt, about the axis through \(O\), is in the direction of motion of the belt

\[M_{\mathrm{O}} = (T_- - T_+)\,R , \tag{26.59}\]

and the belt acts on the pulley with the opposite moment. The power the pulley hands to the belt is \(P = M_{\mathrm{O}}\,\omega = (T_- - T_+)\,v\).

Proof

We must show that the friction of the pulley on the belt carries the difference of the span forces. We apply the law of angular momentum to a piece of belt that is a fixed set of particles, as in section 26.1.

  1. The piece is the set of particles that at time \(t_0\) occupies the whole arc on the pulley and a length \(a > 0\) of each of the two spans. Its length \(s\) is constant because the belt does not stretch (idealization 3 below estimates the error of this assumption as \(4\cdot 10^{-4}\)).
  2. Every particle of the piece has the velocity \(\vek v\) of size \(v\) in the same sense of turning, in a span along a line at distance \(R\) from \(O\), on the arc along a circle of radius \(R\). The angular momentum of a point mass \(m\) about \(O\) is \(\vek r\times m\vek v\). Its size is \(m\,v\) times the distance from \(O\) to the line along which \(\vek v\) points. On the arc and in a span this distance is the lever arm \(R\), so the size is \(m\,v\,R\) on both. The angular momentum of the piece is therefore \(\mu\,v\,R\,s\) in the sense of turning and stays constant as long as the piece has this form. Its time derivative is zero.
  3. The forces of the two spans at the ends of the piece lie on the lines of the spans at distance \(R\) from \(O\), so by definition 2.37 the sizes of their moments are \(R\,T_-\) and \(R\,T_+\). \(T_-\) pulls the piece back, against the motion, \(T_+\) forward, so the total moment in the direction of motion is \(-R\,T_- + R\,T_+\).
  4. The normal forces of the pulley on the arc point along the radius, where \(\vek r\parallel\vek F\), so their vector product is zero (definition 2.37). The friction forces are tangential. Their total moment about \(O\) we denote \(M_{\mathrm{O}}\), in the direction of motion.
  5. The sum of the moments on the piece is the derivative of its angular momentum, which is zero by step 2: \(-R\,T_- + R\,T_+ + M_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\). The forward moments, \(R\,T_+\) and \(M_{\mathrm{O}}\), therefore add up to the backward moment \(R\,T_-\), with the numbers of the example below \(90 + 360 = 450\) N m. Equation (26.59) follows.
  6. The sum of the magnitudes of the friction forces, taken with the sign of the direction of motion, is \(M_{\mathrm{O}}/R\), because each acts at distance \(R\) from \(O\). Each moves its particle with speed \(v\) along its own direction, so the power is \(P = (M_{\mathrm{O}}/R)\,v = M_{\mathrm{O}}\,\omega\). By Newton's third law the belt acts on the pulley with the opposite moment.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The books we have contain no theory of belt friction (a search for "capstan" and "belt friction" in books/txt had no hits), so the lemma is our own computation from the law of angular momentum.

The lemma says that the span forces differ exactly when the pulley gives or takes power. At the driving pulley \(M_{\mathrm{O}} > 0\) because it acts on the belt in the direction of its motion, so the span arriving on it is more tense than the one leaving it: \(T_- > T_+\). On the figure 26.60 this is the bottom span with the force \(T_1\), which we call the tight span (napeti razpon), and the top one with the smaller force \(T_2\) the slack span (ohlapni razpon). The word slack says that the belt there is less tense than in the other span. At the driven pulley it is the other way round: the belt acts on the pulley, so \(M_{\mathrm{O}} < 0\) and the span leaving it is the more tense.

A test on numbers. We choose the steel band \(0{,}9\times 50\) mm of example A of section 26.1 with mass \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m for the drive of figure 26.60. The dimensions of the band, the pulley radius \(R = 0{,}1\) m, the axis distance \(L = 1\) m and the stresses are our choice, because none of the sources gives belt data. Let the tight span have the stress \(\sigma_1 = 100\) MPa and the slack one \(\sigma_2 = 20\) MPa. With the cross-section \(A = 4{,}5\cdot 10^{-5}\) m\(^2\) the forces are \(T_1 = 4500\) N and \(T_2 = 900\) N. The moment of the driving pulley with the lever arm \(R\) is \((T_1 - T_2)R = 3600\ \text{N}\cdot 0{,}1\ \text{m} = 360\) N m. At the speed \(v = 40\) m/s we have \(\omega = v/R = 400\) 1/s, that is 3820 revolutions per minute, and the power is \((T_1 - T_2)\,v = 144\) kW (num-09.out, part A).

We see the same power in another way if we look at a cross-section of a span instead of at the pulley. This view tells along which path the power travels, which the moment on the pulley does not show. The part of the belt that has already passed the cross-section pulls the part behind it with the span force \(T\) in the direction of travel. Force times the path in one second is the work \(T\,v\) that the front part hands to the rear part every second. So the power flows through the cross-section against the direction of travel. In the tight span the belt runs from the driven pulley to the driving one, so the power \(T_1 v\) \(= 4500\ \text{N}\cdot 40\ \text{m/s} = 180\) kW flows from the driving pulley to the driven one. In the slack span the power \(T_2 v\) \(= 900\ \text{N}\cdot 40\ \text{m/s} = 36\) kW returns to the driving pulley, which is why the upper blue arrow is five times shorter than the lower one. The driven pulley keeps the difference \(180 - 36 = 144\) kW, the power of the lemma. The kinetic energy that the belt carries along is the same in both spans and cancels over the circuit.

An example that fails the requirement of the lemma is a drive without load. If the belt is mounted with the same force in both spans, \(T_- = T_+ = 2700\) N, then by equation (26.59) \(M_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\) and \(P = 0\). The pulleys turn but the belt carries nothing. The lemma also requires constant speed: during start-up the angular momentum of the piece is not constant (step 2) and equation (26.59) does not hold.

The third requirement of the lemma is running without slip. What does it cost when it fails? If the belt slips on the driving pulley, then \(v < \omega R\). Equation (26.59) still holds, because step 5 does not use the speed of the pulley. The power changes: the friction forces act on the pulley at its rim, which has the speed \(\omega R\), so the pulley gives \(M_{\mathrm{O}}\,\omega\), while the belt by step 6 receives only \((M_{\mathrm{O}}/R)\,v\). The difference \(M_{\mathrm{O}}\,(\omega - v/R)\) turns into heat through friction. With \(1\) % of slip, \(v = 0{,}99\,\omega R\), the pulley must give \(144/0{,}99 = 145{,}45\) kW for the same \(144\) kW on the belt, so \(1{,}45\) kW goes into heat. When the belt starts to slip is decided by friction, which the sources of the book do not treat, so we do not compute that limit.

Now we can write the model. We state it with six idealizations and give each a measure where we can compute one.

  1. The axes of the pulleys are fixed and the pulleys turn uniformly: the pulleys do not excite the belt's vibration and the belt does not act back on them. According to the source this holds for a drive with fixed-centre pulleys, and for a drive with a tensioner it is only an approximation (CHEN2005, PDF p. 4).
  2. The point where a span leaves a pulley is an eyelet: the displacement of the span there is zero. A wave in the span is therefore reflected completely by the pulley. According to the source a wave at an attached component is partly transmitted and partly reflected (CHEN2005, PDF p. 4). How much a real drive would deviate we cannot say, because the sources give no measure.
  3. The same belt runs with the same speed \(v\) in all spans. The mass flow \(\mu v\) is constant along the belt, and the mass per length at a strain \(\varepsilon\) is smaller by the factor \(1/(1+\varepsilon)\). By Hooke's law (theorem 3.19) the spans have the strains \(\sigma_1/E = 5{,}10\cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(\sigma_2/E = 1{,}02\cdot 10^{-4}\) (\(E = 196\) GPa). The speeds in the spans differ by the factor \((1+\varepsilon_1)/(1+\varepsilon_2) - 1 = 4{,}1\cdot 10^{-4}\), at \(v = 40\) m/s by \(0{,}016\) m/s.
  4. The force in each span is constant along the span (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, assumption 2) and the slope is small, \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}01\), as in definition 13.2.
  5. The weight of the belt is neglected, so the spans in the figure are straight. What this costs is shown in figure 26.63 for the slack span, where the weight is largest compared with the force. Without weight the span is straight between the eyelets. The weight \(\mu g L = 3{,}44\) N, which is \(0{,}38\) % of \(T_2\), makes it sag by \(d\) at the middle. The sag follows from the balance of moments of the left half of the span of length \(L\) about the left eyelet: its weight \(\mu g L/2\) acts at the distance \(L/4\) from the eyelet, and the force \(T_2\) at the middle, where the span is horizontal, has the lever arm \(d\). From \(T_2\,d = (\mu g L/2)(L/4)\) the span at rest has the sag \(d = \mu g L^2/(8T_2) = 0{,}48\) mm. The string then has the shape of the parabola \(w = -4d\,x(L - x)/L^2\) with the sag \(d\) at the middle, so the slope at the eyelet is \(4d/L = 4\cdot 0{,}48\cdot 10^{-3}/1 = 0{,}0019\). When the belt runs, we add the weight \(-\mu g\) on the right of equation (26.5). A shape that does not change in time satisfies \((T_2 - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mu g\), so it is the same parabola with \(T_2 - \mu v^2\) in place of \(T_2\). At \(v = 40\) m/s we have \(T_2 - \mu v^2 = 338{,}4\) N, the span sags by \(1{,}27\) mm and the slope at the eyelet is \(0{,}0051\), which is still below the bound \(0{,}01\). So the idealization fails when the slack span is so close to its critical speed that \(T_2 - \mu v^2\) falls below \(\mu g L/(2\cdot 0{,}01) = 172\) N, that is above \(v = 45{,}5\) m/s.
  6. A span is a string, not a beam. By theorem 26.37 the bending stiffness of the belt raises the critical speed of a span by the factor that is the square root of one plus the ratio of the buckling force of the band to the force of the span. With hinged ends the buckling force of our band is \(5{,}876\) N (example of section 26.7). The critical speed of the tight span therefore rises by \(0{,}065\) % (\(5{,}876/4500 = 0{,}0013\)), that of the slack span by \(0{,}33\) % (\(5{,}876/900 = 0{,}0065\)). With clamped ends the buckling force is \(23{,}503\) N and the shifts are \(0{,}26\) % and \(1{,}3\) %. The speed is below the critical speed of every span, \(v < c_{\mathrm{j}}\) (definition 26.20).
Notation. \(v\) is the transport speed as in section 26.1 and is not the deflection \(v\) of chapter 5. We number the spans with \(j\), \(T_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the force of the \(j\)-th span, not a kinetic energy. We write power as \(P\), which is not the compressive force of a column. The order of an excitation is denoted \(m\), so that it does not meet the span index.
Definition 26.44 Belt drive of strings (jermenski pogon z razponi)

A belt drive of strings is a system of a belt of mass \(\mu\) per unit length that runs with constant speed \(v\) over pulleys with fixed axes, in which each of the spans \(j = 1, \dots, N\) is a moving string (definition 26.3) of length \(L_{\mathrm{j}}\) between its eyelets, tension force \(T_{\mathrm{j}}\) and transverse displacement \(w_{\mathrm{j}}(x, t)\), \(x \in [0, L_{\mathrm{j}}]\). The eyelets of a span are its contact points with the pulleys, \(w_{\mathrm{j}}(0, t) = w_{\mathrm{j}}(L_{\mathrm{j}}, t) = 0\). The model holds with idealizations 1 to 6 above.

Source: CHEN2005 §2.4.2 (PDF p. 4): the transverse vibration of belt spans is an example of a moving string, and so is Ulsoy and co-workers' model (CHEN2005, PDF p. 15). The name and the notation are ours, and so are the measures in idealizations 3 and 5.

Idealizations 1 and 2 are the reason why we can treat the spans each by itself: no span has an unknown or a condition that it shares with another. What does that mean for the drive?

Theorem 26.45 Spans of a belt drive and the critical belt speed (razponi pogona in kritična hitrost jermena)

Let a belt drive of strings be given by definition 26.44 and let \(c_{\mathrm{j}} = \sqrt{T_{\mathrm{j}}/\mu}\) be the wave speed of span \(j\) (definition 13.4). For a span \(j\) with \(v < c_{\mathrm{j}}\) the modes of the span have the natural angular frequencies

\[\omega_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{n}} = \frac{n\pi c_{\mathrm{j}}}{L_{\mathrm{j}}}\left(1 - \frac{v^2}{c_{\mathrm{j}}^2}\right) , \qquad n = 1, 2, \dots , \tag{26.60}\]

which are all positive. The drive has all its spans subcritical exactly when \(v < c_{\min} = \sqrt{T_{\min}/\mu}\), where \(T_{\min}\) is the smallest of the span forces. When the belt speed increases from zero, the span with the smallest force, the slack span, is the first to reach the critical speed.

Proof

We must show that the spans do not affect each other, that they get their frequencies from section 26.3, and that the subcriticality condition singles out the slackest span.

  1. By definition 26.44 span \(j\) is a moving string with its own displacement \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\), length \(L_{\mathrm{j}}\) and force \(T_{\mathrm{j}}\), with the same \(\mu\) and \(v\) for all spans. Its condition at the eyelets contains only \(w_{\mathrm{j}}\). The problems of different spans have no common unknown and no common condition, so we solve them each by itself.
  2. For span \(j\) with \(v < c_{\mathrm{j}}\) theorem 26.13 with \(c = c_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(L = L_{\mathrm{j}}\) gives the modes and the frequencies (26.60).
  3. The frequency (26.60) is positive exactly when the factor \(1 - v^2/c_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) is positive, that is for \(v < c_{\mathrm{j}}\). At \(v = c_{\mathrm{j}}\) the factor is zero and the span is critical by definition 26.20. For \(v > c_{\mathrm{j}}\) the factor is negative.
  4. The root \(\sqrt{T_{\mathrm{j}}/\mu}\) increases with \(T_{\mathrm{j}}\), so a smaller force has a smaller speed \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\). The condition \(v < c_{\mathrm{j}}\) for every \(j\) therefore holds exactly when \(v\) lies in the band below the smallest speed, \(v < \min_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}} = \sqrt{T_{\min}/\mu}\).
  5. When \(v\) increases from zero, the first span at which \(v\) reaches \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the one with the smallest \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\), so with the smallest force \(T_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Source: The theorem is not from a source, it follows from theorem 26.13. The source says only that the belt critical speed is one of four mechanisms of transverse instability (CHEN2005, PDF p. 15).

The theorem says that a drive is judged by its slackest span. We test it on the drive of this section. We shall draw the lowest frequency of the two spans against the speed. First the axes: horizontally the speed \(v\) in m/s, vertically the frequency \(f = \omega/(2\pi)\) in Hz. By equation (26.60) the lowest frequency of a span is \(f_1^{(j)} = \dfrac{c_{\mathrm{j}}}{2L}\left(1 - v^2/c_{\mathrm{j}}^2\right)\), a parabola that falls from \(c_{\mathrm{j}}/(2L)\) at \(v = 0\) to zero at \(v = c_{\mathrm{j}}\). For the tight span (\(j = 1\)) we have \(c_1 = \sqrt{T_1/\mu} = 113{,}23\) m/s and \(f_1^{(1)}\) falls from \(56{,}61\) Hz, for the slack one (\(j = 2\)) \(c_2 = 50{,}64\) m/s and the frequency falls from \(25{,}32\) Hz. The speeds \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are the zeros of the parabolas. For \(v = 20, 30, 40\) and \(50\) m/s we get (num-09.out, part B):

\(v\) (m/s) \(v/c_1\) \(f_1^{(1)}\) (Hz) \(v/c_2\) \(f_1^{(2)}\) (Hz)
0 0 56,61 0 25,32
20 0,177 54,85 0,395 21,37
30 0,265 52,64 0,592 16,43
40 0,353 49,55 0,790 9,52
50 0,442 45,57 0,987 0,63

At \(v = 40\) m/s both frequencies are positive: \(49{,}55\) Hz for the tight and \(9{,}52\) Hz for the slack span. Span \(j = 2\) is at \(v/c_2 = 0{,}790\) near its critical speed and has only \(38\) % of its frequency at rest (\(9{,}52/25{,}32 = 0{,}376\)), while the tight span at \(v/c_1 = 0{,}353\) has \(0{,}875\) of its frequency at rest. In the slack span the two waves travel with the speeds \(c_2 + v = 90{,}64\) m/s with the running belt and \(c_2 - v = 10{,}64\) m/s against it (since \(c_2 - v > 0\), the wave against the flow still travels, but slowly). The critical speed of the slack span is \(c_2 = \sqrt{\sigma_2/\rho} = 50{,}64\) m/s and does not depend on the cross-section of the band, because \(\mu\) cancels. At this speed the tight span still has \(45{,}29\) Hz and \(v^2/c_1^2 = \sigma_2/\sigma_1 = 0{,}2\).

An example that fails the test. Let the slack span have only \(10\) MPa, with the same stress in the tight span. Then the critical speed \(c_2\) moves from \(50{,}64\) to \(c_2' = 35{,}81\) m/s, by \(14{,}83\) m/s to the left, across the vertical line \(v = 40\) m/s, and \(v/c_2' = 1{,}117\). The dashed parabola falls to zero before we reach the vertical line. The span is supercritical, and the model with two fixed eyelets claims nothing there (section 26.4). The tight span is meanwhile far below its critical speed, \(v/c_1 = 0{,}353\), its parabola is high at \(v = 40\) m/s. A test with the mean stress \(55\) MPa would give \(\bar c = 83{,}97\) m/s, far to the right of the vertical line, and would wrongly let the drive pass. The theorem judges by the smallest force, not by the mean. A span at \(15\) MPa is just below the limit: \(c = 43{,}85\) m/s, \(v/c = 0{,}912\) and \(f_1 = 3{,}68\) Hz (num-09.out, part C).

The next mechanism that the source knows for a span is belt resonance. Sack determined, according to the source, the natural frequencies of a moving string from the resonance relation, that is from the condition that the frequency of the excitation equals the natural one (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2). In a drive one cause of excitation is kinematic because the belt is closed. Whatever is fixed to the belt, for instance a joint, returns to the same pulley after one circuit. The length of the closed belt is \(\Lambda = 2L + 2\pi R\), two straight spans and two half-circles. For \(L = 1\) m and \(R = 0{,}1\) m we have \(\Lambda = 2{,}6283\) m, at \(v = 40\) m/s a circuit takes \(65{,}7\) ms and repeats with the frequency \(15{,}22\) Hz, which is the height of the line \(m = 1\) on the vertical line. That a joint really excites the span is our assumption. If we accept it, the condition for resonance of order \(m\) is

\[\frac{m\,v}{\Lambda} = \frac{c}{2L}\left(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\right) \iff \frac{2mL}{\Lambda}\,\frac{v}{c} = 1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2} , \tag{26.61}\]

where \(m\) is an integer and \(c\) the wave speed of the span. The right-hand form shows that the solution \(v/c = -mL/\Lambda + \sqrt{(mL/\Lambda)^2 + 1}\) does not depend on the force of the span. The grey lines \(m\,v/\Lambda\) in figure 26.65 grow with \(v\) and the parabola falls, so for each \(m\) there is exactly one solution. For \(m = 1\) we get it at \(v/c = 0{,}690\), that is at \(78{,}07\) m/s for the tight and \(34{,}91\) m/s for the slack span, for \(m = 2\) at \(v/c = 0{,}496\), that is \(56{,}12\) and \(25{,}10\) m/s (num-09.out, part F). In a start-up to \(40\) m/s the slack span crosses the solutions \(m = 1\) to \(4\) (\(m = 4\) at \(15{,}15\) m/s, \(m = 3\) at \(19{,}04\) m/s), the tight one of these only \(m = 4\) at \(33{,}87\) m/s, because \(m = 3\) comes only at \(42{,}58\) m/s. Solutions with \(m > 4\) are at still lower speeds, for \(m = 5\) at \(27{,}95\) m/s in the tight and \(12{,}50\) m/s in the slack span, so both spans cross them. What happens there the equation does not say: the response to excitation is beyond this chapter, the source treats it with a Green's function (WM1990, PDF p. 3 and 4), which we do not derive.

Let us finally see what the chapter has covered of the four mechanisms that Ulsoy and co-workers distinguish according to the source (CHEN2005, PDF p. 15).

mechanism what it means where in the chapter
tensioner resonance (resonanca napenjalnika) the tensioner, a pulley with a moving centre, vibrates as a rigid body, the spans are its springs not covered, idealization 1
belt resonance (resonanca jermena) the frequency of the excitation matches a natural frequency of a span section 26.3, this section
Mathieu instabilities from tension variation (Mathieujeva nestabilnost) the tension varies periodically, so a coefficient of the equation varies not covered, the source mentions it (CHEN2005, PDF p. 11)
belt critical speed (kritična hitrost jermena) \(v = c_{\mathrm{j}}\) of a span section 26.4, theorem 26.45

The name Mathieu is carried by the equation that the source gets when it inserts the variation \(P_1\cos\Omega t\) of the tension about a mean \(P_0\) into a model with one mode (CHEN2005, PDF p. 11). Where the name comes from is not in the sources we have, so we do not state the origin of the name. The excitation here is parametric (parametrično): a coefficient of the equation varies, the tension force \(P_0 + P_1\cos\Omega t\), and by the source there is no transverse external force. In external excitation it is the other way round, the tension \(P_0\) is constant and a force \(F\cos\Omega t\) pushes the span transversely. This goes beyond the chapter.

The model leaves out more. Nonlinear and viscoelastic strings and the coupling with the rotation of the pulleys are treated elsewhere according to the source (CHEN2005, PDF p. 4, 14 and 15). Friction between the belt and the pulley and the centrifugal contribution to the belt force on a pulley are in no source of the book. So we do not compute with slip, and lemma 26.43 does not need these things, since it uses only the span forces and the speed.

The section has shown that a belt drive with pulleys of fixed axes is a set of separate moving strings and that the critical speed of the drive belongs to the slackest span. The lemma on the moment explained where a slack span comes from at all, and the theorem gave the criterion, tested on an example that the drive passes and on an example that it does not. What goes beyond the model is listed with its sources, and the connections with other chapters are in section 26.10.

26.10 Connections

The abbreviations of subjects are the same as in section 1.19. In this chapter we let the string known from chapter 13 run at speed \(v\) through two fixed eyelets (očesci) and took it as the model of a belt span (razpon). Now we ask where the results come back from and where they go: what of the earlier chapters remained at \(v = 0\), what is proved here for the first time, and what we leave to the chapters that follow. The numbers are for a steel band \(0{,}9 \times 50\) mm, span length \(L = 1\) m and tension \(100\) MPa (\(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, \(T = 4500\) N, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s). The band, the length and the tension are our choice, we have no data on real belts in the books (section 26.9).

  • The string at speed zero (VD, DSK, chapter 13): at \(v = 0\) the equation of theorem 26.4 becomes the wave equation of theorem 13.3, the modes of theorem 26.13 become the modes of theorem 13.7, and the natural frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \dfrac{n\pi c}{L}\,(1 - v^2/c^2)\) become \(n\pi c/L\). For \(v \ne 0\) the standing wave of section 13.2 is no longer a solution, as lemma 26.11 of section 26.3 proves, so the promise of chapter 13 is kept and the strings of that chapter are the case \(v = 0\). The factor \(1 - v^2/c^2\) multiplies all frequencies equally, so the drop at \(40\) m/s is the same for \(f_1\) and for \(f_3\), \(12{,}5\) %. The first drops from \(56{,}61\) Hz at \(v = 0\) to \(54{,}85\) Hz at \(20\) m/s, \(49{,}55\) Hz at \(40\) m/s and \(28{,}35\) Hz at \(80\) m/s. The curve \(f_1\) reaches half of the starting value at \(v = c/\sqrt{2} = 80{,}06\) m/s, just to the right of the last dot.
  • Travelling waves (VD, chapter 13): lemma 13.5 showed only that \(F(x - ct)\) and \(G(x + ct)\) are solutions, and the converse, that every solution is a sum of such waves, we did not prove for the string. Lemma 26.6 proves it for every \(v \ge 0\), so also for \(v = 0\). At \(v = 40\) m/s the speed of waves is downstream \(c + v = 153{,}23\) m/s and upstream \(c - v = 73{,}23\) m/s, at \(v = 0\) both are \(113{,}23\) m/s. This is where the factor of the previous item comes from: the way downstream takes \(6{,}526\) ms, the way upstream \(13{,}656\) ms, so the round trip takes \(20{,}182\) ms instead of \(17{,}664\) ms. The slow way back loses more time than the fast way forward gains, the difference is \(2{,}518\) ms, and one round trip per \(20{,}182\) ms is the frequency \(49{,}55\) Hz.
  • The column and the critical speed (DSK, chapter 8): the static equation of the moving beam (section 26.7) is the column equation of theorems 8.150 and 8.151 with the compressive force \(P = \mu v^2 - T\). The critical speed (kritična hitrost) is the speed at which the equilibrium position turns into a family of positions: for the string it is \(v = c\), where \(P = 0\) and every shape with the two ends held is in equilibrium (lemma 26.19), because the force of the tension on a piece is then, at every curvature, exactly the force the piece needs to run along the curve, also for the other two shapes, and for the beam \(v_{\mathrm{c}}^2 = (T + \pi^2 E I/L^2)/\mu\) with pinned supports and \((T + 4\pi^2 E I/L^2)/\mu\) with clamped ends (theorem 26.37). It has its name because the way of moving breaks at it: below it the frequencies fall, at it a natural frequency is zero. For our band the bending stiffness is \(E I = 0{,}59535\) N m\(^2\) and the Euler loads are \(5{,}876\) N with pinned supports and \(23{,}503\) N with clamped ends, which is \(0{,}13\) % and \(0{,}52\) % of the force \(T = 4500\) N. So bending raises the critical speed by only \(0{,}0653\) % and \(0{,}2608\) %: the parabola reaches both dashed lines already within the magnified neighbourhood of \(v = c\), which is \(0{,}36\) m/s wide. A thin band is therefore a string, as the model of section 26.1 assumes.
  • The conserved quantity (DSK, chapter 8): the functional \(\mathcal{E}^*\) of theorem 26.21 is the energy integral \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) of theorem 8.124.
